author: Yasmine Benabderrahmane
title: Is "khawa khawa" a North African myth?
content:
In the haze of

el ghorba

 — the strangeness and alienation of living abroad — I gravitate toward the Maghrebi diaspora. For a moment, we relax our tongues from the unnatural twists of Arabic dialects foreign to us and speak in the Maghrebi

darija

s. Desperate to latch onto whatever whispers of home exist elsewhere, we claim that we are

khawa khawa

.

Among the Algerians, Moroccans, and Tunisians,

khawa khawa

 is an official nod to an unofficial alliance, loosely translating to

brotherhood

. It is an ode to our shared cultures and history in the face of North African identity discourses.

But what began as a salve for colonialism was lost in the monotonous chants for brotherhood.

Before the 19th century, North African states were “undefined” to European cartographers and authorities alike. Hence, like the concept of the Middle East and the Sahel, the Maghreb was prone to imperial invention. Unsurprisingly, this coincided with the Scramble for Africa — when the insatiable greed of European colonial powers took interest in dividing the African continent among themselves.

Encompassing other colonial legacies, the borders born out of the Scramble engineered the ethnic rivalries that persist in Africa today. Through the newly devised borders and the infamous “divide and conquer” regimes, the Maghreb was branded as distinct.

Despite the existing racial diversity of the region, the French colonial regimes rebranded the Maghreb as a biracial society: Amazigh or Arab. While the Amazigh identity was mislabeled in proximity to the whiteness of Europe, the Arab identity became an accusation of settler colonialism. North Africa became a geographic body for the Francophonie world, distanced from its neighboring regions’ cultures, politics, and society.

In 1962, Algeria — the last of France’s Maghrebi colonies — declared independence. In the years that followed, the Maghrebi people looked inwards and toward rebuilding the identity of North Africa. Thus,

khawa khawa

 was born and reinforced by the diaspora that fled their homes in the wake of political instability. It became a card dealt in moments of desperation to bond to something, or someone, that vaguely resembled home.

Khawa khawa

, and the brotherhood that blossomed with it, became the means to redress an identity obscured by European colonialism.

True

khawa khawa

 culture demands communal harmony void of ego. But when politics becomes inevitably entangled in the national identity of communities, the culture of Maghrebi brotherhood falls flat.

Shortly after 1962, newly independent Algeria and Morocco fell into border disputes. The following decades spiraled into attempted land grabs, fits of cultural monopolies, and accusations of expansionist ambitions. In response, the people cried out

khawa khawa; our governments do not define our brotherhood

!

But too often, the politics override the social bonds of Algerians and Moroccans (and occasionally, Tunisians). With the rise of the internet, discourse shifted, and social media became a useful mirror for the abstractions of the Maghrebi identity.

Most recently, the

khawa khawa

 culture was dramatically pronounced dead on social media platforms, following the 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON). Almost overnight, the football tournament became a litmus test for Algerian-Moroccan relations and spiraled into a warped perception of North African relations. A futile online back-and-forth that began as shared banter turned into personal attacks and political scrutiny.

The post-AFCON

guerre

 between Algerians and Moroccans — which coincided with the recent

UN support

 for Moroccan plans over the Western Sahara, disapproved by the Algerian government — is a recurring phenomenon of how Maghrebi culture wages war parallel to the political tensions of its respective countries. Despite the adamant denial, online Maghrebi communities fall into the habit of using our governments to verify the authenticity of

khawa khawa

.

The problem rests in the fact that both communities — Algerian and Moroccan — fall into the habit of claiming the minority of hateful comments as the consensus among the entirety of both nations. We see assertions made that we cannot prove, except that they are too insulting and their wounds far too inflicting to recover from. It has become a pattern of malice between both nations that resurfaces regardless of how loudly

khawa khawa

 is chanted.

Perhaps the fault is also in the fragility …

author: Francis Annagu
title: Nigeria has not decided how to regulate Chinese businesses. Who will decide?
content:
In mid-September 2026, traders in the auto spare parts section of the Lagos International Trade Fair Complex

protested against Chinese traders who sell directly to customers

. One protester

said

 the Chinese had ‘built warehouses, rented shops and are now selling as we do as retailers.’ Police called the protesters

‘a few miscreants’

.


Nigeria already has rules for foreign businesses. But the government has not said what it wants from Chinese businesses, or who will carry out the policy. In the two weeks after the protest, the police, a market board, a minister’s aide and a governor all spoke. None said whether the rules will change. Mining shows the same gap. In both, a policy question is being handled as a policing problem.


Competition over one supply chain


Retailer John Chidebere

told Premium Times

 that goods from China take two to three months to arrive and leave him little profit. Meanwhile,

Chinese businesses can sell directly

 to local customers at wholesale prices. Nigeria imported

N11.01 trillion

 of goods from China in the first half of 2026, nearly 40 per cent of its imports, according to National Bureau of Statistics data.

SBM Intelligence

 says the trade deficit is ‘substantially a symptom of Nigeria’s broader industrial and macroeconomic environment, not a cause in itself.’ Commentator

Martin Beck Nworah

 said: ‘once the wholesaler becomes the middleman, the retailer is edged out.’ So this is a fight inside one supply chain, not only Nigerians against Chinese competitors.


Protesters rally outdoors in Nigeria, October 2020


What the traders are asking for


Newsclick

 reported placards reading ‘The Chinese must go.’ But Chief Osigwe told Premium Times that Chinese traders should leave the market and trade elsewhere,

not leave Nigeria

. Trader Clement Ebere said: ‘I’m not saying the Chinese should leave, but it should be negotiated.’ The association’s president,

Nnamdi Ngozi Emechebe

, said asking the Chinese to leave Nigeria was not an option.

Some of the Chinese wholesalers

 approached by Premium Times declined to comment. So the slogan and the demand did not match. The traders want Chinese businesses out of retail, not out of Nigeria.


The law allows it


A

BusinessDay legal explainer

 says the Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission (NIPC) Act lets foreigners invest in most businesses.

The Act’s short list of banned areas

 covers arms and ammunition, narcotic drugs, and military and paramilitary clothing, plus anything the Federal Executive Council adds. Retail is not on it. Foreigners still need visas,

business permits and expatriate quotas

. So the legal question is whether these businesses have the right permits. The political question is bigger: does Nigeria want foreign companies in retail at all?


The

Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise

 and a

Daily Trust editorial

 of 2 October both ask for the rules on foreign retailers to be reviewed. Neither asks for a ban. The rules exist. What is missing is a decision on whether to change them.


Institutions have spoken, but no decision taken


Police Area Commander ACP Chike Oti said the protesters had

been cautioned

 and arrests would follow, but

no arrest had been reported

 in the coverage I found. Veronica Ndanusa, who heads the

Lagos International Trade Fair Complex Management Board

, a body under the Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment,

told traders to stay calm

 and said foreign investors who

follow the law

 would be protected.


Ms Ndanusa spoke about investors, not about whether foreigners should be in retail. I found no public statement on that question, or on the protest, from the Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission, the trade ministry itself, or the Lagos State Government. The nearest Lagos voice was the governor’s new-media aide, Jubril Gawat,

sharing a video of a police officer

 speaking about arrests.


Political comments filled the gap. Lere Olayinka, an aide to FCT Minister Nyesom Wike,

mocked the protesters on X

. Abia Governor Alex Otti, on 29 September, said Igbo traders were

‘moving from the market to manufacturing’

. Actor

Joseph Okechukwu

 claimed the federal government brought Chinese people in to destroy Igbo businesses. The report quoting him gave no evidence.


The same gap in mining


Local gold miners at work in Kano State, Nigeria, August 2022.


On 3 September 2026, Premium Times reported that Niger State’s commissioner had asked …

author: Soreti Kadir
title: Finfinnee is the Third Space
content:
At the end of 2010, I took a trip to Ethiopia to visit my family. At the time, my parents worked in Bole, the commercial centre of Addis Ababa. Being only 16, my movements were more or less regulated by my parents, which meant that I would travel with them into the city each day, after which it was the extent of my curiosity and creativity (and pocket money) that determined what I did until evening, when I would head back to our house on the outskirts of the city. Slowly, interactions with the staff at a nearby cafe, just a few hundred meters from the building where my family worked, became routine. 


Over the two months that I was in Ethiopia, with much of this time spent in Addis Ababa, we spent most of our lunch breaks together, hanging out on the steps of the cafe, sharing stories to pass the time. One day, the conversation of our relationship to ‘Ethiopia’, as a national identity, came up. It’s important to note that I was raised in the Oromo diaspora, a community that, in the years my mother and I migrated to Australia, was made up mostly of political refugees who fled the country after the adoption of the “Transitional Period Charter of Ethiopia” and the official establishment of a transitional government. 


This eventually led to the Tigrayan People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) monopolizing power within the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), a process that resulted in the isolation of those seeking political power within the EPRDF through the ballot. Given the size and economic importance of the Oromia region, it was the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF), amongst others, that became a key target of political violence, creating political communities in exile exactly like the one that I grew up in.


I inherited a different definition of Ethiopia, coloured by memories and experiences of violence and displacement that informed my relationship to the state as a place of unbelonging for those who shared my identity. The day that the conversation with these two new friends wandered into political territory, we all engaged passionately, striving to reflect the extent of both our personal experiences and hopes for our country. They found my reflections to be overly nostalgic and antagonistic towards the country’s future.  Unconcerned for the good of the future. I found their insistence that we shared a national identity to be inaccurate and offensive. We agreed on little, and I found it exhilarating. 


That evening, I was restlessly anticipating the opportunity to tell my mother about what I thought was the most exciting experience of my trip to date. In recounting the story, I almost gave my mother a heart attack. Angry, afraid, and in shock, my mother warned me sternly against ever engaging in such conversation in public again. She asked me many questions about who these men were, how I knew them, and if we’d ever had such conversations before. What I was blind to, and what was the daily lived experience of my parents, was that Addis Ababa, primarily but not exclusively, was a heavily surveilled city, the State looking for the people doing exactly what I found myself doing that day – discussing the political reality of our country. Thereafter, I was careful, out of curiosity more than fear (being 16 with a high risk tolerance will do that), and refrained from fully-fledged conversations, opting for quiet enquiry when the opportunity presented itself. Although our conversation never veered down the road of politics again, I continued to visit my friends every day and remember rushing to say a heartfelt goodbye on the day I was due to fly back to Australia. 


For this piece, I will centre the discussion on Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, as opposed to extending the conversation to other parts of the country which exist with their own nuances and political realities, requiring more space for analysis than I have here. I share the introductory anecdote to forward the idea that, in Ethiopia, to nurture spaces of connection, community-building, and care, we must first invest in collective repair of the damage wrought by decades of state surveillance that has defined the range and breadth of relational life the city space can hold, and from the legacy of what can only be defined as settler colonialism. ‘Where’, figuratively and literally, can this process of repair take place? I argue that it must take place in Finfinnee, geographically the same location as Addis Ababa, but sociologically and …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.


But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?


The history beneath the headline


Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. Khnata bint Bakkar intervened in eighteenth-century dynastic politics.


Across the region,

Dihya

 is remembered as an Amazigh queen who led resistance to the Arab conquest in the Aurès, in present-day Algeria, during the late seventh century. Tuareg oral tradition remembers

Tin Hinan

 as a queen and founding ancestress of noble lineages in the Ahaggar, in present-day southern Algeria.


These histories expose how male authority is made to appear natural. Fatima Mernissi’s

The Forgotten Queens of Islam


challenges that selective memory. Colonialism also reorganised authority: French Protectorate administrators

reshaped

 customary courts around imperial priorities. What survives as tradition can carry the history of political intervention. 


Religious interpretation can give exclusion another claim to permanence. Islamist and other conservative opponents invoke this

hadith

 against women’s political authority:


«لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً»


Usually translated as saying that a people governed by a woman will not prosper, it becomes a prohibition irrespective of her competence. Asma Lamrabet, a

Moroccan Islamic feminist thinker

, questions turning a

narration linked

 to Persia’s dynastic succession into a universal ban. She reads it against the Qur’anic Queen of Sheba, whose judgement demonstrates capable leadership. Her argument contests male authority’s claim to divine necessity.


PAM’s promises and its record


Women have long contested how authority is distributed within the family. Fatima Sadiqi

documents

the Union de l’Action Féminine’s 1992 million-signature campaign to reform the Moudawana, Morocco’s family code. The 2004 reform abolished wives’ duty of obedience but retained unequal inheritance and exceptions to the marriage age of eighteen. Proposals announced in December 2024 left fundamental equality demands unresolved. In October 2025, more than sixty civil society organisations and public figures

joined to call for comprehensive reform

. Rights in Morocco have advanced through organised demands, not the gender of an officeholder.


PAM, a centre-right party founded in 2008,

advocates

 social modernisation and positions itself against the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD). It entered government in 2021 alongside the National Rally of Independents and conservative nationalist Istiqlal. Opposition to Islamist conservatism, however, does not itself entail reforming the laws and economic conditions that subordinate women.


PAM’s

2026 programme

 promises improved widow pensions, childcare, safe transport, a women’s enterprise fund and labour inspection. The commitments leave inheritance equality, abortion reform and decriminalisation of consensual same sex relations unaddressed. Mansouri called for

banning child marriage

 without exceptions in 2024, yet PAM’s electoral programme

omits that commitment

. Employment can support independence, but a wage does not cancel criminalisation or unequal property rights. The programme leaves those constraints intact.


Even PAM’s narrow promise to increase …

author: WoMin
title: Press Release | Women’s Climate Assembly strengthens Pan African solidarity, women-led resistance and the struggle for a just future
content:
“

Empowering women is a radical way to transform the world!

” –

Ivorian activist


The fourth regional

Women’s Climate Assembly

 (WCA), held in Yaoundé, Cameroon, from 5–8 October 2026, concluded with a powerful reaffirmation of African women’s determination to defend their lands, territories, livelihoods and communities, and to demand climate justice and reparations.


Under the theme, “

Our lands, our voices: African women united for climate justice and reparations!

”, the Assembly convened over 75 women community leaders, activists, feminist organisations, civil society groups and allies from twelve countries including Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Guinea-Conakry, Liberia, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Senegal and Zambia.


The gathering provided a vital space for women on the frontlines of the climate crisis, extractive industries, land dispossession and environmental destruction to share their experiences, strengthen relationships across borders and build collective strategies for change.


As the Assembly closed, one message rang clear: African women are not merely bearing the costs of the climate crisis. They are leading the struggle for solutions, defending their communities and shaping the future they want.


“

There’s an adage in my village that women cannot build a nation. The Women’s Climate Assembly has proved that women build nations. We counter this adage with the unity and solidarity of African women!”

 –

DRC activist-participant


Turning shared struggles into collective power


From communities confronting oil and gas expansion and destructive mining to women defending forests, seeds, water sources and ancestral lands, participants brought forward the lived realities of communities too often excluded from decisions about their territories and futures.


Through collective reflection, popular education and movement-building, women connected struggles that may take place in different countries but are rooted in common systems of exploitation, inequality and environmental destruction.


Designed by women activists and members of the WCA Steering Committee, the thematic teach-ins explored a range of political concepts, questions and practices, including:


The erosion of farmers’ seeds

: A challenge for building resilient and sustainable food systems. What solutions are there for preserving our seed heritage?  


Nature Commons

: The defence of the Congo Basin’s forests.


Counting the Costs of Mal/Bad Development and Demanding reparations

: The case of the African Development Bank campaign.


Fighting some of the false solutions to the climate crisis

: Gas extraction, enclosure of our forests and lands for carbon trading, green conservation and more.


Building democratic, accountable, ‘loving’ leadership

: Why are these principles so important to feminist leadership? What else do we feel is critical to leading as feminists?


Lessons on organising and movement building

: Growing National/sub-regional grassroots movements.


Building knowledge from what we know

: Building feminist popular knowledge as the basis for Building Women’s Power. How can we go about doing this locally in our communities and beyond that.


The WCA celebrated the knowledge, resistance and organising power of rural, Indigenous, peasant and working-class women. The

Each One, Teach One

 sessions embodied this spirit of knowledge-sharing, collective learning and liberation. On Day Two, participants exchanged practical skills, crafts and tools, sharing techniques for making baobab candies, producing eco-briquettes from cassava and creating seed bricks to cultivate and protect Indigenous seeds. Weaving, cloth-dyeing, beadwork and other practices also featured, affirming the value of knowledge held, practised and passed down through generations of women.


The gathering reaffirmed the importance of strengthening a Pan African ecofeminist movement that recognises the connections between the climate crisis, extractivism, gender injustice, food insecurity and the loss of community control over natural resources.


It also reinforced a fundamental principle: communities must have the power to determine their own futures, including the right to say NO to destructive development projects that threaten their lands, livelihoods and ways of life.


Climate justice means reparations, not empty promises


Africa contributes relatively little to global greenhouse gas …

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: Mada Masr
title: As Sisi vows to leave power by 2030, sources differ on whether he really means it
content:
Speaking at the 44th Cultural and Educational Symposium of the Egyptian Armed Forces on

Wednesday

, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi

said

 Egypt’s “Constitution would not be touched.”

 


His remarks came as part of a longer speech warning against a return to the demonstrations and protests that swept the country after 2011, alongside a series of other political messages, including a

declaration

 that he

would

 “never tire of protecting Egypt.”


He reiterated similar messages again on

Thursday,

 during a speech at the Police Academy’s graduation ceremony, saying he would continue working “until the final day” of his presidential term in 2030.


With

talk

 of lifting presidential term limits already a feature of political conversations in the leadup to the 2025 parliamentary election, a parliamentary source told Mada Masr at the time, Sisi’s comments sparked immediate queries about how long the president will remain in power.

 


Speaking on condition of anonymity, three parliamentary sources close to a sovereign security agency told Mada Masr that Sisi’s pledge not to touch the Constitution is inseparable from a broader plan to reshape the country’s political landscape, and is driven by his desire to avoid the mistakes of ousted President Hosny Mubarak, whose three decades in power fostered the widespread resentment that would lead to the 2011 revolution.


But his remarks were described differently by a judicial source and an opposition party source, who said the president’s remarks were a “political maneuver” intended to diffuse public anger while leaving his political future up to the public. They said the statement also leaves the door open for a peaceful transfer of power, or, the judicial source said, it could pave the way for a “popular call” for Sisi to remain in office on the grounds that no suitable successor is ready to take over. 


The three parliamentary sources and a government source agreed that the president’s pledge not to touch the Constitution was consistent with Sisi’s personal desire not to remain in power beyond 2030.


A parliamentarian with a military background recalled Sisi saying during closed sessions that he wouldn’t wait for the defense minister “to tell me to go to Sharm el-Sheikh,” alluding to Mubarak’s departure for the

Red Sea

 resort in the midst of the January 25 revolution.

 In early February 2011, then-Vice President Omar Soliman announced Mubarak’s resignation after 30 years in power and said the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces, headed by then-Defense Minister Mohamed Hussein Tantawy, would assume power. 


The same parliamentarian added that the remainder of Sisi’s presidency could see the government implement several of the constitutional provisions

introduced

 in 2019, including the one that allows the president to appoint a vice president.

 He suggested that the president could make such an appointment to ensure a smoother transfer of power.


Article 150-bis of the Constitution allows the president to appoint one or more vice presidents, define their roles, delegate some of his powers to them, remove them from office and accept their resignations.


The judicial source told Mada Masr that Sisi’s remarks about not remaining in power beyond 2030 sent positive signals that could help ease public anger and discontent with the executive branch over the country’s economic and political conditions, and could  spark public debate about his successor.


The source also said that Sisi’s remarks do not rule out efforts to extend his presidency before his current term expires, suggesting that a reinterpretation of the constitution could be put forward, or that the president, or one-fifth of the House, could exercise their constitutional prerogative to propose amendments to its text.


The party source, who heads an opposition party represented in the House of Representatives, said it was too early to determine whether the Constitution would be amended. 


“Not before 2028,” the source said. The call for constitutional amendments cannot come from the president himself, he said, adding that, “others make the call, but not now.” He described the current political climate is not conducive to raising the issue, saying “there’s no rush.”


The source said Egyptians are going through a difficult period and needed someone to speak to them clearly about the state of the country and where it is headed, pointing to the deterioration of public services and political and …

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Memorial service held for victims of the Strand mass shooting
content:
In the early hours of Sunday morning, 27 September, gunmen opened fire on patrons at a shisanyama in Lwandle, near Cape Town, killing ten people. “Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities. Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained. Lwandle police have opened murder and attempted murder cases,” said the police. The community believes the mass shooting is related to the extortion racket that is ravaging Cape Town townships.


One of the victims, Khululekani Ndlovu, will be laid to rest this weekend. The nine other people killed will be buried next weekend in the Eastern Cape. The Nomzamo Community Hall in Strand, south east of Cape Town, was packed with mourners and members of political parties for the memorial service.


Speaking to

Elitsha

, the chairperson of the police board in South Africa, Francina Lukas, said that extortion and business rivalry and lack of opportunities for young people are some of the factors contributing to high crime rates in the townships of Cape Town. She said that the lack of trust the community has in the police contributes to high crime rate.


“The police need to do much more than what they are doing in terms of compliance to make sure that businesses in the township comply with their licenses and bylaws. But the issue of trust is still a burning issue in our communities. So we need to overcome that issue to see that trust in the police is restored,” she said.


Families of the Strand 10


Speaking on behalf of the Sikweza family who lost their daughter, Avuyile, her uncle, Luyanda Macokeni, said she had plans to return to school next year. The 20-year-old passed her matric in 2024. She applied to continue her education next year and had just received responses from two universities offering her a place to study. She was expected to make a choice between the two. “Avuyile is supposed to the one burying us as elders but we are the ones burying her. It’s not God’s will that we are here today, it is because of someone’s will,” he said.


Siyathemba Jilaji was one of the victims who died on his way to the hospital, according to his friend. “He said he was going to change in the car so when the shooting began, I thought he was still in the car. A bullet grazed me under my arm. After the shooting, I went to the car to check for him. But, I didn’t know that he was amongst the bodies that were lying next to the entrance that I ran past,” she said.


Sivenathi Manxiwa’s father, Lubabalo Ndamane, said that he is not going to forgive the person who murdered his son. “I also don’t want to know who they are. Even if they can be arrested, I would not go to court. I leave everything to God and God will deal with him. I want to know what drove him to shoot at the young people who were out enjoying themselves,” he said.


The 10 people who died during the mass shooting in Strand last weekend

.

Photo from Facebook

.


The police said that the investigation into the mass murder is still ongoing.

author: Marcus Baram
title: Aging Coal Plants Turn Into a Midterm Fight Over Energy Costs
content:
Climate and energy battles are running through campaigns in Michigan, Colorado, Indiana, and beyond.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Craig Unit 1, a coal-fired power plant distinguished by tall exhaust smokestacks that rise above a rolling landscape in northwestern Colorado, was scheduled to close for good at the end of 2025 amid pressure from environmental advocates, public interest groups and state officials.

But on Dec. 30, Energy Secretary Chris Wright ordered it to keep burning coal. The unit had suffered a mechanical failure 11 days earlier and was not even running. Wright has since renewed the order three times — most recently on Sept. 25, extending the plant’s life through Christmas Day, a full year past its retirement date.

Its operator, Tri-State Generation and Transmission, is a nonprofit rural cooperative, and in January it joined co-owner Platte River Power Authority, a public power agency, in arguing that Wright’s orders violate the Constitution and federal law — a fight that has since reached a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. A co-op and a municipal utility suing the executive branch for the right to close their own coal plant was not what Congress had in mind in 1935, when it wrote the emergency provision that the Energy Department is now leaning on.

Data centers and gas pump prices have dominated the energy story in this midterm cycle — polls show broad opposition to the artificial intelligence build-out over utility bills and grid strain. But with just weeks until Election Day, a second tier of climate and energy battles is running through campaigns in Michigan, Colorado, Indiana and beyond: forced coal plant extensions, canceled plans for offshore wind farms, repealed clean energy tax credits, drought, state preemption of local climate rules and a drumbeat of federal rollbacks. None of these issues poll as high as affordability. But all of them, say the people trying to turn them into votes, are essential to the affordability debate.

Starting in May 2025, the Energy Department invoked Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act to order Consumers Energy’s J.H. Campbell plant in West Olive, Michigan, to stay online past its planned retirement, then renewed the order five more times.

Similar mandates followed for Craig and for the Schahfer and Culley plants in Indiana, each justified by grid reliability. On Sept. 11, a unanimous D.C. Circuit panel, in an opinion written by Judge Cornelia Pillard, ruled that the first two Campbell orders were illegal — no genuine emergency existed to justify overriding Michigan’s regulators.

Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School, said the provision had been dormant for decades after some early wartime use. “Over the past 20 to 30 years it’s really been used almost exclusively for weather-related events,” he said, “and it only lasts a few days.”

Nothing like Wright’s coal orders had been tried. “In every prior instance there’s been some entity, whether a utility, a grid operator or a state regulator, that’s asked for these orders. Here it’s [the Department of Energy] acting on its own,” he said. “No one had asked for it. And to the contrary, some had said, ’Please don’t do this.’”

The administration has until roughly the end of October to decide whether to appeal. If it lets the ruling stand, Peskoe said, “I think the other orders for the other plants will fall pretty quickly.”

Utility giant Consumers Energy put the net cost of running Campbell from May 23, 2025, through June 30 of this year at $295 million, after wholesale market revenue. Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel’s office has cited that figure, against nearly $600 million in savings the retirement was supposed to deliver. In August, federal regulators let Consumers Energy spread the costs across the grid’s north and central regions — from North Dakota to Indiana. That means Wisconsin ratepayers, whose share one estimate puts at $117 million, could wind up paying for a Michigan coal plant. The recent appeals court decision overturning the Energy Department’s order could spare taxpayers those costs.

Brian Wheeler, spokesperson for Consumers Energy, said the utility would work to ensure “everyone who benefits from power from the Campbell plant across the Midwest pays their fair share.” Nessel, who has challenged all six orders, said …

author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: Treaty rights and voting access at centre of Alberta referendum
content:
As Albertans prepare to vote on the province’s future in Canada, Siksika Nation Chief Samuel Crowfoot says the separation debate raises questions about who would honour First Nations treaties and protect the rights they guarantee.


“There’s too many unanswered questions and there’s been no consultation with First Nations, and that’s a requirement as protected by the Constitution.” Crowfoot said.


Crowfoot’s great-great-great-grandfather, chief Crowfoot, was an original signatory of Treaty 7, which established a relationship between the Blackfoot people and the Crown. That treaty predates Alberta’s entry into Confederation in 1905.


The Oct. 19 referendum will ask Albertans whether the province should begin the process of separating from Canada. For First Nations, the question extends beyond provincial politics to treaty obligations, sovereignty and the Crown’s responsibility to uphold agreements protected by the Constitution.


Chief of Siksika Nation, Samuel Crowfoot poses for a photo in his traditional homelands close to where Treaty 7 was signed. Photo: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs/APTN.


Siksika Nation, Piikani Nation, the Blood Tribe and Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation challenged the decision. On May 13, the Alberta Court of King’s Bench ruled that Alberta breached its duty to consult First Nations in the process leading to the approval of a citizen-led separation petition.


Crowfoot says it’s because of First Nation’s taking legal action that the vote is non-binding, meaning it would not itself make Alberta independent, but it could influence the next steps in the separation debate.


The province and the petition organizer appealed the ruling.


Carly Fox, a lawyer and member of the Kainai Nation, emphasized to APTN News how Alberta had hired outside private practice counsel to handle the appeal rather than relying on Alberta Justice.


“That shows that they’re really interested and willing to put a lot of effort and public money into this, which I think is really upsetting,” Fox said.


Voter Information sessions raise questions 


Fox has been holding information sessions for Siksika Nation and other members of the Blackfoot Confederacy to explain the referendum questions and their potential implications.


“Even though treaty rights are a collective entitlement, I think as an individual, to me, it was important for me to vote and to defend my treaty rights,” Fox said.


She said the referendum questions about immigration could leave voters with a misleading impression of existing rules around access to public services.


“There’s rules for eligibility for income support and for education and for health care,” Fox said. “It’s not a free-for-all, but the way that the questions are framed makes it seem like that.”


Carly Fox is a lawyer and member of the Blood Tribe who has held information sessions to answer questions and create discussion around the referendum and its potential implications for Indigenous communities.  Photo: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs/APTN.


Crowfoot said the referendum’s questions about immigration also raise concerns for the Blackfoot Confederacy, whose members have family and cultural ties on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border.


The Confederacy includes Siksika Nation, Piikani Nation and the Kainai Nation, also known as the Blood Tribe, in Alberta, as well as the Blackfeet Tribe in Montana.


“Those discussions about immigration don’t take into account First Nations and the unique position that we’re in. And so we have concerns about that,” Crowfoot said.


He said many Siksika members are married to members of the Blackfeet Tribe in Montana, raising questions about how potential changes to immigration rules could affect their ability to cross the border.


“Is that something that can be seen as another obstacle to keep them from their traditional homelands?” he said.


Referendum street signs along the Trans-Canada highway in Calgary. Photo: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs/APTN.


Federal Responsibility


Prime Minister Mark Carney attended a Forever Canadian Rally in Calgary on Friday and urged  Albertans to vote to keep Canada united, but there was no mention of recognizing treaty rights and the role First Nations played in challenging the separation petition.


Fox called the rally a missed opportunity to build a stronger nation-to-nation relationship.


“I think it would be really nice for him to fully understand First Nations rights and understand our sovereignty and understand why …

author: Andrea
title: ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᖅᓯᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᖁᕕᐊᓲᑎᖃᕐᑐᑦ ᓯᐅᕗᓕᐅᕐᑎᐅᕙᒃᑐᓂᒃ, ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᐅᕙᒃᑐᓂ
content:
For the English version of this story, please see

Nunavut Sport and Recreation awards gala honours leaders, volunteers

.


ᓯᕗᓕᐅᕐᑎᐅᓂᖅ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᐅᕙᖕᓂᖅ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᓯᒪᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᐅᕙᓂ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ ᐅᕙᓂ ᐊᕐᓴᕐᓃᑦ ᑐᔪᕐᒥᕕᒃᒥ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 3-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ.


ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑕᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᒥᕐᖑᐃᕐᓯᕐᕕᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖏᑦ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᑐᙵᓱᒃᑎᑦᑎᔨᐅᖃᑕᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᐅᑯᓂᖓ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᖏᓐᓂ.


ᓄᕗᐊᓕᐊ ᑭᐅᕆᐅ ᑭᙵᕐᓂ ᓄᓇᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᑖᖅᑎᑕᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐆᒥᖓ ᑳᒻ ᐃᐅ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓂ ᓯᕗᓕᐅᕐᑎᐅᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᓵᓚᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᕆᕙᒃᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐊᐅᔭᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᒪᔨᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᔭᐅᓕᖅᖢᖢᓂ ᕼᐋᒻᒪᓚᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕌᓂᒃᑳᖓᑕ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᖏᓐᓄᑦ.


“ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᖅ ᐱᒻᒪᕆᐊᓘᒻᒪ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓄᑦ ᓲᖃᐃᒻᒪ ᖃᓄᐃᑦᑕᐃᓕᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᕈᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᕐᒨᖓᓂᖓᓄᑦ, ᐃᓱᒪᒃᑯᓪᓗ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓯᒪᓂᕐᓴᐅᔾᔪᑎᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᕐᓴᕈᑎᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐃᓅᓯᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᑐᕈᓐᓇᖅᑐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓅᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᕐᒧᑦ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᑭᐅᕆᐅ ᕙᐃᔅᐳᒃᑯ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 8-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ.


ᐅᓇ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓕᒃ 18-ᓂ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑎ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᖅ 40-ᖏᓐᓃᑦᑐᓂ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓕᖕᓂ 5-ᓂ 12-ᓄ 4:00 ᐅᓪᓗᒃᑯᑦ 6:00 ᑎᑭᓐᓇᓱᖕᓂᖓᓂ ᐱᓇᓱᐊᕈᓯᐅᑉ ᐃᓗᐊᒍᑦ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᒃᑯᕕᒃᒥᑦ.


ᑐᓴᕐᓈᖅᑕᐅᔪᑦ ᐅᑯᐊ ᐃᙱᖅᖢᑎ Black Eyed Peas ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᓯᖏᑦ ᐃᙱᕐᑏᑦ ᑐᓴᕐᓈᕈᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᓂᐱᑭᓵᓯᒪᓪᓗᓂ, ᑭᐅᕆᐅ ᑖᒃᑯᓂᖓ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᐅᓪᓗ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᖏᑦᑕᓕ ᐊᓯᐊᒎᖓᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᕋᓱᒃᖢᓂ.


ᐃᒡᓘ ᐃᓗᐊᓂ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᐅᔪᓐᓇᖅᑐᓂᒃ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᕋᓱᒃᖢᓂ ᐃᓱᒫᓘᑎᖃᕋᓂ “ᐃᓐᓇᕐᓄᑦ ᐱᒡᒍᓴᐅᑎᐅᓇᔭᙳᐊᖅᑐᓂᒃ.”


“ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᐅᔪᑦ ᓲᕐᓗ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᖕᒦᖅᑰᔨᓐᓇᕈᓐᓃᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᓱᕈᓰᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᓂ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᕐᓂᕐᓴᐅᓕᖃᑦᑕᕐᒪᑕ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.


ᐅᑯᐊ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓕᐅᕋᓱᒐᑎᒃ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᑦ ᖁᕕᐊᓲᑎᖃᓚᐅᕐᒥᔪᑦ ᑭᙵᐃᑦ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓂ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᐅᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒧᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᓪᓗᑎᒃ.


“ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᔨᐅᕙᒃᑐᑦ ᐆᒻᒪᑎᒋᔭᐅᒻᒪᕆᒃᑐᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᖏᓐᓂᒃ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᔨ ᑐᑭᒧᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᔨᖓ ᐃᐅᕋᓐ ᕌᐱᓐᓴᓐ ᐅᖄᓚᐅᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᐱᕐᓱᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 8-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ.


ᖁᓕᐅᓪᓗᑎᒃ (10) ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᑦ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓖᑦ 13-ᓂ 19-ᒧ ᑖᒃᑯᐊ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᒪᓂᒻᒪᐃᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᐅᓗᕆᐊᓇᙱᑦᑐᒥ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓄᑦ ᐅᐸᒃᑕᐅᕙᒃᑐᓂ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.


ᕕᕝᕗᐊᕆᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᑖᒃᑯᐊ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᑦ 200 ᐅᖓᑖᓃᑦᑐᓂᒃ ᕚᓚᓐᑕᐃᓐᔅ ᑕᐃᒥ (ᓇᒡᓕᒍᓱᖕᓇᒥ) ᐅᓪᓛᕈᒻᒥᑕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᑦ, ᕌᐱᓐᓴᓐ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.


“ᐅᑯᐊ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᑦ ᐃᓱᒪᒋᔭᖃᑦᑎᐊᖅᖢᑎᒃ, ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᒌᑦᑎᐊᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᒃᑯᒋᔭᖃᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑲᑦᑕᖅᑐᑦ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ. “ᐊᓯᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐃᓱᒪᒋᔭᐅᑦᑎᐊᓕᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᑦ, ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᐱᕈᖅᑎᑦᑎᕙᓪᓕᐊᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᓯᒪᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᕙᖕᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓯᕗᓕᐅᖅᑎᐅᕙᖕᓂᖅ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᖓᓂᖓᓂᒃ.”


ᐃᖃᓗᐃᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᐸᐅᔭᖓᓂ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᑐᑭᒧᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᔨ ᐳᕆᑕᓐ ᒪᒃᓂᐅᓪ ᑐᓂᔭᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᕐᒥᒃ ᓯᕗᓕᐅᖅᑎᐅᓂᖓᓄᑦ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒧᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᒥ.


ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ, ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖏᑦ ᕼᐋᑭᖅᑎᐅᓂᑯᕕᓂᕐᒥ ᔪᐊᑎᓐ ᑐᑐᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓅᔪᓐᓃᕐᓯᒪᓕᕐᑐᒥ ᐅᑭᐅᕐᑕᖅᑐᕐᒥ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑎᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᐃᔨᐅᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᑯᒥ ᐊᑏᒪ ᕼᐊᓪᓚᕆᒥ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᑖᖅᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ (Hall of Fame) ᑖᓐᓇᓗ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᑕᐅᓵᕐᓂᑰᓪᓗᓂ.


ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᑐᓂᓯᓚᐅᕐᒥᔪᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓂ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑎᓄᑦ, ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᔨᖏᓐᓄᑦ, ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᐅᕙᒃᑐᓄᑦ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ.


ᖁᙱᐊᖅᑐᑦ ᐃᓚᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ 100 ᐅᖓᑖᓂ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒻᒪᕆᖕᓂ ᐅᐸᒍᑎᓯᒪᓪᓗᑎᒡᓗ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᐱᓇᓱᐊᕈᓯᐅᑉ ᓄᙳᐊᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᕆᔭᐅᔪᒥ.


ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᐃᓚᖃᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐅᑯᓂᖓ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐹᔅᑭᑦᐹᓪ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᙱᓐᓂᒃ, ᕚᓕᐹᓪ ᓄᓇᕗᑯᓐᓂ, ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᓵᑯᑯᓐᓂᑦ, ᓄᓇᕗᒥ ᐱᖕᐹᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖏᓐᓂ, ᐃᖃᓗᒃᑑᑦᑎᐊᕐᒥ ᐅᓇᑕᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᙱᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐹᑦᒥᓐᑕᓐᑯᓐᓂ ᑐᙵᓱᒃᑎᑦᑎᔨᐅᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᖕᒥ ᐃᖃᐃᓕᓴᕐᕕᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 3-ᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 4-ᒥ.

author: Kevin Carson
title: Review. CLR James: Cultivator of the Popular Will, by Matthew Quest
content:
Matthew Quest.

CLR James: Cultivator of the Popular Will. A Study of the History and Politics of World Revolution

 (Brill, 2026).


As Matthew Quest notes in his appendix, “Top Ten Reasons We Don’t Know More about CLR James,” CLR James is a relatively obscure thinker even among the African-American left. This is doubly so on the left more generally. According to Quest, James’ thought occupies a marginal position on the left primarily because his fundamental orientation — an affinity for direct democracy and workers’ self-management — is fundamentally at odds with the centralized, mass-based politics of the Old Left, whether Marxist-Leninist or Social Democratic. He was hostile to the British Labour Party and Atlee, the US Democratic Party and FDR, and to post-independence African leaders who were lionized elsewhere on the left. He saw nation-states and vanguard parties as mostly destructive rather than helpful, and the history of nationalization by progressive governments as hostile to self-management. James also saw the class reductionism of the dominant currents of the left, with their neglect of racial and anti-colonial dimensions of struggle, as failing to meet the needs of the time.


Quest himself is a perfect fit for intellectual biographer of James, as a historian and critic of national liberation movements in Africa and elsewhere in the colonial and post-colonial world, as well as post-independence governments. James’ central values of direct democracy and self-governance resonate strongly with Quest’s hostility — which come through clearly in these quotes from his Preface — to self-serving establishments, Black, revolutionary, and/or “progressive.”


The search for identity and heritage, in all their proper cultural nuances, for those who have known scars, exploitation, and who are overcoming insecurity, cannot be permitted to be captured by those who define freedom as managing subordinate lives. This is how all who fatefully embrace the state define it. These are the facts of the long duration of post-civil rights, post-colonial existence.


…Hopefully, we have now learned that the challenge to respectability politics without opposition to elite representative government is a fraud….


We are living in an affirmative action empire and ethnically plural police state alongside subcontractors of guilt and activists for the government, funded by the white rich, talking about privilege. We have people lecturing us about the problem of ‘colour blindness’ who are not opposed to the police state; they are explicitly part of the boss class who murder, mass incarcerate, and get out the vote for those who exploit.


* * *


…[W]hen I questioned whether the working people of Cuba actually governed that country, many dedicated revolutionaries, socialists, and anti- imperialists replied that it did not matter. For most insulted by the historical denial of self-determination of conquered peoples and for most organising for some future socialism or communism, it did not matter whether ordinary people directly governed or not. This should shake those who are not Machiavellians to the core. We should not be so thirsty for empowerment that we will accept a half-made or second-hand society as a dwelling to sustain our search for liberation.


…No workers or youth to whom we were introduced asked questions about their contradictions. Surely, ordinary people in Cuba asked these questions but were not featured on the directed tours and cultural events. This raised questions about the democratic content and the political economy of the socialist future and the ethics of those who took part in such projects.


* * *


CLR James famously said: ‘Political treachery is not the monopoly of the white race’. He also said there are Black people who treat Black toilers like ‘colonial trustees’, and while they talk of desiring ‘independence’ and ‘power’ they already live a ‘delightful’ existence at the toilers’ expense.


James’ life (1901-1989) spanned the Russian Revolution, the rise and fracturing of Marxism-Leninism, and postwar national liberation movements, and intersected with them at numerous points.


Born in Trinidad, he lived in numerous countries over the course of his lifetime. His activist career was wide-ranging and global; as Quest writes, “James and his associates worked for an American revolution, a Caribbean revolution, African revolution, and world revolution.” He authored numerous historical works, including

The …

author: Halie Moses
title: The Z Factor: Young Voters and the 2026 Midterms
content:
Generation Z voters (aged 18-29) are predicted to make a significant impact on the upcoming 2026 Midterm elections. This has not always been the case, as student and youth voter turnout has historically remained low. Only 47% of Americans aged 18-29 voted in the 2024 election. This year, 50 million Gen Z Americans are eligible to vote.

In October, a report by UCLA’s William Institute examined the political priorities and voting intentions of Gen Z adults ahead of the 2026 midterms. The study found that nearly 74 percent of respondents said they were likely or certain to vote. These numbers come as no surprise to those who work with students, spend time organizing on college campuses, or identify as Gen Z during the Trump Administration. Rising living costs, ICE raids, attacks on reproductive rights access, sexual assault cases, climate change, and unwanted wars have directly impacted their lives and are driving them to the polls with a passion for change.

Leela Strong, Director of CIRCLE, who works to empower the youth vote, reflected: “Young people are sending us clear signals, not only of dissatisfaction with our politics and deep economic concerns, but also of a strong desire to take action and drive change.” Organizations such as When We All Vote are working to engage young people by connecting their priorities with the issues and candidates on their ballots. Opportunities to participate alongside friends and classmates can also encourage young people to become more involved in politics.

Campus organizing is another part of these efforts. The Feminist Majority Foundation’s Feminist Campus program is actively working to get the student vote out. Students can help their peers register to vote, understand their ballot, and march to the polls in solidarity. These efforts are particularly important for first-time voters, who may need guidance.

Not only are young people planning to vote, but they are also planning to vote overwhelmingly Democratic. In the September Economist/YouthGov Poll, when asked who they will cast their ballot for, 54% of 18-29-year-olds said the Democratic candidate, compared with 22% who said the Republican candidate. The same survey found a sentiment among youth that reflects that the Republican Party is too extreme. When asked, “Do you think the Republican Party is too extreme?” 65% of 18- 29-year-olds replied yes. In contrast, only 29% believe the Democratic Party is too extreme. These results reflect the views of respondents at the time of the survey and do not necessarily predict how young people will vote in November.

These numbers are significant and show promising signs that young people are empowered to change the course of our political and social reality. Voter registration, accessible election information, and campus organizing can help young people navigate the voting process and participate in decisions that affect their futures. To learn more, head to vote411.org/feminist.

author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: As parts of the Nicola River run dry, a father fears what his children will inherit
content:
Brian Holmes, a councillor for the Upper Nicola Band, walks through a dry stretch of the Nicola River on Sept. 18, 2026, a few minutes downstream from his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in the Nicola Valley, in B.C.’s southern interior.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


On this stretch of the Nicola River, Brian Holmes misses the sound of water. 


“This is heartbreaking,” he quietly says to himself as he prepares to park above a kilometre-long stretch where no surface water remains.


In the absence of the river’s flow, birds can be heard in the thick vegetation, their calls occasionally joined by a horse neighing in the distance or a car passing along Douglas Lake Road above.


The 44-year-old Upper Nicola Band (UNB) member and father of two leaves his vehicle and disappears into the bush separating the river from a small ranch below the road, a few minutes downstream from his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in the Nicola Valley, in “B.C.’s” southern interior. 


He re-emerges from the bush and makes his way down a steep slope into the exposed riverbed, where large boulders rise from a channel that should be running with water on this warm mid-September morning.


The Nicola River winds roughly 210 kilometres through syilx and Nlakaʼpamux homelands. It flows from its headwaters on the Thompson-Okanagan Plateau, down through Douglas and Nicola lakes before passing through Merritt, and eventually joining the Thompson River northeast of Lytton at Spences Bridge.


But along this one-kilometre dry stretch between Douglas and Nicola Lakes, just around the corner from the community’s drinking water, the waterway resembles more of a meandering valley of rocks.


“I’ve been looking at it enough that it’s numb to me now. This didn’t happen yesterday. It’s been like this for the last month,” said Holmes.


He said that it’s tough to see dried-up sections of the river, especially “when you know there should be water.”


“It’s supposed to be the major river system in this watershed, but it doesn’t have any water flowing through it over the surface,” Holmes said.


“We’ve seen a little bit of a flow coming out of Douglas Lake, but it’s going to get sucked in by the groundwater now. There is a little trickle, but then it just disappears partway down. Any water that pops up anywhere is all groundwater.”


Just upstream, on a bend in the river, there’s a deep hole in the waterway that Holmes and his friends used as a makeshift natural swimming pool every summer when they were children.


Brian Holmes, a councillor for the Upper Nicola Band, stands near a deep hole in the Nicola River that he and his friends swam in as children, in his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake) on Sept. 18, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


“I don’t know if you would swim in it now,” he said, citing health concerns from a buildup of harmful algae blooms in the water.


“I’m hoping by the time (my sons) get to my age, they can enjoy it. If we’re in these (drought) cycles — hopefully we can survive long enough.”


He walks across the dry riverbed, using the boulders as stepping stones, then stops for a moment and looks downstream to where water should be flowing.


Brian Holmes, a councillor for the Upper Nicola Band, walks through a dry stretch of the Nicola River on Sept. 18, 2026, a few minutes downstream from his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in the Nicola Valley, in B.C.’s southern interior.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


“It’s like another world, man. It’s — I don’t know. It just makes me think about missing that sound of water flowing,” Holmes said.


“When you walk down a stream, and there’s no water, it’s like losing a relative, losing a part of you. It’s just hard to explain.”


A few dozen kilometres up the river from this spot, where the stream converges with Chapperon Creek before flowing into Douglas Lake, IndigiNews observed smaller dry patches along the waterway’s surface as well.


A dry patch of the Nicola River, at its confluence with Chapperon Creek northeast of Douglas Lake, on Sept. 18, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


The watershed entered the growing season with little room to spare. In March, “B.C.’s” River Forecast Centre

forecast seasonal inflows

 to the Nicola River and Nicola Lake at just 40 to 60 per cent of normal, citing low snowpack, dry weather and already-low flows.


By mid-June, the Nicola basin was a Level 4 on

the province’s drought scale

, the second-highest rating. It remained at that level in mid-July and had reached …

author: Admin101
title: Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense
content:
Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN) is excited to announce the publication of

Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense

.


Drawing on organizing experiences of Black Rose/Rosa Negra members across the United States, this pamphlet explores how workers, neighbors, and communities are building collective resistance to ICE and defending their immigrant coworkers, classmates, and loved ones. By connecting struggles across workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods, the

transversal organizing

 approach we prioritize builds solidarity across different sectors of society to confront the interconnected structures of domination that shape our lives.


You can find a downloadable PDF version of the pamphlet at the end of this text.


Two Years of Trump II: Immigrants in the Crosshairs, Resistance Under Attack


Upon returning to office, Donald Trump wasted little time fulfilling his white supremacist campaign pledge of “Mass Deportations Now.” Via a flurry of executive orders and congressional acts his administration reinstated the reviled “family separation” policy; directed virtually unlimited resources to stop a fictitious “invasion” of the country’s borders; and sought to end birthright citizenship. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents blitzed Los Angeles in June 2025 with spectacular raids, followed shortly by similar operations in dozens of cities across the country including New York City; Chicago, IL; New Orleans, LA; and Durham, NC. This “shock and awe” strategy culminated in Operation Metro Surge, a months-long invasion of the Minnesota Twin Cities that deported over 2,000 residents. 


Meanwhile, support for the deportation machine plummeted as collective action against it swelled. Everyday people covered their cars, lawns, and lips with the slogan “Abolish ICE;” as of July 2026, nearly 50% of US adults support such a measure. Both May Days since Trump’s second inauguration centered immigrant defense in their celebrations. Rapid-response networks that keep watch for ICE, document kidnappings, and sometimes disrupt them spread wildly. Know-your-rights training flourished at worksites and community centers. Millions of Red Cards–wallet-sized cards outlining the holder’s constitutional protections around interactions with ICE and other police–were distributed at schools, churches, restaurants, and municipal buildings. Children and their parents caged in concentration camps went on hunger strike as constituents bombarded politicians’ hotlines and town halls demanding humanitarian treatment and release outside their walls.


Popular responses in St. Paul and Minneapolis demonstrate the possibilities of mass resistance. Like the Los Angeles Tenant Union’s community defense centers that countered ICE’s Southern California invasion, organizers reactivated dormant neighborhood networks from the 2020 uprising and began building new ones when word spread that Commander-at-Large Greg Bovino was bringing his paramilitary forces to town. Once Operation Metro Surge launched, everyday Minnesotans refined sophisticated systems to track, delay, and disrupt arrests. ICE agents retaliated by killing rapid-responder Renée Good and shooting Julio C. Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan immigrant targeted for deportation. Instead of cowering from the naked clampdown, neighborhood networks coordinated with unions, churches, and other civil societal organizations to shut down their cities on January 23rd. In its wake, Trump ousted Bovino and immigration enforcement plummeted.


But July 2026 saw record high immigrant detentions since Trump’s return to office with little public opposition. What explains it? ICE’s tactical shifts undoubtedly played a role. Bovino replacement and “Border Czar” Tom Homan traded provocative street operations with quiet detainers at jails and prisons and “targeted operations” at sites protected from activist impediment like airports. Escalating repression has also raised the costs of resistance. ICE’s bevy of brutality has included intimidation, beatings, and shootings, culminating in murdering Good and rapid-responder Alex Pretti. Federal grand juries fish from the shadows for information about our movements, stoking fears of informants that slow our organizing. From the Prairieland defendants to the Minnesota 15 and more, indictments and convictions on flimsy charges could make prosecuting dissidents even easier. Evidentiary discovery in the …

author: Valerie Anne
title: ‘The Body’ Is a Sapphic, Ritual-Gone-Wrong Teen Horror Show Coming to Netflix
content:
Do you ever feel like a show was made just for you using all your favorite media keywords? That’s how I felt when I first heard about Netflix’s The Body. I saw Catholic school, dancers, ritual-gone-wrong, horror and I was beyond sold.

And in case those words and phrases didn’t make it obvious: The story is also sapphic. Writer and creator Quinn Shephard (who acted in movies like The Miseducation of Cameron Post and wrote/directed episodes of Under the Bridge) started writing the show the year she came out. She says: “It’s satirizing some of the trauma of growing up queer and repressed and the confusion around that.”

A lot of the main cast of girls are relative newcomers on the scene (aka they don’t have Wikipedia “personal life” pages yet) so I’m not sure who among them are queer, but the show WILL feature lesbian reality star Gabby Windey in a recurring role as a coach. Also, almost all of the episodes have women listed as writers.

The show looks freaky and weird in all the best ways, and I can’t wait. I hope it’s just as fun as shows like Yellowjackets and even Mike Flanagan’s Carrie. May the teens-getting-into-supernatural-mischief genre never die.

The series drops next month and you can watch the full official trailer right now!

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Tablets Make Communication Easier Behind Bars – But Deaf People Are Left Behind
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


Tablet computers have revolutionized communication inside prisons for hearing prisoners. Prison systems from across the country — including in

New York

,

California

, and

Illinois

 — have

distributed tens of thousands

 of tablets to incarcerated people, which they can use to call home, watch movies, message loved ones, or attend virtual classes (although they are often

charged predatory fees

 for accessing these benefits). As of 2022,

25 state prison systems

 had tablet distribution programs, according to the Electronic Privacy Information Center. 


But as the rollout of such tablets continues, many deaf incarcerated people have been left behind. 


Disability justice organization HEARD points out that

it’s

unknown

 how many deaf people are incarcerated in U.S. prisons, but a

2015 report

 by the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimated that 6.2 percent of incarcerated people in

state

 and

federal

 prisons have a hearing disability, which would equal about 71,000 people.


Daniel Valenzuela, who is deaf, is incarcerated at Danville Correctional Center in Illinois. Last year, the Illinois Department of Corrections (IDOC)

distributed tablets

 to all incarcerated people. But IDOC blocks videophone capabilities, preventing Valenzuela from communicating in his primary language, American Sign Language (ASL).  


In September, Valenzuela sued the IDOC director for violating the Americans with Disabilities Act.


“I have six kids, four grandkids, and one of my sons is in the military. I cherish and love my family so much,” said Valenzuela in a

press release

 announcing the lawsuit. “I just want to tell them happy birthday and I am so grieved when I can’t call because I don’t want them to think I forgot.”


There are at least three other deaf individuals at Danville who primarily use ASL to communicate, according to the

complaint

 filed by Disability Rights Advocates, Equip for Equality, and the law firm Much Shelist. 


“Across the Illinois Department of Corrections, people can use tablets to communicate with their loved ones, which has been a game changer in removing restrictions on communication,” Valenzuela’s attorney, Rachel Weisberg, the directing attorney at Disability Rights Advocates, told

Truthout

. “But for Mr. Valenzuela and other deaf people who use American Sign Language, that same access simply isn’t available.” 


IDOC did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.


Last year, in addition to distributing tablets to incarcerated people, IDOC

announced

 it would provide every incarcerated person with 775 free domestic phone call minutes per month. In a press release,

IDOC said

 that these initiatives, working in tandem, “enhance family connections and increase access to technology that supports rehabilitation.” 


But deaf prisoners are excluded from accessing these critical programs. 


Unlike hearing prisoners who can use their tablets to make calls from their cells, Valenzuela must get a guard’s permission to walk to another building to use the one videophone that’s available to him. In at least one instance, Valenzuela had to go out in the pouring rain to use the videophone, according to the complaint. 


“When prison officials don’t communicate with deaf/disabled people in ways they can understand, they may be written up for being ‘non-compliant.'”


The videophone is often unavailable because the unit itself breaks down, the prison is on lockdown, or a guard denies his request, according to the complaint. Last year, Valenzuela was unable to speak with his family during the holidays because the phone was not working for 54 straight days, from November 2025 to January 2026. However, if the tablets malfunction, there are several backup phones that incarcerated hearing people can use, the complaint says.


“We’re asking for equal access, as that’s what the law requires,” said Weisberg. “Equal access is not static — it must reflect the benefits currently offered to others and account for the needs of people with disabilities as technology and communication systems evolve.”


These issues are not limited to Illinois. Advocates say incarcerated deaf people have to contend with discriminatory communication practices in prisons throughout the country.


“In prisons where we’ve seen scores of deaf/disabled people, there may only be 2 videophones,” Kah Mendoza, the communications coordinator for

HEARD

, told …

author: Alison Avigayil Ramer
title: After October 7, I learned that movements need grief spaces
content:
This article

After October 7, I learned that movements need grief spaces

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Since the massacres on Oct. 7, now three years ago, the news has brought a steady stream of horror and broken promises. The ceasefire in Gaza has been broken thousands of times; the ceasefire with Iran only holds until the next strike. Many of us have responded by going numb or turning away. Over these three years, I’ve come to believe that collective mourning can help movements build sturdier organizing infrastructure, move through paralysis and numbness, and get back to the long-term work of creating systemic change.


I’ve spent nearly two decades living and working as a human rights defender, mostly in Palestine and Israel. For years, I responded to atrocities the way much of the dominant organizing culture did at the time: strategically. I prepared statements, launched campaigns and mobilized our base. I worked through several wars and the ongoing ethnic cleansing and genocide. Even though my colleagues and I were often physically together, we rarely had the opportunity to collectively mourn. In fact, mourning was often seen as something only the privileged could afford. As organizers and solidarity activists, we were the ones who needed to push past the pain and keep mobilizing.


And then, after each war, large swaths of colleagues and organizers would burn out, and our movement would suffer a setback. Movement researchers Paul Gorski and Cher Chen, studying U.S. human rights and social justice activists, found that an estimated 50 to 60 percent of organizers eventually walk away from movement work and never return, burned out by a culture that treats overwork and self-sacrifice as necessary. That culture also leaves no room to mourn and process the secondary trauma that accumulates, hastening burnout. These kinds of cycles make it especially hard for movements seeking systemic change to sustain themselves.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


When Hamas attacked Israel in October 2023 and I was waiting in anticipation of the retaliation against Gaza, I knew I couldn’t respond with the same kind of organizing strategy that we usually use: preparation of advocacy statements, social media campaigns and fundraising appeals. I knew that while some people should and would continue that work, there also needed to be spaces for organizers and our base to mourn. And so, on Oct. 8, I opened a space for collective mourning online, sharing it in the many community, political and religious groups I was a part of, for anyone who needed somewhere to process what they were witnessing and feeling. Dozens of people joined: primarily my Jewish community at first, and then people from many faiths and chapters of my life, from Palestine to Palo Alto. 


As the assault on Gaza and the genocide continued, the room stayed open. More colleagues, including community organizers, artists, chaplains and psychologists, joined me in facilitating, and we held space for hundreds of people from across our communities to mourn together. We formed a collective called the

Social Change Sanctuary

 and developed a format that included facilitation and participation from attendees. Over time, we were invited to hold spaces for other communities in mourning. We’ve held spaces to grieve the ongoing genocide; climate catastrophes like the fires in Los Angeles; ICE raids, arrests and murders; and the war on Iran.


The Social Change Sanctuary hosts an Interdependence Day circle in 2025. (Alison Avigayil Ramer)


Participants repeatedly shared the difference it made in their lives to know they had a consistent space to mourn.


“In daily life, when something hurts, I turn away, I distract myself,” one participant told us. “But the collective mourning practice helped me move through the frozenness that constant news induced — helped me stop doomscrolling — and I’m able to return to my work.”


That participant went on to organize her community and raised $20,000 for refugees in Gaza. 


Another participant returned to their role as a chaplain, and extended her work to include “movement chaplaincy” holding one-on-one spaces for people doing solidarity work. 


Many participants also shared how witnessing the news with others enabled them to feel the emotions provoked by the headlines, leaving them feeling less isolated and more connected. That is co-regulation happening at …

author: Aallyah Wright
title: Organizers Are Pushing to Reach “Forgotten” Black Voters Ahead of the Midterms
content:
The efforts target college students, first-time voters, and the formerly incarcerated, particularly in the South.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Kamora Greggs returned to her college campus with voting on her mind. She’d just visited her home in Jackson, Mississippi, about three hours away, when her mom encouraged her to exercise her right.

“And don’t have anybody change your mind about what you want to do,” Greggs recalled.

As a first time voter, the 19-year-old health and kinesiology major wanted to know more about the process, the role of government, and hear directly from her peers about why they thought voting is important.

She and dozens of other Coahoma Community College students participated in a September town hall – playing games like Levels, learning history and the power of the ballot box — at their school in Clarksdale.

“It’s a good way to learn with your friends,” Greggs said. “It really impacted me and made me want to actually get out there and spread the word and make sure other people my age know that it’s a good idea to get registered to vote.”

With Election Day just weeks away, the experience is part of the Voting Is No Laughing Matter Tour. Rita Brent, an Emmy-winning comedian from Jackson, partnered with the Southern Poverty Law Center to host the five-stop campus initiative, which aims to empower students at the ballot box.

“To witness young people who are not only civically engaged but genuinely concerned about the state of our communities, our country, and the world gives me tremendous hope,” Brent said. “Their passion for justice, thirst for knowledge and their commitment to creating meaningful change remind me that our future is in capable hands.”

It mirrors renewed energy in civic engagement nationwide. It is one of several efforts focused on what some are calling the forgotten voters: college students, first-time voters, and the formerly incarcerated.

In another effort to mobilize younger voters, companies and groups transformed campus spaces into art installations, alongside on-site voter registration. And in North Carolina, a group is working to engage more with formerly incarcerated people who don’t always utilize their right to vote.

Since the weakening of the Voting Rights Act, attention has shifted to the South, where many communities are underserved, organizers told Capital B. The region is both a battleground and testing ground for voting rights. Decades of voter suppression, gerrymandering or redistricting, and landmark decisions such as Louisiana v. Callais have shaped the current political landscape.

In Mississippi, citizens don’t have an option when it comes to whether to vote or not, said Waikinya Clanton, the state’s director for the SPLC. Despite the decline in voter participation, it’s more about conditions, racism, and restricting access and opportunity.

In the Magnolia State, an appeals court recently refused to overturn a centuries-old lifetime voting ban for those with certain felony convictions, which was embedded in the state’s constitution. Nearly 60% of people who lost their right under this law were Black. Mississippi also does not offer early voting or drop boxes.

“So many people have felt disillusioned by the fact that they don’t feel like their vote matters. It can be depressing for people who are really trying to find their way out,” Clanton said. “For folks to be working so adamantly to make people feel like their votes don’t matter, that’s a problem.”

Over the past five years, 86 million eligible voters — about one-third nationwide — live in states that have passed more restrictive voting and election-related laws, according to a new report by the Movement Advancement Project. It is disproportionately impacting Black adults in the South, said Brian Hinkle, author of the report and senior democracy program manager for MAP.

“It was really striking that we saw that the Americans who live in the states with the most restrictive voting laws are disproportionately Black. While that was also true in 2021, the proportion has nearly doubled in the last five years, from 27% to over 48%,” Hinkle said.

According to the MAP report, the 2020 election and subsequent Jan. 6 attack prompted an unprecedented wave of state legislation limiting voter access. For example, 13 states passed laws that gave state legislatures the power to interfere …
