title: Abogados del caso Lautaro presentaron recurso de nulidad de sentencia en la Corte de Apelaciones de Temuco
content:
El día jueves 15 de octubre se llevó a cabo la vista de los recursos de nulidad que las defensas de Pelentaro Llaitul, Jorge Caniupil, Juan Carlos Mardones, Luis Menares Chanilao, para que la Corte de Apelaciones invalide la sentencia definitiva del Tribunal Oral de Temuco, que el pasado 13 de julio de este año resolvió condenarlos por ataques incendiarios ocurridos en noviembre del 2022 en dos fundos cercanos a Lautaro, y posteriormente la quema de una camioneta en el sector de Cholchol.


Se solicita a la corte de apelaciones que invalide de sentencia y que dicte sentencia de reemplazo, porque la defensa considera errores jurídicos como condenar dos veces por un mismo delito, o por delitos que no fueron realmente demostrados y considera que están cumpliendo adicionalmente penas que fueron mucho más altas que las que en derecho correspondían.


Según Marco Oñate Escobar, uno de los abogados defensores:


“

Este es un proceso muy sesgado que se llevó a cabo en contra de ellos, solo por ser perteneciente a la Coordinadora Arauco Malleco.


En el juicio oral se pedían penas, que en la sumatoria llegaban casi a 100 años en algunos de los casos. La fiscalía, esta es la historia que no cuentan ellos, fueron derrotados en más de la mitad de sus imputaciones, se recalificaron las figuras penales más gravosas, era una supuesta flagrancia, y entonces intentaron imputar delitos lo máximo que se pudiera a fin de incrementar y elevar las penas y que sean penas de cárcel. Situación que, si bien es cierto, hay condenas, son notoriamente bajas si hacemos un cálculo, una relación con lo que se pedía al comienzo”.


Palabras de Ernesto Llaitul, werken de los presos políticos Mapuche de la CAM:


“

N

osotros, como organización y como comunidades en lucha, he

mos


sido enfático

s


en decir que esto se debe a una persecución política en contra de militantes Mapuche, del movimiento Mapuche


a

utonomista, en específico de nuestra organización, de la coordinadora


Arauco Malleco.


El día de hoy, nosotros no acatamos el fallo, la sentencia condenatoria, no reconocemos tampoco la existencia, la participación de nuestros peñis en este hecho, pero hacemos esta alegación política, como muy bien lo dice el abogado, en relación a circunstancias técnicas o prácticas en las que nosotros tenemos hoy día que desenvolvernos dentro de lo que exige la ley”.


Familiares y comunidad se mantendrán a la espera de que la corte, el día 4 de noviembre de 2026, a las 8 de la mañana, comunique la sentencia donde se acojan los recursos presentados.

author: Andrés
title: No soy amigo de los que cooperan, los quiero fuera fuera fuera
content:
La pierna de un jubilado que cae por el chorro de un hidramte


La decadencia moral y generalizada de un país se mide por la cantidad de recursos empleados en contra de la propia población, y de la vida misma. Que todo gobierno autoritario invierte onerosos recursos en las Armas es un hecho más que probado. De lo que se habla bastante menos es que en países donde el trabajo formal se viene erosionando desde hace tanto, los puestos en las policías y fuerzas armadas los ocupan en amplia mayoría las clases socioeconómicas más vulnerables. Y entonces la extorsión del trabajo estable opera sobre los sujetos al punto de quebrar todo principio, cortar los trazos democráticos y convertir a los “servidores del orden” en cómplices de un poder que no los quiere más que dentro de una institución cuyo funcionamiento mafioso los subordina, los presiona. Y en muchos casos termina descerebrándolos al punto en que ni siquiera pueden abrir los ojos ante la traición que cometen cada vez que apuntan un arma, empuñan un palo, empujan a un compatriota, golpean a un viejo, gasean a una niña, ahorcan entre varios a un hombre solo, disparan a un joven, lo esconden, gasean a la población y lastiman toda posibilidad de concordia. El todos contra todos y cada uno contra sí mismo está a la orden del día bajo esta gestión fascista.

Por Andrés Manrique (ANRed).


El  jubilado golpeado por la presión del hidrante, apuntado por la Policía Federal


Quienes cobran para ir a pegar, disparar y ahogar a estudiantes, a discapacitados, a viejos se cuentan entre lo más bajo de los traidores. Si era el último círculo, cuando además se detenta la fuerza física, se suma una vuelta más.


“Vos te pasaste al otro lado de la vereda”


Tirarle gas a un viejo de camperita, empujarlo.


Pegarle con el puño a toda carrera y por la espalda a un fotorreportero en la cara.


Echarle la moto de alta cilindrada a alguien que va en paz por la vereda.


La Policía Federal agolpeando con el hidrante al jubilado de espaldas


Acorralar a dos fotógrafos en un zaguán y dispararle a quemarropa: contra el abdomen, a las piernas, a la cabeza: en la cara y a los ojos.


Clavarte la rodilla en la espalda cuando estás en el piso, boca abajo, desarmado, reducido por el sobrepeso de aquel al que un trote lo haría infartar, mientras otro te lastima las muñecas con el precinto, y un tercero apoya todo su odio contra las vértebras de tu cuello.


Amedrentar con los escudos, con las tonfas, acelerando las motos, haciendo chasquear las  escopetas, con  bombas de estruendo, postas de goma y armas mal llamadas no letales, con las que no se cansan de matar o herir de gravedad. Revolear bastones, batiendo el aerosol de gas pimienta sobre la cara de una nena, de una anciana, de una vecina que pierde su  bolsa de compras.


“Esa es la diferencia entre la gorra y la visera”


Gasear a pibes con carteles, irse encima de discapacitados. Golpear con la escopeta, salir a cazar a compatriotas que protestan. Salir a cazar fantasmas en manada. Seguir órdenes, aunque vayan en contra de todos los principios. Golpear a alguien indefenso, lastimar entre muchos a uno solo.


Miserable soldadesca del brazo tilingo del poder que nos ahoga. Dése vuelta, reconozca dónde está su enemigo. Identifiquelo, usted sabe que la mano que le pone el sueldo es la misma que lo va a someter a la mazmorra cuando no sirva más.


¿Más traidor que un desclasado?


¿Peor traidor que alguien al que han entrenado para que se odie a sí tanto que odia a todo el que tiene a su alrededor?

author: Redação
title: Treme Terra: um Data Center chegando à Amazônia
content:
17 de outubro de 2026 · Primeiro data center de IA da Amazônia avança em Belém sem licenciamento ambiental e preocupa por poluição sonora

Em junho de 2026, a empresa Elea Data Centers anunciou a construção do primeiro primeiro data center de inteligência artificial da Amazônia, que será instalado em Belém. A poluição sonora contínua está entre as preocupações que cercam o projeto — que até aqui avança sem licenciamento ambiental. No mesmo território, pulsa um outro som com um quê futurista que, no entanto, é marcado pela marginalização: a aparelhagem. E aí, quem pode fazer barulho?

author: Darío Aranda
title: Las cuentas no cierran en Vaca Muerta: la fuga de dólares que oculta el relato extractivo
content:
Por Natalia Concina


La explotación de Vaca Muerta permitió el ingreso al país de casi dos mil millones de dólares entre lo que vendió y lo que pidió como préstamo durante 2026. Lejos de quedarse en el país,

esas divisas volvieron al exterior y le permitieron a las empresas petroleras y de diferentes rubros fugar sus ganancias

. Un nuevo estudio del grupo de investigación EJES confirma que el yacimiento de petróleo no convencional permite hoy sostener la estabilidad cambiaria, pero

consolida a los sectores de poder concentrado y genera una millonaria deuda a futuro

.


Durante la primera parte del año, las empresas que explotan Vaca Muerta pidieron préstamos por 936 millones de dólares mensuales promedio, una cifra incluso superior a las divisas que generaron por las ventas al exterior de hidrocarburos (que rondaron en un promedio de 754 millones por mes).


Esta inyección de divisas extranjeras es la que garantiza hoy la estabilidad cambiaria, es decir, que el precio de la moneda estadounidense esté más o menos estable. Sin embargo,

los dólares que ingresan por el endeudamiento privado son un problema para toda la sociedad

 porque —a futuro— utilizarán los dólares que genera toda la economía. ¿Por qué? Porque para cancelar sus deudas la empresas comprarán los dólares disponibles en el Banco Central, que a su vez ingresarán por las exportaciones u otros mecanismo (como podría ser esta de toma de deuda).


En otras palabras, Vaca Muerta permite hoy la “sostenibilidad” del modelo a través de estos dólares de los que se nutren, además de las empresas petroleras, los sectores corporativos más concentrados de la economía local para remitir sus ganancias al exterior, un proceso que se intensificó desde diciembre pasado.

Una especie de puerta giratoria de dólares

, aunque las deudas quedan.


Foto: Martín Álvarez Mullally


Estas conclusiones son los pilares más importantes d

el informe “

¿A dónde van los dólares de Vaca Muerta”,


el tercer estudio realizado por el Enlace por la Justicia Energética y Socioambiental (EJES)”

, una articulación de organizaciones que desde 2024 analiza sistemáticamente los números del yacimiento no convencional en forma crítica, exponiendo sus implicancias ocultas detrás del supuesto boom energético.


“El análisis de los datos del Banco Central de 2025 y lo que va de 2026 permite consolidar dos miradas respecto a Vaca Muerta: por un lado, que su función es traer dólares y no se está pensando en eslabonar un conjunto de actividades económicas a partir del yacimiento; por el otro, que

lo único que dejará al país son deudas

”, asegura a Tierra Viva el economista Marco Kofman, autor del trabajo.


¿A dónde van los dólares de Vaca Muerta? - EJES


Récord de ventas


En los primeros cinco meses de 2026, el país exportó 314.000 barriles diarios de petróleo, acumulando un total de 3.773 millones de dólares, lo que da un promedio de 754 millones por mes. No sólo se aumentó la cantidad de crudo sino que coincidió con un precio internacional relativamente elevado.


De las diez primeras empresas que comercializan internacionalmente el crudo argentino, hay cinco que exportan más del 50 por ciento de su producción local. Respecto al gas de Vaca Muerta, se vende al exterior sólo entre el cuatro y el cinco por ciento.


Pese a la orientación exportadora, el informe destaca que en los últimos años Argentina disminuyó la importación de hidrocarburos drásticamente, parte por la producción de Vaca Muerta, parte por la crisis en la producción local. En ese contexto, la balanza comercial energética (diferencia entre la compra y la venta de petróleo y gas) es favorable para la Argentina, que pasó de estar en rojo a tener un superávit de 3.000 millones de dólares acumulado sólo en los primeros cinco meses de 2026.


“A este ingreso de dólares por ventas (dólares comerciales),

se le suman los dólares financieros, es decir los que ingresan por toma de deuda de las empresas


que funcionan como un respirador artificial del modelo de Milei

y le permite que el dólar se mantenga estable, sin tener que devaluar ni poner controles cambiarios”, explica Kofman.


Foto: Depositphotos


El trabajo de EJES explica que de los 22.617 millones de dólares que el sector privado ingresó al país por la vía del endeudamiento, 14.441 millones —casi el 64 por ciento del total— fueron aportados por las empresas energéticas; en los primeros cinco meses del año, ese endeudamiento fue de 936 millones de dólares promedio …

author: La Zarzamora
title: DESPEDIR A JUAN…
content:
Esta mañana nuestro compañero Juan Aliste Vega ha partido de su cuerpo, cuerpo que el poder mantuvo en encierro los últimos 16 años, cuerpo que practicó el conflicto y lo materializó en acciones armadas, que acompañó su vida en el álgido recorrido de ser él. Fue en el hospital penitenciario de Santiago, donde en compañia y calma, se fugó definitivamente.

Aún no podemos confirmar donde ni como será su despedida, ló que sí sabemos es que serán muchas, en muchos territorios, en las calles, en los puentes, en las jaulas, en avenidas y carreteras.

Juan Aliste es y será reivindicado, pese a los esfuerzos incansables de la prensa del enemigo y de sus múltiples intentos de desprestigiarlo, nosotrxs sus compañerxs sabemos que en este momento estamos despidiendo a un guerrero de gran envergadura. Pese a sus miserables conjunciones de palabras, el mundo sabe quien es Juan y en todos los territorios se levantará fuego en su memoria.

Que desesperanza deben sentir los poderosos, al saber que amamos pese a estar en guerra, que nuestra historia es escrita por nosotrxs, pese a sus asquerosos relatos oficiales, tan indignos como ellos mismos.

Hoy es un día de nuestra propia historia, hoy parte el guerrero combatiente que se alzó en armas contra la dictadura y la pestilente democracia de burgueses y traidores, el que no se dejó abatir, el que atacó y acertó, el que siguió compartiendo conocimientos y enseñanzas pese al encierro, el que enviaba notas y saludos, el que hacía llegar sus palabras a actividades y espacios.

Cada vez es más difícil despedir, esto no es una noticia, ni tampoco un comunicado, es nuestro adiós a un hermano…

A nosotrxs ahora nos quedará volver a mirarnos, tensionar el encierro de nuestrxs compañerxs, cuestionarnos y autocriticarnos, dejar de hacernos tolerantes al encarcelamiento, dejar de normalizar la sociedad carcelaria y hacer. Arduo camino nos dejas.

Juan que tu fuga sea eterna querido compañero.

Ternura y ataque frontal por ti y por todxs nuestrxs muertxs.

title: Revista Crítica Anticapitalista 6 – La Comuna, la clase y la lucha de clases
content:
PRESENTACION


¿Qué relación existe entre la Comuna como forma política de la emancipación social y la clase, entendida ésta no como categoría positivizada y sociológica, sino en su carácter dual y contradictorio? ¿Es la Comuna una manera de entender la clase y la lucha de clases en clave no identitaria, no positivizada? ¿La oposición entre Comuna y clase es algo derivado de una concepción anti-dialéctica de la lucha de clases? En ese campo ¿a qué dialéctica nos referimos? ¿A la dialéctica hegeliana orientada a la síntesis estatal como forma política de la identidad? ¿A la dialéctica negativa que la cuestiona? ¿La lucha de clases, entendida en clave dialéctica no-identitaria, permite entender la Comuna como proceso contradictorio de disolución de la clase? ¿Implica esto un desafío a nuestro concepto de proletariado y a la idea de revolución calcada en el canon leninista?

author: Rizomatica
title: 83,000 hectáreas, 400 familias y 150 actores colectivos consolidan inclusión y participación relevante: Destacan al espacio costero (ECMPO) Mañihueico-Huinay
content:
La microserie «Zonas de Resguardo» estrenó su tercer capítulo sobre el ECMPO Mañihueico-Huinay, el espacio costero más extenso del sur de Chile, con 83.000 hectáreas, 400 familias y 150 convenios de uso. Por su parte, el geógrafo Álvaro Montaña destaca que la ley permite incluir a múltiples usuarios y genera un nuevo equilibrio de poder.


La ECMPO más grande del sur de Chile


El Espacio Costero Marino de Pueblos Originarios (ECMPO) Mañihueico-Huinay, en Hualaihué, es el más extenso del sur de Chile: 83.833 hectáreas de mar, 16 años de tramitación, decenas de organizaciones incluidas y 9.368 personas viviendo en su entorno. La Ley 20.249 permite que comunidades indígenas administren un espacio costero y que otras organizaciones locales participen como usuarios del mar, según establece el artículo 11. Pesca, choritos, algas, mariscos y turismo forman parte de la economía y la vida de Hualaihué, y la pregunta que surge es qué significa esto para el futuro del mar en Chile.


La inclusión como cambio de paradigma


Consultado al geógrafo Álvaro Montaña, quien desde Chiloé ha apoyado técnicamente algunos procesos de Espacios Costeros

, señala: «El artículo 11 de la ley que crea los espacios marinos costeros de pueblos originarios establece algo que es inédito en las figuras de administración territorial de la playa y el mar de Chile. Permite la inclusión. Si bien esta ley surge por una demanda de las comunidades indígenas y solo puede ser invocada por ellas, en la administración de los espacios marinos, las comunidades indígenas pueden integrar a otros usuarios. Juntas de vecinos, comités productivos, escuelas, centros de investigación, personas naturales, empresas, ya una serie de actores que se vinculan al uso y al manejo de los recursos del mar».


Montaña agrega que esto «sin duda genera un nuevo equilibrio de poder en la administración territorial de la playa y el mar porque transfiere poder a las comunidades locales, quienes hacen la gobernanza, toman las decisiones sobre el uso de sus espacios comunes». Y sostiene: «Este es, a mi juicio, uno de los aportes principales de la ley de los espacios costeros marinos de pueblos originarios porque permite esta inclusión de usuarios. Y a mi juicio, el espacio costero de Mañihueico-Huinay es un ejemplo, un modelo en el sur de Chile de cómo la ley de espacios costeros integra y da cabida a orilleros, pescadores, buzos, armadores y una serie de organizaciones sociales, culturales, ambientales y productivas que conviven a orillas del mar».


Vivir en una isla: la voz de Yohana Coñuecar


En el marco del tercer capítulo de la microserie

«

Zonas de Resguardo

«

, Yohana Coñuecar Llancapani,

destacada dirigenta, relata su experiencia: «Es algo que es muy difícil de explicar, pero muy fácil de sentir. Que esa relación con el mar en ningún rato se corta. Está ahí, constante, latiendo como la sangre, como del corazón». Yohana vive en la isla Llanchid, en la comunidad AdMapu kaLafken, en el espacio territorial de los Coñuecar Llancapani. «Vivir en una isla es único, así que los desafíos que implica vivir acá sean siempre constantes», dice.


«Nosotros dependemos del mar», afirma. «El hecho de vivir en una isla implica que tu única conexión con el mundo exterior es a través de la navegación. El hecho de que se pueda bajar a mariscar cuando quieras comer una cazuela de marisco, un curanto, no sé. Vas al mar, no vas al mercado, aquí vas al mar directo a buscar los recursos. Y además porque toda la gente de acá sabe dónde están los recursos. Dónde están las almejas, dónde están las chorras, dónde ir a buscar choritos, dónde ir a buscar piures, qué sé yo. Entonces hay un conocer constante de la gente de la isla sobre nuestro propio espacio».


Sobre el ECMPO, detalla: «El espacio costero Mañihueico-Huinay es un espacio costero de 83.833 hectáreas. Y como es un espacio costero como de fiordos, es el espacio costero más grande otorgado en el sur de Chile». Y agrega: «Este espacio costero reconoce a 150 actores, algunos individuales y otros más en organizaciones. Así que tiene una inclusión importante de pensamiento local. El uso de la habitabilidad habla en el fondo de un uso histórico de vivir cerca del mar. Que implica no solamente tener la casa cerca del mar, sino que es tener la casa y todos los elementos necesarios para vivir. Y eso que hoy día esté acreditado y puesto como un derecho, no nos habla solamente de un derecho presente, también habla de un derecho futuro».

author: anred
title: Apuntes apurados tras la movilización frente al Congreso: “En algún momento hay que pegar el salto”
content:
El textual del título, “En algún momento hay que pegar el salto”, fue dicho por un estudiante de secundaria (16 o 17 años) que estaba en la marcha frente al Congreso (ver video adjunto). Más precisamente, estas fueron sus palabras, cuando la represión ya se había desatado: “Es lógico tener miedo, pero en algún momento hay que pegar el salto y empezar a combatir, hacer lo que haga falta”. Uno de sus compañeros agregó: “Somos hijos de trabajadores, es importante que peleemos por todos”. Como toda persona medianamente informada, los pibes sabían lo que iba a pasar: el gobierno ordenaría una represión para meter miedo, como parte de su apuesta estratégica que es quebrar la voluntad de lucha del pueblo, desmovilizar. Esta vez, sin embargo, la jornada tuvo su particularidad. Hay elementos auspiciosos, a pesar del fracaso parlamentario en el intento de voltear el DNU 12/70 y la prepotencia gubernamental. Estos son algunos puntos fuertes que no debemos dejar pasar. Por Pablo Solana | Reporte Ancora / Imagen Andres Manrique


1. Conflicto universitario I: no fueron solo marchas.

 La toma del Palacio Pizzurno el 7 de octubre sorprendió al gobierno y envalentonó a los estudiantes. Entraron por la fuerza, mantuvieron una sentada y forzaron a las autoridades a atender el reclamo, todo en medio de un esquema de seguridad desbordado por el efecto sorpresa y por la decisión del grupo que planificó la toma. Con ese antecedente, se llegó al día 15 con asambleas en decenas de universidades, tomas en unas cuantas y no solo de Buenos Aires, vigilias, sentadas y semaforazos en colegios en distintas ciudades. En una lucha encabezada por dirigentes del sector poco propensos a la confrontación, la acción directa por abajo gana espacio.


2. Conflicto universitario II: ya nadie está a salvo.

 Un análisis más o menos compartido hasta ahora decía que el gobierno sabía que no era el mismo costo si reprimía a desocupados o jubilados revoltosos, que si se metía con la comunidad universitaria; que había un factor de clase (media, pequeño burguesa) que de algún modo “protegía” las movilizaciones por la universidad pública. Bueno, eso ya no pasa. A diferencia de las cuatro anteriores, esta marcha fue enfrentada sin contemplación. ¿Cuánto falta para que se animen a reprimir, también, una marcha por el 24 de marzo?


3. La movilización se sostiene a pesar de los gases.

 Ya venía pasando en marchas anteriores, pero esta vez la consistencia de la movilización popular se plasmó en una imagen poco habitual. Además del activismo que resiste, de la “juventud revueltista” que se va forjando en cada enfrentamiento con la cana, en el Congreso esta vez convivió el acto de la Universidad con escenas de enfrentamientos en paralelo, a pocos metros, sobre Hirigoyen y sobre Rivadavia. Los dirigentes de la FUA terminaron el acto lagrimeando por los gases. Si hace un año el Frente de Sindicatos Unidos, Fresu, había instalado un palco casi sobre avenida de Mayo para distanciarse de los revoltosos, esta vez el escenario estuvo lejos de las vallas, pero ocupando el centro de la Plaza. Es saludable la decisión de ocupar el espacio público pese a la certeza represiva, más allá de las críticas a la dirigencia de las Universidades.


4. “Es importante que peleemos por todo”.

 La convocatoria universitaria fue central, pero también estuvo en agenda la defensa de la Ley de Tierras (desdibujada por el paso atrás de la Corte), la Emergencia en Discapacidad, y la posibilidad de voltear el DNU 70/12. Por fuera de las agrupaciones estudiantiles y las columnas universitarias, se vio una cantidad importante de manifestantes que estaban allí “por todo”. El antecedente de la Marcha de la Bronca no es circunstancial: aún no es masivo, pero crece un ánimo de confrontación política en las calles contra el gobierno, que no se ciñe a tal o cual “defensa” reivindicativa puntual.


5. “Empezar a combatir, hacer lo que haga falta”.

 Dicha por un pibe de colegio, la frase debe ser puesta en su contexto y en la perspectiva de largo plazo. Pero la claridad de esa sentencia no se limita al activismo estudiantil que se va radicalizando. El enfrentamiento a la represión es cada vez más organizado. La influencia de la revuelta chilena gana espacio: esta vez se vieron baldes apaga-gases y guantes para devolverlos, a ambos lados de la plaza; también aparecieron músicos trompetistas, no ya en las columnas, sino acompañando al activismo de la resistencia: dando ánimo a quienes combaten. Esa mística …

title: Four DEM Party Youth Council members detained in Mardin
content:
Turkish police detained four members of the DEM Party’s Youth Council during house raids in the central district of Artuklu in Mardin on Friday evening. Those detained were identified as Mahsum Çalhan, Serhat Akpınar, Abdulkadir Elmas, and Bilal Elmas.

The detentions were reportedly linked to the hanging of a banner. The four young men were taken to police headquarters. After interrogations at the police headquarters, they were brought before the prosecutor’s office on allegations of “making propaganda for an illegal organization.”

The four young men were then released under judicial supervision.

author: rti_admin
title: The IITs: Tragic Failures That Beget More Tragedies
content:
From a social perspective, the IITs are tragic failures that beget more tragedies.

But you already know the IITs are the pinnacle of Indian aspirations, achievements, accolades, blah-di-blah, right? How about we celebrate by taking a closer look at the graduates, the faculty, and the institution?

The institutional charter, briefly. The IITs were conceived in 1946 to support the country’s industrial development and help meet the nation’s technological challenges. Parliament’s 1961 Act declares them institutions of national importance. It charges them with instruction and research, and with the advancement of learning and dissemination of knowledge. The same Act says every institute shall be open to persons of either sex and of whatever race, creed, caste or class, in admitting or appointing students and teachers alike. [1] Later laws reserve seats for SC, ST and OBC students, PhD seats included, and, since 2019, teaching posts at every rank.

Start with the product. As any IIT alum would confirm, a majority of IIT graduates wouldn’t be able to properly describe what ‘engineering’ is. Poorly educated and narrowly conditioned to chase status from a young age, most of them used to end up in finance or as middle management in US IT firms, but have lately diversified into mercenary ouroboros via IIT coaching and YouTube influencing. The institute’s own numbers: in IIT Bombay’s placement report for 2023–24, 29% of offers were in engineering and technology. The rest went to IT, consulting, finance, analytics and “other”. [2]

The defence is usually the famous founders. Let’s do the math. Seats went from about 2k a year in the 80s to about 20k now, so total grads ~400k. Unicorn founders ~117, high value startup founders maybe four thousand if you’re generous. So, 0.03% and 1%. [3, 4] Like unicorns, these founders are statistical anomalies. Sensible folks within the system will themselves readily acknowledge that their success is mostly despite it rather than because of it. And given the stated mission, funnelling billions in public subsidy into private equity accumulation for a minuscule minority is cause for shame rather than something to tom-tom about.

This is the deal then. Ruin your childhood to join an exclusive band of svayambhu achievers. Concoct jagatguru-brand gig economy “innovations” for exploiting cheap labor. Garland each other for contributions to the economic miracle of jobless growth and extractive digital feudalism. Parade your arrogant indifference or offer defensive apologies for the mockery of a social contract, dressed up in a lazy pragmatism argument about success.

By the way, who’s even there to teach them? Across all 23 IITs, 4,804 of 12,498 sanctioned teaching posts stood vacant in January 2026, or 38.4%. [5] It was 38.3% in December 2022. [6] In the nine IITs that disclosed the breakdown, about 60% of the empty posts were reserved ones. [5] Cryogenic sthiratva.

Sour grapes? I was there, eating them for four lost years. So chill. First week in the hostel, the rank was a common icebreaker question you asked people along with where they were from and in what department. Some hesitant answers made me stop asking. Only the rare, confident stud would openly declare he was SC, came through the preparatory course etc. The term in use was ‘schaddu’, and people would murmur in the early semesters, but soon some of them were ahead on GPA, and the murmurs lost voice. Years later, a friend who got a PhD mentioned feeling conflicted using reservations since their father was also a PhD and they went to good schools. Not long ago, an alum stated that even though they got in via reservation, everything after was earned by merit. I couldn’t make out if this was being defensive or proud. I don’t remember hearing of any campus suicides, and only learned about them from ‘The Death of Merit’ documentary. [7]

A decade after graduation and on another continent, the sourness still stung, in an interview by another pitiable alum. I was struggling for purpose and careening across career lanes. Unusual for an IIT grad, and he got suspicious… maybe I was a ‘category candidate’? So he asked for my rank, and then I asked for his, and then he said that’s not relevant, and then I agreed, and the interview went downhill. So, no chill.

Then the people who run the place. Do the IITs still hire blatantly sexist dogs as professors? It used to be de rigueur in several departments. A lot of the students were of a similar breed …

author: groundxero
title: Another One Bites the Dust: Construction Workers’ Not So Quiet Battle For Survival Ahead of Delhi’s Long Winter
content:
The ‘annual ban’ on construction work through the winter seasons in Delhi that has become tradition over the last half a decade due to an acute air pollution crisis in the city, has this year, become a starvation sentence.


 


by

Mouli Sharma


 


15 October 2026, New Delhi:

 The rain falls in sheets on Thursday morning, ice cold and sudden like it can only get during mid-October weeks as Autumn bleeds into Winter. The wide, planned roads of Delhi’s Civil Lines region don’t flood quite so much as Shankar Road and its tributaries (or, god forbid, Gurgaon) but it’s enough to drench the lower halves of even the umbrella havers stuck underneath foot-over bridges and bus stops. 


 


Needless to say, the roads are abandoned. At the T-Point facing the DRDO office, a lone rickshaw puller stops abruptly, shivering as he holds the thin gamchha protecting his head tighter over him and runs to the shelter of the bridge. I stand there, too. Water has been steadily gathering at the top, and has now begun flooding down the stairs, soaking his sandalled feet and into my socks and shoes. When the rain slows, for a minute, I make to leave, aiming for the bus stop 50 metres away in case it starts up again.


 


The rickshaw puller warns me not to do that. I tell him I have somewhere to be. He asks me where I’m trying to go. I tell him there’s a protest today at Vikas Bhawan. 


 


“Look at the weather. No one’s protesting in the middle of this. Only a lunatic would be out there today.”


 


He is, of course, wrong. 


***


 


At Thursday noon, nearly 50 construction workers led a march from Vikas Bhawan to the Sushruta Trauma Centre, led by the AICCTU’s Building Workers’ Union, many of them travelling from faraway districts like Burari and Okhla. This was ahead of an announcement by the Delhi government that construction work in the city would be banned for a period of three months between November and January, ostensibly due to air pollution concerns, except the Supreme Court’s directions that such a blanket ban on work must be accompanied by the provision of minimum wages to aggrieved workers are not only nowhere close to being fulfilled, but are in fact being violated for a consecutive season since the Rekha Gupta led BJP came to power in 2025. 


 


“The Welfare board website has been down for nearly four months now,” said Ranjan Kuswaha, a mason and secretary of the local Burari unit of the Building Workers’ Union. “They said they were making a new one. And now that they have, they’ve already announced a seasonal ban less than two weeks away, beginning on November 1st and ending on January 31st. And till now this website is taking neither new registrations nor renewals. How on earth is the worker supposed to survive?”


 


Kushwaha further highlighted the plight of the migrant worker, so many of whom come to Delhi to work contractually on the many building and developmental projects undertaken here annually, who will now be left destitute. 


 


Advocate Surya Prakash Union said that a majority of the workers associated with the BWU hail from Supaul and Saharsa, two of Bihar’s poorest districts. 


“Most of our workers come from the poorest regions,” Surya Prakash, AICCTU; Infographic via BWU.


“We demand that this website be fixed at the earliest, and that registrations and renewals be completed as soon as possible and the workers be provided their labour cards,” Kuswaha said. 


 


There is also the matter of alleged gross corruption within this “welfare board” itself—the Delhi Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board (DBoCWWB), an organisation founded in 2002 in reference to the 1996 BoCW Act, which is apparently as much of a handful as it as a mouthful, according to the workers whose welfare it proclaims to oversee.


 


“On paper, the welfare framework for Delhi’s construction workers promises them wide-ranging support in almost all spheres of life: from maternity care, pension, housing, healthcare, education and even free daily commute on govt buses,” wrote Ishita Jairath for the Times of India in her scathing January 2026 report,

Hands That Build Delhi Brick By Brick Out Of Welfare Framework. 


 


The ground reality, however, was that the intended beneficiaries she asked about the schemes meant for them had nothing more than a “blank look”.


 


“Bitto, a marble and tile worker from Mangolpuri, didn’t know his children are eligible for education assistance,” Jairath wrote. “Preeti, a …

author: Brian Hioe
title: In A First, China Sanctions Ministers of Diplomatic Allies of Taiwan
content:
THE CHINESE GOVERNMENT has sanctioned two government ministers from diplomatic allies of Taiwan. These would be Belizean Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca and Paraguayan Minister of Information Gustavo Villate. Such sanctions prevent them and their family members from doing business in China.

China does not appear to have sanctioned ministers of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies in the past. This would be a new means, then, of pressuring countries to switch ties from Taiwan to China.

Taiwan is larger than all of its diplomatic allies, whether measured in terms of the size of population or economy. The main reason why Taiwan maintains ties with its diplomatic allies is so that they can speak up for it in international organizations in which Taiwan is not a member.

That being said, Taiwan has also long been accused of “dollar diplomacy”–paying off diplomatic allies through infrastructure investment deals or slush money to high-ranking politicians in return for recognition. Indeed, one notes that many of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies are countries that have questionable human rights records.

Though China offers much the same to such allies in return for switching recognition, Taiwan is unable to outspend China. China is, of course, much larger than Taiwan. Likewise, small states risk being shut ouf of the lucrative–and much larger–Chinese market if they retain ties with Taiwan.

At times, the question of whether to maintain ties with Taiwan or break them in favor of Taiwan is a dividing issue between the two major political parties of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies. Another question for such countries, however, is that of ties with the US. The US does not diplomatically recognize Taiwan either, but it has in the past sought to shore up Taiwan’s existing diplomatic allies, maintaining ties with it. Indeed, one notes that Taiwan’s existing diplomatic allies are often also closer to the US, rather than China, and this proves another means of the US extending its influence in Latin and Central America, or among Pacific states.

The Chinese government has sanctioned American government officials such as Marco Rubio in the past, over hawkish stances on China, criticism of China’s human rights record, and support for Hong Kong. It may not be surprising to see China targeting government officials of countries that express support for Taiwan, then. This would follow up on how sanctions on Taiwanese government officials may in themselves be ineffective, seeing as such individuals and their family members may already know better than to do business in China. But it is not impossible that some of those that China eventually targets do, in fact, have business holdings in China. As such, it is to be seen whether this proves an effective means of pressure on diplomatic allies of Taiwan.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Marcos Congress set to pass another corrupt budget, progressives warn
content:
Progressive legislators expressed alarm over the 2027 national budget passed by the House of Representatives (HOR) on Monday, saying it is the opposite of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s promise of cleaner government spending.


“The Marcos budget they are passing is not a budget for Filipinos. It only funds politicians, political dynasties and war and militarism against our people,” the Makabayan Coalition lawmakers said in voting against the measure.


The HOR approved a P7.2-trillion budget for next year, the biggest in the country’s history. With a few alterations to accommodate pet projects of Marcos allies in the chamber, the total amount followed the national expenditure program earlier submitted by Marcos.


How did the budget pass so quickly?


Marcos allies control the HOR. Led by a Speaker loyal to the president and persuaded by the Senior Deputy Speaker who happens to be Marcos’ eldest son Sandro, 282 legislators agreed to the proposed budget.


Only 13 voted against the proposal while a lone representative abstained.


The HOR glowingly described the approved budget as a

 “

boost to public education and health, as well as the country’s preparations for El Niño” now starting to affect the Southeast Asian country.


Opponents of the measure, however, said Marcos’ budget is meant to continue both patronage politics and corruption the Philippine government is notorious for.


Who opposed Marcos’ planned budget?


Of the 254 district representatives of the Philippines Congress – as many as 80 per cent of whom are members of political dynasties – only five voted against the measure. Eight of their fellow oppositionists are party representatives, led by the three members of the progressive Makabayan Coalition.


The few HOR members who opposed the “porky” 2027 proposed General Appropriations Act. (HOR photo)


ACT Teachers Representative Antonio Tinio pointed out that while the Marcos proposal already reduced the budget for public health, the president’s allies further reduced Department of Health’s budget. He said funds on health facilities and equipment, commodities for family health, immunization, nutrition and responsible parenting, Health Promotion and Quick Response Fund would be reduced by billions of pesos.


Tinio also revealed that funds for education would be substantially cut, impacting construction and renovation of classrooms as well as the country’s school computerization program


Contrary to government claims the budget factors in effects of the El Niño, government’s calamity fund was also reduced by P9.5 billion, Tinio revealed.


What does the Marcos budget contain?


 

Appropriations Committee chairperson and Representative Mikaela Angela Suansing was in tears when the HOR approved the budget on Monday night, overjoyed by the approval of the proposal she pushed along for months.


“The House’s budget amendments were guided by the shared judgment of the House to protect key spending priorities, particularly education and healthcare, while responding to the most pressing needs of the Filipino people,” she claimed.


Leaders of the House of Representatives celebrate after passing its version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill. (HOR photo)


Kabataan Youth Represenative Renee Louise Co, however, disagreed with Suansing’s glowing description of their work.


“Mister Speaker, this begs the question: What is taking up all that fiscal space? Year-in, year-out, the national budget is overflowing with pork [barrel],” Co exclaimed in her explanation of her rejection of the proposed budget.


Co revealed that the approved budget retained P361.19 billion for the Marcos government’s controversial infrastructure projects, such flood control and farm-to-market roads.


The budget would also give P136.94 billion to Marcos’ financial assistance programs the young legislator said are used to deodorize the president’s failure to defend the economy against uncertainties brought by the conflicts in West Asia.


Co also flagged the P51.88 billion that would be given to Marcos as “discretionary funds.”


Can the budget still be cleaned?


While the HOR holds the Philippine government’s “power of the purse,” the proposed 2027 budget has yet to go through the Philippine Senate before it is signed into law.

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: On liberal opportunism and the “purity” smear
content:
Photo from Naga City Tourism Facebook page

Accusing leftists and activists of demanding a “useless politics of purity” is a classic liberal defense mechanism designed to shift the burden of moral failure onto the critic.

Why did former Vice President and now Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo roll out the pink carpet for the Zionist war machine? When Robredo hosted Israeli Ambassador Dana Kursh for an official courtesy visit, she was not merely performing the routine gestures of local hospitality. She was actively welcoming and legitimizing representatives of the US-Israeli genocidal apparatus. This intervention centers an anti-imperialist analysis to dismantle the liberal apologetics surrounding this act. Rather than an isolated error in judgment, this diplomatic encounter exposes the persistent, foundational tension within the Philippine political landscape: the contradiction between liberal reformism and anti-imperialist national liberation.

Dismissing progressives’ critique of Robredo’s hosting of the Israeli envoy as mere “political purism” is politically and morally impoverished. The underlying mechanism demands a total, systematic critique. To understand why her defenders deploy the “politics of purity” accusation, and why that defense completely falls apart when examining real power dynamics and economic interests, we must lay bare both the liberal class position and the ideological sleight of hand at work.

To make sense of Robredo’s pivot toward imperial hospitality, we must look directly at the liberal class position. Her stance is neither an accidental misstep nor a personal failure of political intelligence but the direct expression of her class character and political alignment. Liberal reformism in the global periphery operates strictly within the legal, institutional, and geopolitical framework dictated by US imperialism.

While Robredo served as a focal point against the overt state terrorism of the Marcos-Duterte dynasties, her opposition was strictly intra-class—a feud over how to manage the neocolonial state, pitting rule-of-law decorum against autocratic violence.

Because her political legitimacy rests upon acceptance by the global capitalist order, her opposition stops at the border of imperial interest. When forced to choose between international solidarity with an anti-imperialist national liberation movement and alignment with the Washington-Tel Aviv axis, liberal reformists invariably side with the imperial core. They cannot critique the drain of value, the extraction of labor, or the military hegemony of US imperialism because their entire political project depends on remaining within that very apparatus.

This structural subservience explains why defenders deploy the “purity politics” weapon whenever that alignment is exposed. Accusing leftists and activists of demanding a “useless politics of purity” is a classic liberal defense mechanism designed to shift the burden of moral failure onto the critic. From a materialist standpoint, this argument relies on three ideological fallacies:

First, it replaces a materialist baseline with ideological absolution. Opposition to active genocide, ethnic cleansing, and imperialist aggression is not a performative or elevated ideological standard; it is the absolute baseline of human solidarity and anti-imperialist struggle. Labeling principled opposition to mass slaughter as “purity” redefines baseline morality as an unreasonable demand, attempting to pass off complicity as pragmatic maturity.

Second, it operates on the logic of liberal idealism, which treats political stances as abstract moral choices made in a vacuum. Political actions reflect concrete class interests. Shielding a public figure from accountability for legitimizing a settler-colonial state serves a specific political function: it conditions the middle forces to accept imperial violence as a routine, acceptable feature of global diplomacy.

Third, it trades scientific alignment for unprincipled unity. Transformative praxis distinguishes between principled unity—built on anti-imperialist struggle and mass interest—and unprincipled unity, which colludes with reaction to preserve electoral coalitions. Demanding that the progressive movement remain silent on international solidarity to protect a liberal politician’s image trades human rights and anti-imperialist consciousness for temporary electoral expediency.

This dynamic reveals the distinct role of the middle forces—segments of the …

author: chuang
title: “Every War Is a World War”: Interview with a Member of Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine
content:
The following is an interview with friends from Taiwan who have formed the umbrella coalition Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP). The interview includes an overview of the rifts in the Taiwanese left, and the frustration of TWAFP organizers carving out their place amid divisions between pro-unification and independence, or pro- and anti-American positions, in the contentious and highly polarized politics on the island.


The organizer recounts their efforts to confront Taiwan’s growing ties with Israel and direct support for the genocide in Palestine. They speak with sadness that, even as Taiwan is now the fourth-largest supplier of arms to Israel, surpassing mainland China, most Taiwanese care little for the distant genocide and the struggle in Palestine seems far away. And yet, TWAFP has led successful demonstrations, pulled together a broad coalition of disparate groups in support of Palestine, and conducted research to expose Taiwan’s complicity in the ongoing genocide.


Be sure to read their

report


from 2025, outlining specific pathways of material component support for Israel, including radar, armor, and an array of military hardware.


See also a recent

piece

 submitted to us, outlining Taiwan’s deepening ties with Israel under the DPP government.


–

Chuang


Q: To begin, let’s just set the stage. Over the last few years, the Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP) has helped to organize the largest mobilizations against the genocide in Palestine seen in Taiwan. Can you tell us a little about how TWAFP formed and maybe review some of the protests it has organized?


A:

Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP)

 was founded in April of 2024. Prior to this, Taiwan had already seen several groups doing Palestine advocacy work arise spontaneously, including Palestine Action Front, Taiwan Palestine Solidarity Network, and Parallel Government. As its name suggests, TWAFP is an “Alliance” that brings together groups that were already involved in initiatives related to Palestine. In addition to the three groups already mentioned, the alliance also includes a migrant worker organization, the

Taiwan International Workers’ Association (TIWA)

; the human rights organization, Taiwan Association for Human Rights; the cultural collective, Taiwan Rave & Punk Solidarity Front for Palestine; the gender issues group, Queer Margins; and the Christian group, Taiwan Olive Branch Peace Collective. From 2024 to today, we have organized one petitioning campaign, issued two open letters, held one candlelight vigil, hosted one book club meeting, staged five protest actions, held three press conferences, and organized three marches. In the future, we plan to engage in a number of other activities, many of which may be smaller in scale.


Q: TWAFP also did some very interesting research on material links between Taiwan and Israel. We can link to the report here, but can you briefly go over the main findings, and maybe go over any new information that you’ve found since that report was released? For example, have there been more details since then?

      


A: In September of 2025, we released our report,

Taiwanese Companies’ Complicity in Israel’s Ongoing Genocide

, which identified specific manufacturers assisting Israel in the production of military weapons, including via the production of components. For example: Gloria Material Technology Corp (GMTC) supplies superalloys and high-grade steel produced through electroslag remelting, while ADLINK Technology supplies embedded computing systems and industrial-grade computers. In another case, Transcom marketed its vertically integrated capabilities—spanning chip design to module production—to enter the Israeli defense supply chain and is now a key, long-term supplier of components for the EL/M-2084 multi-mission radar, which is a core element of the Israeli “Iron Dome” air defense system designed by Israeli defense company Elta.

author: ALR Editors
title: Announcing Asian Labour School Oct-Nov 2026 Semester
content:
Dear friends,


We are back with an amazing list of new and returning courses for the Asian Labour School. If you are interested in

acquiring democratic facilitation skills, navigating conflicts and taking collective care, working cooperatively, strengthening a union core or leading your own radical walking tours

, please check out the course information below and study with Asian Labour School.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Chie Matsumoto


We all have attended meetings where decisions were made by only a few members, most outspoken ones or someone at the top. We may have once thought, “Why am I even here?” and left without saying a word. Democracy starts in the smallest conversations, dialogues and meetings by raking in most diverse opinions and ideas, piecing them together to create something new and meaningful to all participants.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Facilitators: Emi Do and Matt Noyes


Worker cooperatives are enterprises that are owned and governed by workers. When all of our working experiences have been in profit-maximizing enterprises, or in workplaces that are structured hierarchically, it is no wonder that we can encounter challenges when attempting to work together cooperatively. In this course we will explore the challenges and tensions when there are no bosses to hate!


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Facilitator: Nash Tysmans


Movements are built through relationships. Yet the pressures of organizing (urgency, conflict, exhaustion, political disagreement, and unequal power) can strain those relationships and undermine our collective capacity. How can we build movements that are both effective in challenging injustice and caring in how we work together?


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Sithar Chhim


In order to win any campaign at workplace, unions need to be strong enough to pressure the company. Building a strong and representative committee is the only way to win over the bosses who have well organized structure at workplace compare to workers.


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)


Facilitator: Kevin Lin


Have you ever thought about leading your own radical walking tour to share with friends the significance of places and histories in your city? Leading and participating in a radical walking tour is not only educational but fun and always memorable. A walking tour provides a concrete sense of places, people, and histories. This course will walk you through the conceptualisation, research and logistics of a radical walking tour, and hear ideas and experiences from other participants across Asia.


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)

author: Unknown
title: Ronda Tayfur: Jineolojî enables us to look at problems from different perspectives
content:
The European Jineolojî Conference, held in Haelen, the Netherlands, and titled “The Role of Jineolojî in Building a Democratic and Communal Life,” brought together participants from across Europe. Speaking to ANF, Ronda Tayfur discussed how she came to know Jineolojî, her experiences in the women’s freedom struggle, and the discussions held at the conference.


Tayfur, who works within the Kurdish Women’s Movement in Switzerland, emphasized that Jineolojî is not merely a theoretical field but offers a perspective that helps people approach the problems they encounter in everyday life from different angles.


I first encountered Jineolojî in 2014


Tayfur said she first encountered Jineolojî in 2014, while studying at university in Istanbul. The workshops and discussions she attended during that period helped her develop a new perspective. “I first encountered Jineolojî in 2014, when I was studying at university in Istanbul. It was something entirely new to me. That year was when I first engaged with Jineolojî, attended its workshops, and took part in discussions.


Because of the environment we lived in and the geography in which we grew up, we had always been interested in women’s freedom and gender consciousness. But Jineolojî encouraged us to look at things from a different perspective. That is what drew me to it.”


Tayfur said that since discovering Jineolojî, she has sought to apply its perspective not only in organized political work but throughout every aspect of her life.


“Since then, I have tried, and continue to try, to look at everything through the lens of Jineolojî, not only in my work or in the areas where I am active, but in every part of life. I also try to address the problems I encounter through this perspective. First and foremost, I would speak of the plurality of life. There is no single quest for freedom, just as there is no single way to solve problems. Solutions can also be found by looking at things through different windows.”


Variety of experiences at workshops


Tayfur also spoke about the workshops held as part of the European Jineolojî Conference, noting that she participated in the workshop on Democratic Society and the Democratic Family.


She described the methods used in the workshops as creative and productive, adding that bringing together women from different institutions and fields of work enriched the discussions. She said:  “We held workshops yesterday, and I took part in the Democratic Society and Democratic Family workshop. The working method was genuinely creative and also more productive. We could call this one of the distinctive aspects of Jineolojî. We discussed several issues. Having a workshop with broad participation, bringing together people from different backgrounds and institutions, had its advantages. We discussed these issues from a broad perspective, and everyone brought different viewpoints and opinions.”


Tayfur said that the concepts of the democratic family and democratic society have long been subjects of discussion within the women’s movement. She noted that the conference provided an opportunity to revisit these discussions through the perspective of Jineolojî.


 


Emphasizing the importance of strengthening the links between Jineolojî and the work of the Kurdish Women’s Movement in Switzerland, she said: “The democratic family and democratic society have always been concepts we discuss. But now, through the lens of Jineolojî, we can ask what we have overlooked and what we need to complete or develop further. We can also better understand how to build relationships and work together with Jineolojî and the Kurdish Women’s Movement, of which I am a part and within which I carry out my work.”


The importance of sharing experiences


Tayfur said the conference had also included discussions on the legacy and influence of actually existing socialism. She described these discussions as important for connecting ideas to ongoing work and developing plans for the future. She added: “We also discussed the effects of actually existing socialism today. People do not remain confined to the present moment; they try to connect these discussions with the work they are doing and carrying out. At the very least, they try to develop a plan or program. For us, this is something productive and creative. No matter how much social work we carry out, when we come together like this, we realize that there are still patterns we have not broken and ideas that have not yet …

author: rti_admin
title: No, not the Generation: Political Mobilisation and Changing Grammar of Protest in India
content:
Both academic and non-academic spheres are recurrently using terms like “Gen-Z protest,” “Gen Z’s political anger,” “Gen Z pressure,” “Gen-Z consciousness,” and “Gen Z politics” to describe the follow-up events. US public broadcaster NPR, despite accentuating the statistics of joblessness and inequality across South Asia as latent sources of unrest, concludes its argument by portraying “Gen Z” as an active political force. I feel some edginess with how a demographic detail is so readily treated as an explanation, when it is, at best, merely a description. Young people marching in large numbers, staging sit-ins, occupying public spaces, and facing tear gas are not new phenomena of 2026. These have long been a persistent feature of political activism in India. For instance, Bhagat Singh’s Naujawan Bharat Sabha (1926) had already demonstrated the political mobilization of youth nearly a century before.

Protests against exam-leaks are not new to India. We witnessed similar protests regarding the NEET exam in 2024. However, in 2026 the movement evolved into a mass youth mobilization, garnering national and international attention. It was driver not solely due to the examination scandal, but its collision with an unrelated event. Chief Justice Suryakant likened unemployed youth who turned to media and RTI activism to ‘cockroaches,’. Later he clarified that his remarks were intended merely for those who had entered professions such as the Bar through fake degrees, and not youth in general (Bar & Bench, 2026). Nonetheless, this clarification remained ineffective and within 24 hours a satirical social media account named ‘cockroach Janta Party’ (CJP) was created, open to anyone. This account gained 15000 followers within 24 hours, and over 19 million Instagram followers within a week. The NEET exam-leak and subsequent students-suicides provided impetus, leading tens of thousands of protestors to march towards Parliament Street under the overarching leadership of CJP and veteran Sonam Wangchuk, and ended with the resignation of a union minister.

The protesters were widely framed as a representation of a globally lucid generational style that is exasperated with institutional reverence, smooth in satire, and native to the platforms on which the movement lived. The movement has been routinely presented as a ‘Gen Z phenomena,’ that includes humour, memes, slang, and digital presence as its principal vocabulary. Gen Z has become a dominant frame, or popularised as one. Here, the concern is not whether the specific age-group people participated in the protest, but why this frame has become the media’s preferred explanation of it? Generational categorisation, such as Gen Z, Gen Alpha, Millennial, is neither an analytical lens nor an ideology in itself. A generation is just a demographic category that may have diverse socio-political orientations (Kumar, 2026); different structure[s] of power they may have confronted; and navigated varied trajectories of struggle. This essay raises the question of whether a demographic category is an appropriate explanation of a political mobilisation.

Instagram posts, memes, sarcastic placards, or even irreverent slogans are forms of political expression that should not be mistaken for an account of the politics. Labelling it as ‘Gen Z protest’ can highlight the prominent demographic cohort of protestors. But it does not shed light on the concerns, grievances, institutional failures, leadership, or political orientations that catalyzed these protests. The essay argues that while the youth presence in the protests is not new, the available grammar has shifter in the key dimensions: (a) the mode of communication through which issues, objectives and planned actions are circulated; (b) the mode of mobilisation through which sympathisers are turned into participants; and (c) the mode of campaigning through which a protest sustains public attention and pushes its demands. It is not the generational essence, but rather a recurring structural feature of youth combined with the accessibility of modern media, that explains the difference between the 2026 movement and its predecessors.

Theoretical framework: Beyond the birth-year bracket

A widespread discourse about ‘Gen Z’ typically considers a generation as a straightforward demographic fact demarcated by shared birth years, commonly dated 1997 to 2012. It is presumed to share a psychology, a politics, and a communication style as a consequence of …

author: Sue Bull
title: Socialist Alliance registered with the VEC for the Victorian elections
content:
Socialist Alliance will be on the ballot paper for the Victorian elections on November 28, after its registration lapsed in 2019.

Sue Bolton, Victorian candidate for the seat of Broadmeadows and a veteran Merri-bek City Councillor said she was pleased that Socialist Alliance, which formed in 2001, was registered again.

“We will be on the ballot, with our name and logo, presenting progressive, pro-worker policies.”

Bolton has a stand-out record of working with residents and communities standing up for their rights. She has helped win a number of concessions from the state, including saving the outdoor pool in Fawkner, and winning Merri-bek City Council support to end contracts with companies supporting the Israeli military.

Socialist Alliance is standing a group of candidates in the Northern Metropolitan Region of Naarm/Melbourne and in Djilang/Geelong, who have a record of fighting with vulnerable communities for rights and services.

Its campaign platform is “Fighting for people, not the billionaires” and says the incoming Victorian government must prioritise the needs of ordinary people, before corporate profits.

It is calling for the public sector to be rebuilt, including 100,000 new public houses and a moratorium on building energy hungry mega AI data centres.

Socialist Alliance is running five candidates for the Victorian Legislative Assembly, including Bolton and Jacob Andrewartha in Pascoe Vale, and three in the Northern Metropolitan Region.

In Djilang, the party will contest all four Legislative Assembly seats and three for the Western Victoria Region.

Sarah Hathway, a former councillor for the City of Greater Geelong who is standing in Lara, said there are a number of micro far-right parties, some with progressive sounding names, which have also registered with the Victorian Electoral Commission.

“Having Socialist Alliance registered means workers have a real alternative to the right-wing hypocrites, such as One Nation,” Hathway said.

“These conservative parties blame immigrants for the cost-of-living and housing crises. They whip up racism to distract and confuse people from putting the blame where it really lies — on the billionaires, one third of whom do not even pay tax.”

Tim Gooden, the lead Socialist Alliance candidate for Western Victoria Region and a former secretary of Geelong Trades Hall said: “Workers in the two regions can now vote for candidates who have a proven track record of fighting with communities and are putting forward positive solutions for workers, rather than the hate which is being spewed by the big end of town.”

[Sue Bull is running for Socialist Alliance in the Western Region. For further information and to help out, get in touch with Socialist Alliance Victoria.]

author: Ella Gutteridge
title: Hundreds protest far-right conference in Brisbane
content:
High-profile racists and far-right leaders descended on the Brisbane showgrounds over the weekend of 10 and 11 October for the Conservative Political Action Conference.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson headlined the event. She was joined by Liberal leader Angus Taylor, far-right podcaster Karl Stefanovic, and one of Britain’s least successful politicians, former Prime Minister Liz Truss.

Inside, it was a carnival of reaction. The ABC reported that

Hanson was greeted with

rapturous applause

 as she harangued the Coalition for signing up to net-zero and creating an eSafety commissioner, which she pledged to abolish on the grounds of free speech.

The leader of the National Party, Matt Canavan, cosplayed as a blue-collar worker as he took to the stage to extol the virtues of Australian manufacturing. Despite earlier criticisms, Hanson said that she’d be willing to work with the Coalition to “

throw out this wretched and corrupt Labor government

”.

Outside, hundreds of irreverent high schoolers, trade union activists and community members rallied, waving homemade signs, chanting and drumming. The crowd was a sea of keffiyehs, rainbow flags and signs, with many commenting on Hanson’s close relationship with Australian billionaire Gina Rinehart (“Pauline works for Gina!”).

“Migrants are welcome, racists are not!” was a popular chant, echoing across the showgrounds while conferencegoers streamed out for their lunch break. One Nation recently unveiled

its policy to cut Australia’s immigration intake

 by 750,000 people over three years, including plans to cut visas for the family members of skilled migrants and international students to zero.

“Pauline Hanson wants net zero immigration, but my parents are immigrants, my friends are immigrants, and without them this country would be nothing and fuck Pauline!”, Sam, a high school student, told

Red Flag

.  

The rally heard from Dave Pullen, an Indigenous elder from Inala who ran against Hanson in Ipswich in 1996. Draped in an Indigenous flag, Pullen opened with an acknowledgement of country and of Hanson’s long record of racism towards Indigenous people.

National convenor of the Socialist Party and teacher unionist Rebecca Barrigos highlighted the importance of posing an alternative socialist vision to One Nation and the broader right:

“Today’s rally isn’t just about sending a signal to those inside the conference; it’s about saying we know what you’re doing. They’re fighting for a more competitive, more brutal, more pro-billionaire, anti-worker vision of society, and to that we say, fuck your vision of society! We have an alternative vision.”

There is a long way to go to realise that vision.

Hanson is currently the preferred prime minister to Anthony Albanese

 and is polling at 36 percent in Queensland. While the right has momentum, it still faces opposition. People who oppose One Nation’s vision for the world should rally to our side and put up a fight.

author: AWSM
title: Why I Won’t Vote ~ A SYMPOSIUM #1
content:
Anarchy 37, March 1964, Why I Won’t Vote

Voting : “The instrument and symbol of a freeman’s power to make a fool of himself and a wreck of his country”

The saying that ” only a fool would put a loaded gun into the hands of an idiot ” is an especially apt analogy of government. An idiot (usually well-meaning) considers himself clever enough to run the affairs of a large number of people by taking a seat in parliament. A large number of people, acting like fools, vote for his party’s policy then spend the next few years grumbling about the results. The error in approach is that the voter thinks that he will get what he voted for. If he could vote for those who in fact control the country, say the Governors of the Bank of England, the directors of the industrial corporations and those behind the ministries, the illusion of democracy would be more understandable.

The real centres of power lie far beyond the people’s influence at elections. These remain constant whatever Party is ” in power “. In the terms of centralised ” democracy ” the only possible argument to justify voting is that marginal benefits may be gained. The state only incidentally attends to the well-being of its subjects. Its main concern is its power relation to other states, of which the most perfect expression is in war.

I am on the side of people anywhere who are prepared neither to live nor die for something that in the long run can only militate against survival and the conditions that make life worth living. Our immediate action must, by its nature, be to oppose that pathetic gesture, voting. It must be direct and direction. We can learn to live as free men and women only by organising against the condition we are in.

The Tenants Association, Consumers Association, and Direct Action in industry all provide opportunities for people to experience directing their own lives in positive ways towards positive ends.

Only by direct involvement in society can the individual hope to transform himself and his world. Freedom cannot be given, it must be taken; and the free society can only grow from experiments in the problems (ethical and organisational) of community.

Voting does not, and cannot, mean government by consent. By voting, one acts on the assumptions that certain men are fit to govern, and that a majority is necessarily right. Also should the state, acting in the name of a (frequently fictitious) majority, declare war, the individual loses the right to live, if he ever had it.

To me, voting is complicity with the State and a negative action, therefore I do not vote.

author: Cas Smith
title: Land Forces weapons expo protested in a time of genocide
content:
Around 2000 anti-war activists took to the streets on October 6, in a strong rebuke to the weapons’ manufacturers displaying their wares at the Land Forces International Land Defence Exposition and Western Australian Labor, which welcomed it.

The rally, one of the biggest in recent years, began at Yagan Square near Northbridge, before marching through the city to Elizabeth Quay, close to the Perth Convention Centre.

A “security area” had been set up around the expo venue, which included the Elizabeth Quay train station and several sections of surrounding streets.

A new law, the Land Forces (Special Powers) Act 2026, gave police the “ability to establish checkpoints, cordons, and roadblocks, while also searching people, bags, and vehicles, and issue lawful directions for a 10-day period”, until October 10.

Alongside this, several activists had been told they were banned from the security area, and could face fines of up to $36,000 and three years in prison if they challenged this.

The media coverage of these repressive security initiatives — to which WA Premier Roger Cook had allocated $11.5 million — may have encouraged people to come to the rally, which was hosted by WA Anti-War Collective, Stop AUKUS WA, Nuclear Free WA, Independent and Peaceful Australia Network (IPAN), Friends of Palestine WA (FOPWA), Students for Palestine WA, Right To Protest WA and Extinction Rebellion Western Australia.

It included several creative aspects, including a flash mob dance to the tune of the Temptations’ song “War” and a performance by Drummers for Climate Action.

Noongar Elders Uncle Headley Hayward and Uncle Herbert Bropho gave the Welcome to Country. Adrian Glamorgan (Independent and Peaceful Australia Network and Stop AUKUS WA), Danica Scott (Stop AUKUS WA and Freiends of Palestine WA), Greens MLC Sophie McNeill, Rojin Didari (Students for Palestine WA) and Berlin Guerrero (Migrante and International People’s Struggle) addressed the protest.

Sam Wainwright (Stop AUKUS WA), who MCed the rally, said Labor’s decision to roll out the red carpet for weapons manufacturers indicated his priorities.

“[Land Forces] comes in the context of a worldwide increase in military expenditure, including a 50% increase in military expenditure by Donald Trump. It comes in the context of the genocide in Gaza, and a climate emergency,” Wainwright said.

“It poses the question: What is the real response of our rulers to what are known as the ‘poly crises’ of capitalism. Is it not repression at home and war abroad?”

It was particularly horrific that weapons used in Gaza would be on display at the exhibition, Wainwright added.

“For the last three years, we have begged this federal government to stop sending arms to Israel and to cancel bilateral military ties, because it’s the one thing you’d do if you were serious about stopping the genocide.

“Labor won’t, because it has committed to making Australia one of the 10 major weapons exporters in the world. Roger Cook has said he wants to make weapons exports the number two industry in WA. The place of Israel in the military industrial complex means deepening bilateral military ties with that state.”

Elbit Systems and Rafael were among the Israeli weapons companies featured at Land Forces, alongside Lockheed Martin, which constructs the F-35 fighter jets used in much of the destruction of Gaza.

author: April Holcombe
title: Chinese youth in a very shit time of their lives
content:
Certain quarters of the internet are filling with content lauding contemporary China as an advanced, anti-imperialist, even socialist society. Its unrivalled high-speed rail network and its continued use of Communist jargon have encouraged some disillusioned Western youth to declare themselves in “a very Chinese time of my life”.

State-of-the-art infrastructure and Communist iconography have obvious appeal to a section of people living in decaying, imperialist and increasingly far-right-controlled Western capitalism. But there is a big difference between Instagram China, a Potemkin country showcased by influencers at the invitation of the tourism bureau and marketed to disillusioned Western youth, and the real China, a nuclear superpower ruled by bureaucrat-businessmen.  

Young Chinese people on social media—students, workers and the unemployed—use a very different kind of language than influencers do. Theirs is the language of alienation, exploitation and oppression in a society every bit as capitalist as our own.

“Involution”: an obscure word for a common problem

Ever heard of “involution”? Me neither. This obscure academic term, translated into Chinese (内卷

neijuan

), has entered common parlance among young people trapped in the country’s hypercompetitive economy. Literally meaning “inwardly curling”, anthropologists repurposed the term to describe activities that increase in complexity but lead nowhere. Chinese youth decided it captured their social predicament: instructed to work ever harder to stay ahead of their peers, they end up doing much more without being any better off.

Neijuan

describes many things: the gruelling hours at Big Tech companies; the notoriously competitive university entrance examinations; the apps pushing food delivery workers to ride ever faster; and the impossible social media-influenced beauty standards. The second character is now used as a standalone verb, meaning “to work or try too hard”.

Many young people who reject the

neijuan

 rat race opt instead to “lie flat” (躺平

tang ping

), a vibe somewhere between “quiet quitting” and “bedrotting”. The Ministry of State Security finds it deeply disturbing that anyone would want to lie flat, claiming in a Douyin (like TikTok) video that “an unnamed overseas organisation heavily funds ‘lying flat’ influencers, mass producing short videos promoting ‘anti-involution equals anti-exploitation’”.

Successive surveys show scepticism and pessimism rising sharply. In 2014, 62 percent of 10,000 respondents agreed that “effort is always rewarded in our country”; only 28 percent agreed a decade later. One-fifth blamed “the unfair economic system” for poverty in 2014; more than one-third did a decade later. Two-thirds agreed their families’ lives would improve from 2014-19, but less than half thought so for 2023-28.

“Graduation means unemployment”

University degrees once guaranteed well-paid government or tech jobs, providing the Communist Party’s dictatorship with a large, stable base of middle-class support. But now, often, “graduation means unemployment” (毕业即失业

biye ji shiye

). The gradual slowdown in economic growth has intensified competition for entry-level positions (more than 600 people, for example, applied for one basic Beijing office job in November 2025). Stable employment has given way to job flux. “I have family members who, since the early 2000s, never lost their jobs”, labour researcher Kevin Lin told

Red Flag

. “Last year, my cousin was laid off for the first time. Then he struggled to find another job, got laid off again, and is on to his third job.”

Unemployment is roughly twice the official figure of 5.2 percent, according to estimates by economist Li Daokui. “There are roughly 24 million long-term discouraged unemployed people, which is highly unfavourable for social stability”, the Tsinghua University academic told the China Macroeconomic Forum in July. The youth unemployment rate, officially hitting 17.9 percent that same month, has not included students since it soared past 25 percent in 2024, and hides a vast pool of underemployed youth working as little as one hour per week.

For the first time, the Communist Party’s most recent five-year plan includes no job-creation target. On the other hand, the government has a very clear target of 70 percent AI adoption across key industries by next year, inciting fears of layoffs among many IT workers. “I still can’t shake the feeling that I’m getting closer to being …

author: @ndy
title: From CPAC to NatCon to BACPAC : Trumpism Down Under
