title: Jineolojî must connect with society’s needs, say women at Haelen conference
content:
The European Jineolojî Conference titled “The Role of Jineolojî in Building a Democratic and Communal Life,” is being held in Haelen. The third session focused on “Socializing Knowledge and Decolonizing Science.” Participants discussed collective learning, educational methods, knowledge production and the role of women’s knowledge in building a democratic society.


Presentations were given by Jineolojî Committee members Yasemin Anday and Nûjîn Derya, and Jînda Amed of the European Kurdish Women’s Movement (TJK-E). Topics included educational experiences, research, the social role of academies and strengthening local organization.


Education was the foundation for building a new human being


Reflecting on the Kurdish Freedom Movement’s educational experience and the development of Jineolojî from this legacy, Jînda Amed said education had been a central focus since the movement’s beginnings. Initiated with limited resources under the leadership of Haki Karer and Kemal Pir, educational activities gradually expanded and adopted new methods. Their aim was not only to transmit knowledge but also to shape people’s identities and personalities.


She said education emphasized ethics, morality, love for humanity and nature, women’s liberation and overcoming feudal influences. “Jineolojî, too, grew out of these values. It is their product,” she stated.


Amed stressed the importance of education and self-education in overcoming patriarchal and capitalist mindsets, highlighting personal commitment and self-development. She also emphasized continuing educational and awareness-raising activities from a women’s liberation perspective.


Women's education and organizing in Europe


Amed said educational initiatives in Europe had developed under the leadership of women such as Binevş Agal and Sakine Cansız, despite state repression and patriarchal attitudes. These experiences helped strengthen cultural activities, assemblies and communal organizing.


She said Kurdish women’s educational experiences had offered important answers to the question of how to build a free life. “Women not only overcame patriarchal oppression but also developed an answer to the question, ‘How should we live?’” she said.


Although conferences, training programs and research projects are being conducted, Amed argued that more needs to be done and that academies and committees must become more involved in community life.


She stressed that Jineolojî must strengthen its connection with the socially grounded and internationalist nature of the women’s liberation struggle. Its work should address society’s needs rather than remain confined to academic settings, integrating education and research with social relationships and grassroots organizing.


Anday: Learning must be part of collective life


Jineolojî Committee member Yasemin Anday discussed more than a decade of educational work and alternative learning methods developed in Europe. She said Jineolojî emerged to expose women’s enslavement as a root cause of social problems and to develop knowledge for a free life.


“The dagger in society’s back was women’s enslavement; no social problem could be fundamentally resolved without removing it. Jineolojî emerged as a science that identifies this dagger, pulls it out and replaces it with the knowledge needed for a free life,” she said.


Anday explained that European initiatives drew on the Kurdish Women’s Movement’s experiences of education and self-education. Activities initially took the form of conferences, seminars and reading groups before reaching a new stage with the first European camp in Germany in 2017. These camps made learning part of a shared way of life in which women lived, debated, researched and shared responsibilities.


Emphasizing that knowledge must be experienced collectively and connected to everyday life, Anday said communal living exposed individualistic habits and social contradictions. Practices such as xwebûn (selfhood), hevaltî (companionship), criticism and self-criticism, and tekmil (collective evaluation) created opportunities for women to reflect on themselves and their relationships.


“Communal life is not simply about sharing a space; it requires continuous effort to think together, take responsibility, confront contradictions and transform relationships,” she said.


Anday described methods used in Jineolojî research, including oral history, life stories, small-group activities, theatre, art and memory work, which …

author: Tam Saavedra
title: Conectivas: First Time in (Por primera vez en) CADF
content:
A table of our own: Conectivas First Time in CADF.    

 


 


For many years, we have seen organizations that serve people with disabilities occupy spaces like the Central American Donors Forum (CADF); this year, thanks to WEI’s support, we were able to attend in person, make our voices heard, and become visible in places where we are usually invisible.   

 


We were not there to hear people speak about us; we went there to speak ourselves, for the first time and in first person – as an organization led by women with disabilities.   

 


What did we achieve?

  

 


We facilitated a networking table on women and disability.  

 


We offered support to WEI’s lighting talk on women with disabilities fighting back anti rights movements.   

 


We networked with different actors about how we see – from a human rights perspective- the backlashes in rights we are seeing globally and how we want to be included in the resistance.  

 


They still see us as something apart.

  

 


Most of the donors we engaged in conversations agreed that the disability movement needs funding but struggled to see how to include us into what they are already doing.

Disability. Intersects democracy, protection and gender equality.

Yes, we need specific resources and at the same time. Inclusion in the actions already put in place.   

 


Our accessibility is not enough. We could get there thanks to WEI’s support, but many other women are missing from the conversation. A

rriving is not enough: we need conditions to remain in those spaces

. To guarantee accessibility for women with disability the following spaces are also needed:   

 


Desstined spaces for rest  

 


Physical and menstrual hygiene accommodations  

 


Spaces where we can rest from noise and crowds  

 


To invest in the participation of the female disabled leaders is to invest in the movements:

it strengthens the local networks that already exist to access resources, but also to weave alliances that survive the forum’s duration.   

 


Thank you to Women Enabled International for the technical assistance provided that opened up a space for us without occupying it.

This time we had a table of our own: what comes next is that this stops being the exception.

  

 


In solidarity,  

 


Conectivas

 · October 2026.

fortalece las redes locales que ya existen, tanto para acceder a recursos como para tejer alianzas que duren más que el foro.

author: Santana Simiyu
title: A baby died following FGM in The Gambia. Why did the case end in acquittal?
content:
16th October 2026


A baby died following FGM in The Gambia. Why did the case end in acquittal?


By Santana Simiyu


14 min read


News and Insights


End harmful practices


Africa


Nairobi, Kenya, September 30, 2026:

In May 2026, The Gambia’s High Court acquitted three women prosecuted in connection with the death of an infant following female genital mutilation (FGM). The Court found that the child had died from injuries sustained during FGM, but in her ruling, Justice Janneh upheld a “no case to answer” submission by the defence on the grounds that the prosecution had failed to produce legally admissible evidence establishing the criminal responsibility of the accused. 


The case did not turn on whether FGM had taken place or caused the child’s death, but on whether investigators and prosecutors had gathered and presented sufficient admissible evidence to prove who was responsible. The judgment raises an important question for The Gambia: what does it take to turn laws prohibiting FGM into effective accountability?


Rule of law cannot be selective

 


When news spread that a one-month-old

girl had bled to death following FGM

 in Welingira, in The Gambia’s West Coast Region, the public was understandably outraged. In such cases, people often expect courts to deliver justice by securing convictions. Yet the outcome of

The State v. Fatou Camara and Others

reminds us that the legitimacy of the criminal justice system depends not only on the outcome of a case, but on whether every stage of the justice process, including investigation and law enforcement, adheres to the rule of law. 


The state filed four charges:

performing FGM, conspiracy to commit a felony, aiding and abetting the procedure, and failing to report the act. The

 three accused pleaded not guilty, placing the burden on the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The prosecution called ten witnesses and submitted evidence to support its case. 


The High Court did not dispute the medical evidence that the child died from injuries consistent with circumcision. Nor did it question the seriousness of FGM. Rather, the court insisted that criminal responsibility must be established through legally admissible evidence, and it correctly observed that the strength of a criminal case is measured not by the number of witnesses but by the quality and admissibility of the evidence they provide.


The court’s insistence on admissible evidence should not be dismissed as a mere procedural technicality. It reflects a foundational principle of the rule of law that courts must follow due process and conduct a fair trial. This requires the State to prove criminal responsibility through lawful and reliable evidence before it can convict a person and deprive them of their liberty. A justice system that relaxes evidentiary standards because an offence is particularly grave does not strengthen justice. It weakens it. Ensuring justice for survivors of severe human rights violations like FGM thus requires every actor in the criminal justice chain to ensure that these standards are met so that the burden of proof can be discharged.


The judgment is an institutional critique


Perhaps the most significant aspect of the judgment is not the acquittal itself but the court’s observations regarding the investigation. Rather than merely concluding that the prosecution had failed to establish a prima facie case, Justice Janneh identified concrete investigative deficiencies that undermined the prosecution from the outset. 


Several police witnesses admitted they never visited the scene where the alleged offence occurred. Others testified that their evidence was based largely on information received from colleagues rather than on their own investigative work. Material witnesses were apparently not identified or interviewed, and little effort was made to gather physical or circumstantial evidence capable of independently linking the accused persons to the offences charged.


These were not isolated oversights. Collectively, they reveal systemic weaknesses in how the police and prosecutors investigate FGM cases. The court’s criticism extended beyond the conduct of individual officers. It raised broader institutional questions about investigative capacity, training, supervision, and compliance with statutory procedures in cases involving vulnerable victims.


When criminal investigations fail, justice fails


The evidence established that the infant died from …

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Students Say Cornell Banning Frat Parties and Adding Investigators Insufficient
content:
“Nowhere among these measures is the institutional change that students demand,” said Students for a Democratic Cornell.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Cornell University has suspended parties and social events at fraternity houses for the remainder of the academic year, and will work with state police and their sexual assault investigators on future cases.

The changes came in response to outrage over a gang rape at the university in 2024 that has brought national attention to the issue of sexual violence on college campuses and the failures of administrations to address the problem.

Cornell’s President Michael Kotlikoff announced these changes on Tuesday, after weeks of protest against the administration’s mishandling of the 2024 case that have escalated into calls for Kotlikoff’s resignation.

In 2024, a Cornell student, known by the pseudonym Jane Doe, reported that she had been drugged and raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity on campus. Her case was initially dismissed by the district attorney after university police “summarized” her complaint while omitting mentions of sexual violence and drugging. In mid-September, Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the university, the Chi Phi Fraternity, and the 7 men. Weeks later, NBC reported on court documents and text messages revealing conversations rife with the language of rape culture among the fraternity brothers. Subsequent reporting on the university’s mishandling of Jane Doe’s case prompted protests at Cornell and the reopening of her case by the district attorney.

“I have spent the past weeks listening to students, faculty, staff, parents, alumni, and trustees, who have shared their feelings of deep connection and sympathy with Jane Doe, anger and frustration that this could happen at Cornell, and outrage at the broader prevalence of sexual violence against women in our society,” Kotlikoff wrote in his announcement Tuesday.

In addition to suspending fraternity parties and working with New York State police “trauma-informed criminal investigators,” Koltikoff promised more staffing to support students who come forward with complaints of sexual assault.

But students at Cornell have called these measures insufficient.

Students for a Democratic Cornell (SDC), which organized a protest on campus on October 5 that was attended by thousands of students and faculty members, said that the measures demonstrate a refusal “to make institutional change on sexual violence.”

In a press release shared with Truthout, SDC explained that “Nowhere among these measures is the institutional change that students demand; specifically, there is no mention of reforming Cornell’s corrupt judicial system or an independent investigation not led by the Board of Trustees.”

The group contends that these measures allow the university to skirt the blame for its part in mishandling the 2024 case as well as its role in creating a “campus-wide epidemic” of sexual violence at Cornell.

Saya Taylor, a member of SDC, explained that the group “will continue to push until all of our demands are met – not just a select few that allow the administration to place blame on other parties.”

While the SDC does not view limiting fraternity parties as a useful measure in combatting sexual violence, other groups disagree – as was clear in the chants and slogans calling for banning frats entirely during the October 5 protest.

Kaori Quan of Cornell’s Graduate Student Union (CGSU) told Truthout that the barring of fraternity parties for the remainder of the academic year does not go far enough. “Stopping frat parties for a year does not address the systemic issues on campus that perpetuate rape culture,” she said, “namely, the intertwined nature of donor money and Greek life.”

“Until Greek life is off our campus entirely, Cornell will continue to prioritize the money it brings in over the health and safety of both students and workers.”

Referring to Cornell’s plan to work more closely with state police and investigators, Quan added that “so long as there is money in protecting Greek life, the campus police and the investigators they work with will answer to university administrators, not the students they supposedly protect.”

“CGSU’s stance is that working more closely with state police will do more harm than good,” Quan also told Truthout.

author: Eliel Peterson
title: Death as liberation
content:
Death as liberation is hardly a comfortable political proposition to digest. In a world where Black death is often the common condition, there is a well-established insistence on our living. So what do we make of two of Africa’s greatest filmmakers, Ousmane Sembène and Souleymane Cissé, whose earliest cinematic visions, expressed through their respective debut features

Black Girl

 (1966) and

Den Muso

 (1975), center on the suffering, alienation, and eventual deaths of Black women?

Sembène’s

Black Girl

 is preoccupied with racial violence and the economic exploitation that continues to structure relations between Senegal and France. The film follows Diouana, a young Senegalese woman who accepts employment with a white French family and travels to Antibes believing she is embarking on a new life. While Cissé’s

Den Muso

, turns inward, examining interpersonal violence and the ways patriarchal power consumes family life and communities, weakening the broader social fabric of a nation. The film follows Tenin, a mute young woman who becomes pregnant after being raped, exposing the brutal underbelly of the patriarchal violence imposed upon her. Despite the differences in their circumstances, both films position death as a troubling possibility of liberation for their central characters.

Tenin (Dounamba Dany Coulibaly) in a still from Souleymane Cissé’s

Den Muso

 (1975).

The history of Black resistance has not solely been confined to the preservation of life. From enslaved Africans who leapt from ships during the Middle Passage, to those who faced death in the fight against their oppression,

It is true

 that to rather die than to endure is not a popular or digestible form of liberation. Although these acts are not equivalent, nor do they carry the same weight as the deaths of these fictional characters, Sembène and Cissé, raise an uncomfortable question: what does life mean for a person stripped of agency, recognition, and self-determination?

For Diouana and Tenin, freedom remains out of reach because of the structures governing their everyday lives that continually deny these women full humanity: Tenin’s father and her rapist, Diouana’s white employers. This sustained stripping of humanity produces what I would argue is already a death, albeit a social one, that precedes their physical endings. Sembène and Cissé challenge audiences by asking what is living for the dehumanized. Diouana travels to France only to find her livelihood replaced by isolation and unpaid, alienated labor, while Tenin’s body becomes a site upon which familial and communal shame, punishment, and control are dumped. Death, therefore, is at the core of both films from the outset, existing not only as a shocking culminating event, but as a condition of violence. By the end of each film, Sembène and Cissé are not arguing over whether death is a worthy or noble choice for self-liberation; rather, they position the act of self-annihilation as the only remaining form of control available to their characters, and as an indictment of a society in which death is the only option. 

It is understandable to recoil at the self-inflicted violence that ultimately claims both Diouana and Tenin. One might ask why their rage is not directed solely towards those who harmed them. Why does Tenin’s retaliation extend beyond her rapist? Why doesn’t Diouana exact revenge on her employers and flee France? These questions linger because death feels like an unsatisfying conclusion, one that denies us, as audiences, the catharsis of resistance. We want these women to fight back and survive. We want their suffering to lead somewhere other than death. Yet perhaps the more daunting question is not why these women die, but whether we find their deaths more difficult to accept than the suffering that precedes them. What is ultimately more uncomfortable to confront: their deaths, or the conditions that made life itself unbearable?

Neither film offers an uncomplicated answer. To read Diouana’s and Tenin’s deaths as acts of liberation is not to suggest that their deaths resolve the violence they endure, or that self-annihilation is freedom in any complete sense. Their deaths do not dismantle the structures that dehumanized them. What death offers these women, perhaps then, is not freedom but a final assertion of agency within those systems. This is what makes their endings so devastating: the possibility of control emerges only when the possibility of living on their …

author: JoEllen Chernow
title: What If We Organized Survivors of Sexual Violence?
content:
Every few months America discovers another “monster.” A celebrity. A billionaire. A politician. A religious leader. A professor. A CEO.

The details differ, but the story doesn’t: rape survivors risk everything revealing years of abuse, followed by a burst of public outrage and demands for accountability.

Survivors of Jeffrey Epstein told us about a global rape and sex-trafficking network in which young people were abused and exploited by some of the world’s wealthiest and most influential men. For decades, survivors were ignored, disbelieved, and failed by the institutions around them. Newly released files corroborating their horror stories have resulted in zero US criminal arrests and little tangible accountability.

The #MeToo movement was supposed to interrupt this cycle. For a brief moment in 2017, it seemed possible that we could stop treating each “scandal” as an isolated incident and confront the systems connecting them. Instead, less than three months after the hashtag went viral, the press was full of opinion pieces about how it had all “gone too far.” The backlash flipped #MeToo into #NotAllMen. Outrage faded into fatalism, denial, and eventually business as usual.

As a rape survivor, community activist, and labor organizer, I call bullshit.

The problem isn’t that we keep “discovering” abusive men. It’s that we keep refusing to look at the underlying systems that reproduce sexual violence. Instead, we focus on finding, exposing, and punishing the monster du jour (or not) and then wait for the next one.

What we haven’t built is survivor power. Survivors are a constituency with the potential to change the social, political, and material conditions that enable violence and produce abuses of power.

Survivor power is not simply inviting us to the table or ensuring we are represented in leadership. It begins when we invite survivors to bring their full selves. Survivor power is built in the movement by moving from isolation to connection, from private shame to shared analysis, and from shared analysis to collective action. And because sexual violence is enabled by unequal distributions of power, survivor power means changing the basic conditions that make people vulnerable to violence in the first place: economic precarity, workplace exploitation, racism, misogyny, housing insecurity, and isolation.

We use the term power-based violence more than gender-based or sexual violence with survivors. It shifts our focus from seemingly separate forms of harm toward the throughline that links rape and domestic violence to workplace sexual harassment and coercion to the daily intimidation of strangers shouting obscenities and catcalls.

Survivor power is the power to imagine and build what does not yet exist.

More than 90 percent of adult rape victims are women and over 80 percent of survivors under the age of 18 are girls. Of every 100 survivors, 98 of them are raped by men. The vast majority of male survivors are also assaulted by men. Abusers are almost never strangers.

Sexual abuse and harassment aren’t isolated incidents just because they happen behind closed doors (or on private islands). They are expressions of ideology–a structural pattern of male power and control that reproduces itself from the intimate to the institutional and beyond.

Violence–and the ever-present threat of it–shapes where women go, whom they trust, what jobs they take, how they move through public space, and hundreds of other daily micro-calculations about their bodies and lives. Criminalized survivor and Chicago abolitionist organizer Monica Cosby maps out these similarities in the reframing of State Power and Control Wheel tracing how dynamics familiar from domestic violence–coercion, isolation, surveillance, economic control, threats, and violence–are also wielded through institutions and the state.

Yet we continue funding systems designed primarily to (inadequately) respond to violence while dramatically underinvesting in the people and strategies capable of changing the conditions that produce it. In 2026, the Violence Against Women Act and related sexual and gender-based violence programs received roughly $720 million–less than the cost of the White House renovation. Within these limited resources, funding overwhelmingly flows toward what happens after the harm is done.

The state’s narrow mandate to identify, prosecute and remove the “monster” has failed to make us safe. Only a tiny fraction of sexual assaults result in …

author: Unknown
title: Hande Ortaç ile ‘Sus’ üzerine: ‘Yazı benim mücadele alanım’
content:
Yasemin Seven Erangin [email protected]

Hande Ortaç’ın İletişim Yayınlarından çıkan “Sus” romanı, bir polis operasyonuyla başlayan hikayesi üzerinden şiddet, güç ilişkileri, adalet ve suskunlukla yüzleşiyor. Biri şiddeti iktidar kurmanın aracı olarak kullanan, diğeri ise maruz kaldığı sistematik şiddetin ardından öz savunmaya başvuran iki karakterin hikayesini karşı karşıya getiren roman, suçun yalnızca sonucuna değil, onu doğuran koşullara da bakıyor.

Romanın ilk cümlesinden itibaren güçlü bir “av” metaforu kuruyorsunuz: “Bir av partisinin en masumu avın ta kendisi değil midir?” Sus’u yazarken bu metafor sizin için ne ifade ediyordu?

Roman, tüm İstanbul’u etkisi altına alan bir polis operasyonuyla başlıyor. Avcılar kolluk kuvvetini temsil ediyor. Toplum için tehlikeli olduğuna inandırıldığımız bir katili kovalıyorlar. Roman ilerledikçe ortada iki katil olduğunu anlıyoruz. Hikayeler derinleşirken dışarıdaki av devam ediyor ve günün sonunda sadece biri yakalanacak.

Bu metaforda ısrar ediyorum çünkü söylemi kurma ayrıcalığına sahip olanların peşine düştükleri genellikle en güçsüzler oluyor. Güç sahibinin, iktidar yakınının işlediği suçların çoğunlukla cezalandırılmadığını, hatta alkışlandığını görüyoruz. Gerçek suçlu eğer erkten yanaysa avcıların cephesinde yer alıyor. Romanı yazarken bir avın sonunda mutlaka en masumun öldürüldüğünü hep aklımda tuttum.

Sus, suçun kendisinden çok suçu doğuran koşullarla yüzleştiriyor. Sizce adalet her zaman eşitlik demek midir? Bir insanı suça götüren koşullar, o suçun değerlendirilmesinde ne kadar belirleyici olmalı?

Adaletin eşitlikle değil hakkaniyetle daha sıkı bir ilişkisi olduğunu düşünüyorum. Kadın ve erkek benzer koşullarda, şiddet sarmalında büyümüş iki karakter. Fakat biri eril gücü ve şiddeti iktidar kurmanın aracı olarak görüyor, diğeri ise hayatının her aşamasında şiddet mağduru olmasına rağmen şiddeti araçsallaştırmıyor.

İkisi de birini öldürüyor ama eylemlerinin sebepleri arasında dağlar kadar fark var. Sonuç benzer olsa da iki olayı bağlamlarından bağımsız değerlendirmek mümkün değil. Hayat siyah ve beyazdan ibaret değil, aradaki tüm tonlar da vicdan ve akıl muhasebesi için.

Kadın karakteri, kendisine şiddet uygulayan kocasını öldürüyor. Bir kadının hayatta kalma mücadelesi hangi noktada öz savunmaya dönüşür?

“Öz savunma” kavramını indirgemeden verebilmek için olayları bağlamından koparmadan anlatmaya gayret ettim. Ataerkil şiddetin, karşısındakinin cezayı hak ettiğini düşünüp had bildirmeyi kendinde hak gören yaklaşımını deşifre etmeye çalıştım.

Sistematik şiddetin ve tacizin görünmeyen, konuşulmayan taraflarına yer vermek istedim. “Öz savunma”nın tek bir neden-sonuç düzlemine indirgenemeyecek kadar derin psikolojik bağları olduğunu düşünüyorum. Tek bir anı değil, tüm süreci anlatarak bunu görünür kılmak en büyük amacımdı.

Romanda şiddeti evde, iş yerinde, ilişkilerde ve dijital dünyada farklı biçimleriyle gösteriyorsunuz. Bu şiddet biçimleri aynı toplumsal kaynaktan mı besleniyor?

Dezavantajlı kesimlerin ve hassas kimliklerin sınırları hemen her karşılaşmada aşılabiliyor. Bu gruplara kadınlar ve LGBTİ+’nın yanında engellenen bireyler, çocuklar ve hayvanlar da dahil.

Genç bir kadın okulda, otobüste, sosyal medyada ya da iş yerinde tacize uğrayabiliyor. Medeni olduğunu düşündüğünüz sevgilinizden ya da iş için iletişim kurduğunuz birinden bile beklenmedik bir anda sınır ihlaliyle karşılaşmak mümkün. Bu hadsizliklerin, kontrol etme açlığının ve sınır ihlallerinin en büyük sebebinin güç ilişkilerinde olduğuna inanıyorum. Roman boyunca bu kuşatılmışlığı hissettirmeye gayret ettim.

Erkek karakteri üzerinden sosyal medya trollerini ve dijital dünyadaki kadın düşmanlığını da anlatıyorsunuz. Anonimlik şiddeti artırıyor mu?

Sosyal medya, avatarların ardına sığınarak insana sonsuz bir özgürlük ve hesapsız bir varoluş fırsatı sunuyor. Erkeklik de sıkı kurallara tabi. Makbul bir erkek olursan, oyunu kurallarına göre oynarsan ödülünü alacağın söyleniyor.

Erkeklikten pay alma itkisiyle sosyal medyanın sağladığı güvenli alan birleştiğinde şiddet artıyor. Yüz yüze olmamanın verdiği rahatlıkla şiddet kontrolsüz biçimde büyüyor. Romandaki erkek karakter de erkeklik normlarına uymadığı için zorbalanıyor, ardından şiddeti araçsallaştırmayı seçiyor. Sosyal medya onun için gizlenebileceği ve iktidar kurabileceği bir alan haline geliyor.

Romanın parçalı anlatım biçimi en başından beri tasarladığınız bir yöntem miydi?

“Sus” benim için bu dönemin yaralarıyla yüzleşme …

author: Chris Walker
title: HHS Demands Answers From Orgs Over Support for Youth Gender-Affirming Care
content:
Studies have demonstrated that gender-affirming care for transgender young people can be life-saving treatment.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) sent letters this week to multiple medical organizations, demanding they provide the department with a “clear, current statement” on their positions regarding gender-affirming care for transgender youth.

The organizations in question have expressed support for such care, with many noting that gender-affirming care is based on years of study and careful implementation.

Conversely, HHS framed the letters using non-medical terminology, asking the groups to “answer” for their support of so-called “sex-rejecting procedures for minors.”

The letters from HHS have been sent to the Endocrine Society, the American Psychiatric Association, the American Medical Association, the American Psychological Association, Columbia University trans health expert Asa Radix, and American Academy of Pediatrics CEO Mark Del Monte.

“HHS has asked these organizations for clear answers about their current positions, the evidence supporting their guidance, and whether they intend to change it,” HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in announcing the letters.

In a press release explaining why the letters were sent out, HHS stated it also wants “identification of any planned revisions to their respective guidance, and a timeline for those changes.” The department is giving the organizations 10 business days to respond.

Past statements from some of these organizations note that health care for transgender individuals — including trans children and teenagers — is beneficial, and that denial of such care when it’s warranted is harmful.

“We recognize health as a basic human right for every person, regardless of gender identity or sexual orientation,” reads a statement from the American Psychiatric Association published in 2021. “For gender-diverse individuals, including children and adolescents, this means access to gender-affirming care that is part of comprehensive primary care.”

“Physicians must be able to practice medicine that is informed by their years of medical education, training, experience, and the available evidence, freely and without threat of punishment,” the organization added. “Patients and their physicians, not policymakers, should be the ones to make decisions together about what care is best for them.”

The American Medical Association made a similar statement that same year, writing that:

Physicians are guided by their ethical duty to act in the best interest of their patients and must tailor recommendations about specific interventions and the timing of those interventions to each patient’s unique circumstances. Such decisions must be sensitive to the child’s clinical situation, nurture the child’s short- and long-term development, and balance the need to preserve the child’s opportunity to make important life choices autonomously in the future.

Dozens of other medical organizations, beyond those that HHS sent letters to, have also affirmed the need to preserve gender-affirming care, including for young trans patients.

Gender-affirming care is life-saving for many transgender and/or nonbinary individuals, including for young people. An observational study from late 2025, examining hundreds of trans patients between the ages of 12 and 20 from 2017-2024, found that suicidality rates for these patients dropped by 67 percent after they were given treatments that affirmed their gender identity.

Despite overwhelming evidence demonstrating the benefits of gender-affirming care, dozens of states across the U.S. have banned such treatment options for trans youth and young adults, often using misinformation to justify doing so.

President Donald Trump has also used blatantly false anti-trans talking points in an attempt to scare or anger people into backing Republicans in this year’s midterm elections. Meanwhile, some Democrats have also tried to appeal to voters by claiming they are skeptical of transgender rights, supporting, for example, unfounded bans on trans athletes, disallowing them to participate on teams corresponding to their correct genders.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

"Estrella: Bittersweet Freedom for a 'Bad Mexican'"

We’re joined by Latino USA host Maria Hinojosa as she shares the story of Estrella Diamantina González, an undocumented transgender woman and trafficking survivor from Mexico caught up in the United States’ criminal and immigration systems. This summer, after serving a nine-year sentence in a Texas men’s prison, Diamantina González was released, but she wasn’t free. She was immediately transferred to an immigration detention facility and then deported. Hinojosa, who has been reporting on Diamantina González’s ordeal for the last decade, followed her to Mexico in the new audio documentary “Estrella: Bittersweet Freedom for a 'Bad Mexican.'”

Maria HinojosaPulitzer Prize-winning journalist, founder of Futuro Media and host of Latino USA.

"Estrella: Bittersweet Freedom for a 'Bad Mexican'"

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman.

Soon after President Trump’s inauguration, in February of 2017, one of the first people arrested by immigration agents inside a courtroom was Estrella Diamantina González, a trans woman from Mexico. She was there to get an order of protection against an abusive boyfriend, but she never got the chance. Estrella spent most of the next decade caught up in the U.S. criminal and immigration systems. This summer, after serving a nine-year sentence in a Texas men’s prison, Estrella was deported to Mexico.

Journalist Maria Hinojosa was the first journalist to interview her after that courtroom arrest, and she’s been speaking to her ever since, for about a decade. Maria Hinojosa is the Pulitzer Prize-winning host of Latino USA. A new audio documentary is out today about Estrella, her life, her deportation and the evolving relationship with Maria. author: Maríangeles Guerrero
title: "Creemos en la potencia política de los feminismos para sembrar semillas de esperanza"
content:
Por Mariángeles Guerrero


Desde Córdoba


De todas las provincias, del campo y de la ciudad, llegan mujeres, lesbianas, travestis, trans. Viajan hace 40 años para encontrarse. Para compartir con otras lo que viven cotidianamente en sus territorios, para aprender de otras experiencias, para contar las propias. Este año, el

39° Encuentro Plurinacional de Mujeres, Lesbianas, Travestis, Trans, Bisexuales, Intersexuales y No Binaries

 se realizó el fin de semana pasado en Córdoba capital. Los temas a debatir se organizaron por ejes. En el Eje Soberanía, la soberanía alimentaria tuvo su propio taller. Carina Vallejo, de la Unión de Trabajadoras y Trabajadores de la Tierra (UTT) de Santiago del Estero rescata “la fuerza de poner en común nuestras realidades y darte cuenta de que no estás sola”.


Y añade: ”Poder encontrarnos, escucharnos y ver que las problemáticas del agua, la tierra y el modelo de producción nos atraviesan a todas por igual en distintos puntos del país nos fortalece muchísimo. Nos permite

salir del aislamiento del interior

 y llevar nuestras voces comunitarias a debates colectivos y asambleas de mujeres”.


Dhanna Moyano es travesti, productora caprina en Luján de Cuyo (Mendoza), integrante del Movimiento Nacional Campesino Indígena-Somos Tierra (MNCI-ST) y representante de Argentina en la Coordinadora Latinoamericana de Organizaciones del Campo (CLOC) - Vía Campesina. Fue una de las participantes del Encuentro y señala que la masividad que tuvo es una muestra del enojo que hay hacia el Gobierno. “

Hemos tenido travesticidios, femicidios, ventas de nuestras tierras

. Hoy estamos defendiendo la soberanía alimentaria porque es preocupante para nuestros cuerpos y cuerpas en todo el país. Este 15 de octubre tenemos que salir a defender que no nos vendan las tierras, porque venderlas es despojar a las familias campesinas, a las comunidades indígenas y al colectivo de la diversidad que está retomando ese camino”, denuncia.


Y agrega: “Nos abrazamos, lloramos, porque estamos mal en todo el país pero también estamos dando una gran lucha por un país soberano, libre y con igualdad de derechos para todos y para todas”.


Subraya que las diversidades sexuales son parte de la lucha campesina porque es un proyecto de vida concreto para ellas. “El Estado dice que las travestis nos morimos entre los 35 y 40 años por la calidad de vida que llevamos. Volver al campo implica que esa calidad de vida aumenta, porque es una vida más sana, más saludable”, explica.


Ante el desmantelamiento de las políticas para la agricultura familiar y las políticas de género,

la presencia de la realidad campesina en los debates feministas se vuelve urgente

. En este Encuentro, por primera vez la UTT, el MNCI-ST y el Movimiento Nacional Campesino Indígena marcharon en una misma columna, representando a las organizaciones campesinas.


Carolina Llorens, del MNCI-ST y del Movimiento Campesino de Córdoba (MCC) remarca “la potencia política que tenemos los feminismos de articular luchas ante un horizonte tan fragmentado y sembrar semillas de esperanza y de organización”. Y apunta que ese es el rol que tienen los feminismos campesinos, indígenas y populares. Y que los encuentros son un espacio potenciador de esa presencia política, del protagonismo de las mujeres y las diversidades.


Graciela Salto vive a 60 kilómetros de la localidad de Quimilí (departamento Moreno, al este de Santiago del Estero). Es la primera vez que participa de un Encuentro. “Aquí se dice la verdad, uno no viene con invento, dice lo que conoce. En la vida del campo es muy importante la tierra. Y si la defendemos, es para algo bueno, para algo sano. Es para la familia, para nuestros abuelos, para nuestros hijos”, valora.


Salto participó del Encuentro con la bandera del MNCI en la espalda, junto a su hija y otras compañeras que viajaron con ella. Cuenta que el mensaje que fue a compartir con compañeras de otras provincias es lo que sucede en su territorio: las fumigaciones con agrotóxicos y los desalojos. “No podemos criar animales porque te los envenenan, no podemos poner una fruta o una verdura por el tema del veneno. Y si nos desalojan, ¿adónde vamos a ir? No queremos irnos, somos nacidos y criados en el campo”.


Al encuentro llevó su bandera y la realidad del lugar donde vive. Y vuelve a su casa, dice, “con muchos recuerdos de todo lo que se habló y de las compañeras que conocí”.

author: Aoife Doran
title: Ceuta: Spain must protect trans asylum seekers, not return them to danger
content:
More than two months after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, many remain in precarious conditions, with inadequate access to shelter, essential services and international protection. Among them are trans asylum applicants who have fled persecution, only to face further violence, insecurity and the threat of being returned to danger. Their situation is part of a wider humanitarian crisis affecting people on the move in Ceuta, all of whom deserve safety, dignity and access to protection.


We are deeply concerned by reports of physical assaults, harassment and mistreatment of people seeking protection in Ceuta. A

report by Border Resistance

, a grassroots collective working at the border, documents at least seven alleged incidents of violence against LGBTI people between 21 August and 6 September. One trans woman described being assaulted by police officers after being expelled from a reception centre, stating,

“We are trans, we cannot live on the street because we are attacked.”

 Another described fleeing Morocco after receiving death threats from her family. These testimonies expose the grave risks facing trans and other LGBTI people who seek protection in Ceuta, only to encounter further violence and insecurity. We also reject the racist and dehumanising portrayal of people arriving in Ceuta as an

‘invasion’

, language that fuels discrimination and hostility and undermines the right to seek asylum.


“Trans people in Ceuta face specific and severe risks within a wider humanitarian crisis. Our solidarity is with all migrants in Ceuta: everyone deserves safety, dignity and real access to asylum.”


– Tayri Fadil (she/her), TGEU Board member


For people fleeing persecution because of their gender identity, access to asylum can be a matter of life or death. Morocco continues to criminalise consensual same sex sexual activity, and trans people face serious risks of violence, discrimination and exclusion. Court documents indicate that seven LGBTI people arrested in Fès in August 2026 were each sentenced to eight months in prison, to be served immediately, and fined, while another person received a three-month suspended sentence. Yet Morocco’s inclusion on the EU list of so-called

‘

safe countries of origin’

 risks obscuring these dangers and exposing people with legitimate protection needs to accelerated procedures and removal. As

we warned in February

, treating a country as safe based on general assessments can conceal the specific and sometimes life-threatening persecution experienced by trans people.


“Seeking asylum is already one of the most painful journeys a person can undertake. When you are a BPOC trans person, you may not even make it to safety alive, but to see Spain forcibly return asylum seekers across its borders is unconscionable and constitutes a gross violation of human rights that should alarm all of us.”


–  Purity Tumukwasibwe (she/her), TGEU Board member 


These concerns are particularly urgent following reports of proposed changes to Spain’s asylum procedures that would further restrict safeguards for applicants from countries considered safe. Such proposals reflect the wider shift towards accelerated removals and weakened protection safeguards seen in the EU Returns Regulation, which

we condemned in July

. Any measure that allows applicants to be removed before an effective assessment of the risks they face, including while challenging a negative asylum decision, would expose trans applicants to irreversible harm.


Spain has an obligation under European and international law to ensure effective access to asylum, assess each claim on its individual merits and uphold the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning people to places where they face persecution or other serious harm. These obligations apply regardless of how someone entered the country or whether their country of origin has been designated safe.


We call on the Spanish authorities, with the support and oversight of the European Commission, to take immediate action to:


Guarantee immediate safety and protection for trans and other LGBI asylum seekers in Ceuta, including safe and dignified accommodation, access to essential services and urgent transfers to mainland Spain for those at risk, in coordination with specialist civil society organisations.


Ensure fair and accessible asylum procedures, including confidential identification of protection needs, independent legal …

title: Childfree – Ein pro-choice Rollenspiel
content:
Childfree ist ein LARP darüber, dass dein Körper nur dir gehört. Darüber, sich zu ermächtigen, lebensverändernde Entscheidungen zu treffen und den eigenen Träumen und Projekten zu folgen. Es ist ein LARP über die Entscheidung, eine Schwangerschaft abzubrechen.


Es ist uns eine große Freude, unsere Ausgabe des Rollenspiels „childfree“ von Axiel Cazeneuve vorstellen zu dürfen. Wir hatten dieses Spiel im Jahr 2023 auf Französisch und Englisch herausgebracht. Zwei Jahre später haben unsere Freund*innen von

LarpPunk

 es ins Polnische übersetzt, und nun hat das autonome Gesundheitskollektiv Geko aus Bern es ins Deutsche übersetzt.


Die Möglichkeit, frei über den eigenen Körper zu verfügen, ist nach wie vor ein umkämpftes Thema – und wird es wahrscheinlich auch bleiben, solange Einzelpersonen, Institutionen oder Nationen sich die Macht über andere anmaßen. Mit dieser Neuauflage möchten wir uns solidarisch mit all jenen zeigen, die für den freien Zugang zu Schwangerschaftsabbrüchen kämpfen, sei es durch den Kampf gegen

Abtreibungsgesetze in Polen

 oder durch die Entwicklung von I

T-Sicherheitstools zum Schutz von Pro-Choice-Aktivist*innen in Brasilien

.


Wie alle unsere anderen Produktionen kann „Childfree“ zum freien Preis bestellt werden, und eine PDF-Version steht auf unserer Website kostenlos zur Verfügung. Um das Spiel in gedruckter Form zu bestellen oder bei der Verbreitung und Übersetzung dieses Spiels mitzuhelfen, kontaktiere uns bitte unter evasions@riseup.net.


Einleitung Von Axiel


„Childfree“ ist ein Live-Action-Rollenspiel – die Teilnehmenden schlüpfen physisch in Rollen, um gemeinsam eine Geschichte zu erzählen, ohne dass ein Publikum anwesend ist – für 5 bis 7 Personen, das in insgesamt vier Stunden gespielt wird. Es befasst sich mit Abtreibung, genauer gesagt mit dem freiwilligen Schwangerschaftsabbruch und bietet den Spielerinnen die Möglichkeit, einerseits die gesellschaftlichen Zwänge im Zusammenhang mit Schwangerschaft oder Abtreibung und andererseits die Individualität der schwangeren Person zu verkörpern. Der flexible und nicht-direktive Rahmen des Spiels ermöglicht es den Spielerinnen, verschiedene Situationen zu entwerfen und vorzuschlagen. Das Geschlecht der schwangeren Person, die Details ihres Lebens, der rechtliche Kontext … all dies bleibt ganz den Spielenden überlassen, die dabei durch die Spielunterlagen unterstützt werden, die so klar und einfach wie möglich gehalten sind. Die Entscheidung, die Schwangerschaft abzubrechen oder fortzusetzen, liegt natürlich ebenfalls bei der schwangeren Rolle (und somit bei der Person, die sie spielt). Indem ich eine Erfahrung biete, die vollständig von den Teilnehmenden gemeinsam gestaltet wird, wollte ich ein wenig von dem weitergeben, was ich durch einen freiwilligen Schwangerschaftsabbruch gelernt habe, sowie das Gefühl der Befreiung, das damit einherging.


Ich habe dieses Spiel 2018 geschrieben: Anlässlich der Veröffentlichung der Ausgabe durch Projet Évasions möchte ich auf meine persönliche Erfahrung zurückblicken und darauf, was mich zum Schreiben motiviert hat.


Ein Spiel mit wunderschönen Illustrationen von Nemo


Erfahrungen mit einer freiwilligen Schwangerschaftsunterbrechung in Frankreich im Jahr 2017


Anfang 2017 blieb meine Periode eine Woche aus. Da das ungewöhnlich war und ich zudem starke Schmerzen im unteren Rücken und in der Brust hatte, ging ich los, um einen Schwangerschaftstest zu kaufen. (Auf dem Weg dorthin machte ich einen Abstecher in den Laden um die Ecke, weil ich Heißhunger auf Fruchtgelee hatte. Als ich die einsame Pappschachtel auf dem Förderband vorbeiziehen sah, fragte ich mich, ob es sich wirklich lohnte, den Test zu machen).


Natürlich war das Testergebnis positiv. Als ich die beiden Striche erscheinen sah, versuchte ich zu weinen. Ähm … Nein, das klappt nicht. Ich versuchte zu lachen. Nein. Also griff ich zum Telefon – es war, glaube ich, ein Montag, gegen Mittag – und rief beim „Planning Familial“ an (ein Netzwerk aus Vereinen und aktivistischen Gruppen, das in Frankreich Dienstleistungen im Bereich der sexuellen Gesundheit anbietet). Folgendes habe ich wörtlich gesagt:


– „Hallo, ich habe mir vor neun Monaten bei Ihnen eine Spirale einsetzen lassen, ich habe gerade einen Schwangerschaftstest gemacht und er ist positiv.


Stille.


– Oh Scheiße. Können Sie in zwanzig Minuten vorbeikommen?“


Ich sprang in mein Auto, das mein Partner fuhr, und innerhalb einer halben Stunde waren wir im Planing-Familial 31 …

title: ExisTransInter 2026
content:
Appel de l'

interorga de l'ExisTransInter

 pour l'édition 2026 : rendez-vous vendredi 16 octobre à 19h devant Gare de l'Est à Paris


L'autodétermination au pouvoir


Vendredi 16 octobre à 19h à gare de l'Est

, l'ExisTransInter réunira

les personnes intersexes, les personnes trans, et leurs allié·es

. Notre histoire commune est faite d'entraide et de transmission, de lutte et de résistance, de victoires arrachées. En 2016, nous réclamions déjà le changement d'état civil libre et gratuit, le libre choix des parcours médicaux, l'arrêt des mutilations des enfants intersexes, la reconnaissance de droit pour les personnes migrantes et les travailleur·euses du sexe (

TDS

). Dix ans plus tard, et en l'absence affligeante d'avancées majeures sur ces sujets, notre détermination reste intacte et sans concession. Nous ne voulons plus d'une société où l'accès au droit, au soin, au logement, dépendent de notre conformité aux normes cis et dyadiques –- pas plus que de notre classe sociale, de notre pratique du

TDS

, de nos origines, de notre validité ou de nos titres de séjour.


Dans un contexte politique particulièrement menaçant, nous refusons plus que jamais la réduction de nos vies à des controverses médiatiques, à des paniques morales, à des cases administratives. Nous refusons d'être les boucs émissaires de cel·leux qui alimentent la peur et la haine des minorités.

Nos luttes sont antifascistes, anti-impérialistes, anti-coloniales

. Elle sont, en cela, indissociables de celles des peuples palestinien, congolais, soudanais et iranien.


Enfant·es ou adultes, nos corps nous appartiennent


Nos luttes sont indissociables des luttes féministes et enfantistes

. En ce sens, nous défendons l'autonomie corporelle de tous·tes les enfant·es, dont les droits fondamentaux ne commencent pas à la majorité. De la naissance à l'adolescence, les jeunes sont des personnes, et doivent être écouté·es avant tout.


Tout en prétendant protéger les enfants, les mouvements réactionnaires internationaux continuent les mutilations des enfant·es intersexes, dont le corps doit être “normalisé”. L'extrême-droite et ses lobbies alimentent ainsi un continuum de violences (familiales, sociales, physiques, sexuelles) qui doit absolument cesser. Ils privent les enfant·es trans de soin, violentent les enfants racisé·es, invisibilisent cel·leux qui, en ce moment même, meurent sous des génocides.


Peu importent les rapports, les promesses et les demi-mesures partisanes : les mutilations des enfants inters doivent cesser, et leurs droits doivent être protégés avant 2027. Nous soutenons, en cela, les

propositions de loi n° 1914 et n° 2286

. Un rassemblement pour le droit des personnes inters aura lieu

le 7 novembre à 15h, place Stravinsky

.


La Haute Autorité de Santé (

HAS

) a entamé, en 2026, l'élaboration de recommandations spécifiques sur l'accompagnement des mineur·es trans, dont la publication est prévue pour 2027. Nous condamnons fermement l'exclusion des associations d'auto-support, aux côtés des mineur·es trans et inters depuis des années, de ce processus. Nos savoirs expérientiels doivent être au centre de ces travaux, et le lobbying réactionnaire n'a rien à faire dans un travail scientifique.


Les personnes transinters existent

 

!


Les personnes intersexes représentent environ 13 000 naissances par an. Leurs corps sont en dehors de la binarité des sexes, mais on les assigne malgré tout à un sexe et à un genre à la naissance. Un récent rapport européen montre que 6

3% des personnes inters se déclarent sur le spectre trans/non-binaire

, donc en dehors du genre qui leur a été assigné à la naissance. La panique morale exercée par les réactionnaires à l'encontre des mouvements trans, qui “mutileraient des enfant·es” est hypocrite : ce sont el·leux qui mutilent les enfant·es inters. Les enfant·es transinters subissent ainsi une

double transition forcée

, dans leur chair et dans leur genre. Le rapport indique aussi que

44% des personnes inters estiment avoir subi une thérapie de conversion en France

. Ainsi, pour nombre d'entre nous, le parcours de transition, choisi à l'âge adulte, représente une forme de réparation de nos corps.


Le sexe, tout autant que le genre, est une construction sociale qui, factuellement, n'a rien de binaire. Un des piliers de la transphobie est la haine envers les personnes sortant de la binarité des sexes, d'où l'animosité féroce des réactionnaires, à international, envers la non-binarité. Nous …

author: anred
title: Histórico: Buenos Aires será la sede del 40° Encuentro Plurinacional en 2027
content:
Tras cuatro décadas de recorrido federal y de manera ininterrumpida, el máximo evento de los feminismos y las disidencias regresa al territorio donde nació en 1986. La elección se realizó mediante el tradicional «aplausómetro» durante el cierre de la edición número 39 en Córdoba.

Por ANRed

 


CÓRDOBA — En una jornada cargada de mística, debate y organización colectiva, la Comisión Organizadora del 39° Encuentro Plurinacional de Mujeres, Lesbianas, Travestis, Trans, Bisexuales, Intersexuales y No Binaries anunció que la Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires albergará la próxima edición del evento en 2027. La decisión se tomó a través del histórico sistema de «aplausómetro», el mecanismo asambleario y masivo con el que este espacio federal define democráticamente sus destinos año tras año. Tras la elección de la sede, se procedió a la lectura de las conclusiones de los más de 100 talleres que funcionaron durante el fin de semana.


Este regreso a las callee porteñas tiene una profunda carga simbólica y política. La última vez que el Encuentro se realizó en Buenos Aires fue en su edición fundacional de 1986. En aquel momento, apenas unas 600 mujeres provenientes de diferentes provincias y de diversas comunidades de pueblos originarios se congregaron para sembrar la semilla de una experiencia asamblearia y colectiva que terminaría transformando por completo la historia de los feminismos en la Argentina.


Cuarenta años después de aquella primera convocatoria, el espacio se ha masificado, transformado y complejizado. Con la única y lógica excepción del parate obligado por la pandemia de COVID-19, los Encuentros se sostuvieron de forma ininterrumpida durante cuatro décadas. Su persistencia en el tiempo consolida un formato único en el mundo: un espacio completamente autónomo de los gobiernos y los partidos, federal, plural, autofinanciado y autoconvocado que sirve como usina de organización, debate y posterior lucha en las calles.


De cara al próximo año, el desafío se traslada al centro político del país. En un contexto que demanda la articulación constante frente a las violencias y opresiones, el 40° Encuentro Plurinacional abrirá un nuevo capítulo en Buenos Aires con el objetivo de seguir reconociendo diversidades, compartiendo experiencias desde los territorios y fortaleciendo el tejido social hacia una comunidad más justa e igualitaria.


Todo en pleno año electoral, en el marco de una profunda crisis política social y cultural, en el gobierno de la Libertad Avanza. «Vamos a Buenos Aires a sacar a Milei, contra todos los fascismos. Seremos Nostres quienes les pongamos un freno a estas politicas de precarización de nuestras vidas» cerro una encuentrera.

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Feminist Spaces: Abusive Power and the Accountability We Owe
content:
Feminist spaces are not toxic. Feminism is not toxic. Accountability is not toxic.


So, what is?


This began as my rage, but now it is my love letter to the movement.


A call to do better. To be better. To build spaces worthy of the feminism we claim.


This piece is born from my rage. From the nights I spent questioning whether I was too sensitive, too difficult, too much. From the moments I swallowed my truth because speaking it would cost me opportunities, contracts, references, relationships, or my place in the movement. From the realization that I was being asked to trade my voice for access, my dignity for opportunity, my growth for loyalty and the truth is… I am done trading.


I know I am not alone. This is not just my story. It is the story of countless women, feminists, workers, and young people who have been asked to choose between their voice and their livelihood, between their dignity and their place in the room.


Maybe you know this feeling. The tightness in your chest before a meeting. The way you edit yourself mid-sentence. The calculations you make:

If I say this, will I lose that contract? That reference? That place at the table?


What is toxic is expecting people to be silent because they were “given an opportunity,” as though a job, contract, platform, or salary bought permanent ownership of their voice. What is toxic is calling people ungrateful, difficult, arrogant, or “not humble” because they refuse to shrink themselves to make others comfortable. Humility is not silence. Gratitude is not obedience. Respect is not submission.


Maybe you have been told to fly but only within certain limits. Only as high as someone else is comfortable with. Only as far as someone else can control.


What is toxic is encouraging people to fly, but only if they do not fly too high, too far, too visibly, or beyond control. It is celebrating potential when it serves an image, then resenting growth when it reminds those in power that no one was ever theirs to own. You may have opened a door, but they walked through it. You may have offered an opportunity, but they brought the labour, talent, courage, ideas, and commitment.


None of us are self-made. We are made by community, by people who loved us, taught us, challenged us, believed in us, opened doors, and held us when we needed it.


But we also showed up. We did the work. We learned, took risks, survived uncertainty, and chose growth even when it meant leaving spaces that wanted us to doubt ourselves. You may have witnessed part of our journey, but you do not get to rewrite our story as though you made us.


Let us speak plainly about the people who “hold the keys to the city”. The keys to opportunities, the keys to funding, the keys to visibility, to platforms, to convenings, to donor rooms, to decision-making tables, the keys to who gets hired, who gets promoted, who gets credited, who gets erased. Holding the keys is not itself the problem. The problem is when those keys are used to gatekeep, to exclude, to concentrate power, and to decide who belongs and who is erased. That misuse of power, wielding exclusionary authority as if it were neutral administration—is anti-feminist. 


Paying homage is deeply feminist, and I will acknowledge people who have labored for the movement for years. They have given decades of their lives, their energy, their health, their relationships, their peace. They have stood on frontlines, organized communities, written proposals, managed crises, mentored young feminists, and carried burdens no one else could see.


ON YOUR SHOULDERS WE STAND. WE ARE GRATEFUL. WE HONOR YOU.


But gratitude does not mean silence. Honor does not mean immunity and laboring for the movement does not place anyone above reproach.


Feminism was born out of questioning. It was born of women and gender-diverse people looking at what the world called “normal” and saying: this is not right. This is not just. This must change.


Feminism questioned marriage laws that treated women as property. It questioned workplace policies that excluded women. It questioned medical systems that silenced women’s pain. It questioned political structures that erased women’s voices. It questioned religious doctrines that justified women’s subordination. It questioned cultural practices that normalized violence against women.


Women at community gathering in Ghana. Photo by Random Institute on Unsplash


Feminism itself is a practice of critical interrogation. It is a …

title: Le massacre du 17 octobre 1961 à Paris : « ici on noie les Algériens ! »
content:
Ce jour-là, des dizaines d'Algériens ont été noyés dans la Seine ou massacrés par la police française à Paris. C'est un devoir de justice de ne pas l'oublier. Le 17 octobre 1961 alors que la guerre d'Algérie touche à sa fin, le

FLN

 appelle à une manifestation pacifique dans les rues de Paris pour dénoncer le couvre-feu raciste imposé quelques jours plus tôt aux Algériens et par extension à tous les Maghrébins (obligation d'être sans cesse isolé, et interdiction aux travailleurs algériens de sortir de 20h30 à 5h30, les cafés tenus par des musulmans doivent fermer à 19h...). Cette manifestation rassemble environ 30.000 personnes.


Début de la manifestation pacifique le 17 octobre 1961 à Paris


Le préfet de police de Paris, Maurice Papon, qui a reçu carte blanche des plus hautes autorités, dont de Gaulle, lance, avec 7.000 policiers, une répression sanglante. Il y aura 11.730 arrestations, et peut-être beaucoup plus de 200 morts, noyés ou exécutés, parmi les Algériens.


Ce crime au coeur de l'État français n'a toujours pas été reconnu officiellement alors même que les partisans de la Nostalgérie prônent la promotion de l'oeuvre positive française durant la colonisation dans les programmes scolaires

 

!!!


Le 27 octobre 1961, Claude Bourdet, alors conseiller municipal de Paris et aussi journaliste à "France-Observateur", avait interpellé le préfet de police, Maurice Papon, en plein conseil municipal de Paris sur l'exactitude des faits qui se lisaient dans la presse parisienne, à savoir le repêchage dans la Seine de 150 cadavres d'Algériens depuis le 17 octobre 1961 entre Paris et Rouen.


«

 

Monsieur le Préfet de Police

 

»


Intervention de Claude Bourdet au Conseil municipal de Paris, le 27 octobre 1961


- Les silences de Monsieur Maurice Papon


Claude Bourdet


«

 

J'en viens d'abord aux faits. Il n'est guère besoin de s'étendre. Parlerai-je de ces Algériens couchés sur le trottoir, baignant dans le sang, morts ou mourants, auxquels la Police interdisait qu'on porte secours

 

? Parlerai-je de cette femme enceinte, près de la place de la République, qu'un policier frappait sur le ventre

 

? Parlerai-je de ces cars que l'on vidait devant un commissariat du quartier Latin, en forçant les Algériens qui en sortaient à défiler sous une véritable haie d'honneur, sous des matraques qui s'abattaient sur eux à mesure qu'ils sortaient

 

? J'ai des témoignages de Français et des témoignages de journalistes étrangers. Parlerai-je de cet Algérien interpellé dans le métro et qui portait un enfant dans ses bras

 

? Comme il ne levait pas les bras assez vite, on l'a presque jeté à terre d'une paire de gifles. Ce n'est pas très grave, c'est simplement un enfant qui est marqué à vie

 

!


Je veux seulement mentionner les faits les plus graves et poser des questions. Il s'agit de faits qui, s'ils sont vérifiés, ne peuvent pas s'expliquer par une réaction de violence dans le feu de l'action. Ce sont des faits qui méritent une investigation sérieuse, détaillée, impartiale, contradictoire.


D'abord, est-il vrai qu'au cours de cette journée, il n'y ait pas eu de blessés par balle au sein de la Police

 

? Est-il vrai que les cars radio de la Police aient annoncé au début de la manifestation dix morts parmi les forces de l'ordre, message nécessairement capté par l'ensemble des brigades... et qui devait donc exciter au plus haut point l'ensemble des policiers

 

? C'était peut-être une erreur, c'était peut-être un sabotage, il faudrait le savoir

 

; et peut-être, d'autre part, n'était-ce pas vrai. C'est pour cela que je veux une enquête.


Photo d'Elie Kagan prise le 17 octobre 1961


De même, est-il vrai qu'un grand nombre des blessés ou des morts ont été atteints par des balles du même calibre que celui d'une grande manufacture qui fournit l'armement de la Police

 

? Qu'une grande partie de ces balles ont été tirées à bout portant

 

? Une enquête dans les hôpitaux peut donner ces renseignements. Il est clair que ce n'est pas n'importe quelle enquête et que ceux qui la feraient devraient être couverts par son caractère officiel et savoir qu'ils ne risqueraient rien en disant la vérité.

author: Binoy Kampmark
title: Sportswashing the Racing Circuit: Rwanda and Formula One
content:
Tyrants and demagogues love sports and the governing bodies that preside over them. Despite strictures, injunctions and warnings about dealing with unsavoury regimes, a sporting body or organisation can always be relied on to ignore the fine print of their charters and make a dash for the revenue till. While the candidates for such a list are long – the International Olympic Committee and the world footballing body FIFA figure with amoral sprightliness in that regard – Formula One (F1) has shown itself to be most promiscuous.

In its October 13 statement, FI glows with the announcement that motor racing will “return to Africa for the first time since 1993.” Then, the apartheid government of South Africa, one nearing expiration, still offered their good services to F1 to run the tournament as part of a controversial tradition. (The South African Grand Prix had been something of a fixture since the 1960s, barring the interrupting hiccup in the latter 1980s.) In a ten-year agreement with the Rwandan government, the Formula 1 African Grand Prix will become a part of the racing calendar in the early 2030s, beginning its first race at the still to be completed Bugesera circuit. “The new track will be developed to FIA Grade 1 standards as part of a wider sports, tourism, infrastructure, and commercial development project led by the Rwanda Development Board.”

The language of the announcement resembles the best traditions of sporting colonialism on the hunt for willing consumers. “Africa represents one of the most exciting growth opportunities for the sport, with more than 100 million fans already following F1 across the continent, and almost 60% of fans in key Sub-Saharan African Markets under the age of 35.” The project is celebrated as beneficial with its promise of creating “a legacy of supporting tourism, attracting investment, developing local talent and creating new opportunities for communities and businesses.”

F1 also praises Rwanda for its appeal “as one of Africa’s leading destinations for international events, successfully hosting major sport and global gatherings”. These include, amongst others, the UCI Road World Championships, the ICC Women’s Challenge Trophy, the 2023 FIFA Congress and the Basketball Africa League.

The Rwandan President, Paul Kagame, heaped praise on the project. As is a tendency befalling many African leaders, the decision of one country is treated as having been made for the benefit of an entire, neglected continent. “Today belongs to Africa. For more than three decades, the world’s premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement.”

What, then is there not to like? The answer: much and more besides. For one thing, the motorsport body, despite stipulating the need to respect “internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally” in its own charter, has decided to overlook the distinct unpleasantness of the Kagame regime, one not above using arbitrary detention, torture and stomping on free speech. In its 2026 accounting of the country’s human rights record, Human Rights Watch (HRW) notes continued attacks on freedom of expression and association, including the arrest of Victore Ingabire in June of the unregistered opposition party Development and Liberty for All (DALFA-Umurinzi). Among the charges she faces are forming a criminal group and planning activities with the purpose of inciting public disorder. HRW also notes a lack of progress in investigating the “suspicious deaths of disappearance of critics, journalists, and opposition activists.” Kigali’s spotty record on protecting refugee and migrant rights is reiterated. In terms of foreign policies, a stern eye is trained on the ongoing support for the notorious M23 armed group in eastern Congo, responsible for “mass summary executions, arbitrary detention, torture, forced labor, forced recruitment including child recruitment, forced deportations, sexual violence, and intimidation of journalists and activists.”

In June, the Democratic Republic of Congo filed a case against Rwanda in the International Court of Justice concerning “abuses attributable to Rwanda over a period extending from 1996 to the present day”. author: Ash Sarkar
title: A Motion, a Meltdown, and an Andy Burnham-Shaped Opportunity
content:
They’re calling it the E motion heard around the world, as the fallout continues from the Green party’s ‘Zionism is Racism’ policy, passed at its conference earlier this month.


The motion has dominated the headlines since making it onto the agenda for autumn conference, eclipsing what the leadership had hoped would be the party’s trademark rent controls policy. It kicked off a briefing war, led by GPEW stalwart and second referendum-enthusiast Caroline Lucas. It also prompted 

pointed queries

 from the Equalities and Human Rights Commission.


And now, unwilling to let a good crisis pass him by, prime minister Andy Burnham has piled in, 

ruling out any future coalition

 with the Greens while the policy remains in place. Supporters of the motion may greet this news as a strategic win – distance from Labour cements the Greens’ status as an insurgent, anti-establishment force. But there are rumblings of discontent amongst parts of the Green party of England and Wales.


It’s no secret that Zack Polanski (while publicly supportive of the argument that Israel’s displacement of, and genocide against, the Palestinians is the result of racist ideology) needed this motion like he needed a hole in the head. He was careful to neither unequivocally back nor deride the motion, and warned that it may “create a distraction” by putting Green members and pro-Palestine activists in a position of being attacked.


Whatever the virtues of the motion were, and still might be, Polanski was proved right on this latter point. The days leading up to his unsuccessful attempt to become the MP for Holborn and St Pancras were a storm of negative media coverage, in which he was forced to defend his party against accusations of being a threat to Jewish people. It would be wrong to characterise the byelection loss as a direct result of the ‘Zionism is Racism’ motion. But it didn’t exactly help his efforts to get elected either.


What followed were the first stirrings of Green infighting. For those steeped in the factional bloodletting of Labour party politics, this is all fairly tame stuff: Lucas, the night of the count, 

failing to shut down talk

 of Polanski stepping down, Ellie Chowns 

calling on her leader to “step up”

. But while the Greens might put the ‘civil’ in civil war, this level of publicly-litigated internal division is new for the party.


What’s more, local Green parties and councils have had to manage the reactions of a significant number of Jewish residents and organisations. Haringey council, led by the Greens, found its attempts at overture 

knocked back

 by one local synagogue. “We take it from both the tone and the content of your email that you are deeply embarrassed with the decision taken by your party,” wrote Highgate United Synagogue. “[Your] embarrassment is not enough. If you really want us to feel you do not agree with the racist and genocidal implications of your party’s policy, the least we can expect is for you to publicly resile yourself from that policy and commit yourself and your party colleagues to reverse that policy.”


Enter one Andrew Burnham. Though the early months of his premiership have been marked by his attempts to mend fences with voters alienated from Labour by the party’s moral turpitude on Palestine, the temptation to kick his progressive rivals while they’re down was seemingly too much to resist.


Condemning the motion in the House of Commons at this week’s PMQs, 

Burnham thundered

: “It is wrong, it is antisemitic, and this side of the House will have nothing to do with it.” Polanski, in a statement, hit back, pointing out that he’s the only Jewish leader of a political party and himself a victim of antisemitism – while the prime minister “arms a genocide and locks pensioners up for opposing it”.


Westminster grandstanding has since filtered down to local governance. Yesterday, Labour issued an ultimatum, saying it would scrap any power-sharing deals with Greens in local authorities unless local Green electeds reject the ‘Zionism is Racism’ motion passed by members at conference. According to the New Statesman, such agreements prop up 

more than a dozen local authorities

, including in Bristol. Nice gauntlet you’ve got there, shame if anyone threw it.


Perhaps Alanis Morissette might have something to say about a devolution-loving prime minister imposing the will of the Westminster government on local authorities the minute he thinks it’s advantageous to do so. It’s worth …

author: By L. Cam Anderson, Contributor
title: Jake Lang’s Tour of American Courtrooms Continues
content:
St. Paul, MN – White supremacist agitator and violent J6er Edward Jacob “Jake” Lang Zoomed into a court hearing in St. Paul on Friday, Oct. 9, as the Minnesota state government argued its case against him for kicking over an ice sculpture reading “Prosecute ICE” in front of the State Capitol building in February.


The hearing marked Lang’s second appearance for his

criminal charges

 after the previous hearing scheduled for July was canceled. It saw the state’s attorneys make the case for a hate crime charge in addition to property destruction against Lang that could carry a prison sentence, while Lang’s attorney argued in favor of a pretrial hearing to dismiss the additional charge.


Lang, wearing a polka dot dress shirt beneath a navy blue suit jacket, was making his video call from a familiar location where he frequently gives interviews, sitting in front of a backdrop branded for his “Blessed News Network,” which markets itself as “AI-curated Christian and conservative headlines.”


Jake Lang appearing on a monitor hanging above the court room.


Photo contributed by L. Cam Anderson.


The previous day, Lang was protesting at Cornell University in New York, carrying a sign on campus claiming the “Cornell 7” were innocent, potentially explaining his absence in the Minnesota court room. According to Lang, he was “thrown out” of the campus for this.


[Source: Jake Lang on X]


Throughout the hearing, Lang was quiet and relatively stoic, breaking from this demeanor to shake his head and show disbelief whenever the prosecuting attorney spoke to the judge. It was clear he learned from his run-in with Judge Reid Poland III in Tennessee,

where he was held in contempt of court and jailed for the maximum amount of time after interrupting the trial of Dalton Eatherly

, also known online as “Chud the Builder.”


The bedraggled Brian Karalus, Lang’s attorney, sat at a table in the center of the room across from the two prosecuting attorneys. Karalus, who earlier this year represented Shiloh Hendrix – the woman who was filmed at a park in Rochester calling an 8-year-old the N-word – had only papers before him where the two across from him had laptops.


Brian Karalus, Jake Lang’s attorney.


Photo contributed by L. Cam Anderson.


Lang watched silently over Zoom, suspended above the courtroom from a wall-mounted TV, while Karalus did not contest the government’s first charge against Lang, the destruction of property, but made the case to dismiss the second charge, that the destruction was hate or bias-motivated.


Justifying Lang’s actions as a form of “political speech,” Karalus added in a rambling speech to the judge that the majority of Americans and Minnesotans support deportations.


“Mr. Lang’s political position on this is not in the minority,” Karalus said. “The state might not like some of his antics and his theatrics, but that’s not a crime.”


Contrary to Karalus’ point,

YouGov polling conducted on Jan. 24

, less than two weeks before Lang’s vandalism, revealed that 57% of U.S. adults somewhat or strongly disapproved of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).


On the topic of deportations specifically,

according to Pew Research Center polling from February and March last year

, 51% of U.S. adults distinguish between immigrants who have committed violent crimes from those who have not committed any crimes and have a job. The data reveals that a majority of those polled actually are opposed to deporting such immigrants,

who make up a significant number of those targeted by ICE under the second Trump administration

.


Karalus made the case that the state’s decision to prosecute Lang represented “selective prosecution,” mentioning the

toppling of a Columbus statue

 in front of the State Capitol in 2020.


The statue, which was pulled down by a large group of activists two weeks after the

police murder of George Floyd

felony of first degree criminal destruction of property

.


Forcia ultimately agreed to

a restorative justice sentencing
