author: Marcelo Oliveira
title: Mulheres são maioria das vítimas de violência política, mesmo sendo minoria das candidatas
content:
O primeiro turno da campanha eleitoral de 2026 durou 50 dias e registrou 134 episódios de violência política contra candidatos e candidatas, além de agentes políticos.

Um aumento de 11% em relação aos 121 casos registrados no mesmo período da eleição municipal de 2022.


Os 134 episódios representam um caso de violência política a cada nove horas de campanha.

 E apesar das mulheres serem apenas 35% do total de candidatos, elas foram a maioria (52%) das vítimas do primeiro turno, segundo o levantamento.


Os dados integram a 4ª edição da pesquisa Violência Política e Eleitoral no Brasil, realizada pelas organizações de direitos humanos Terra de Direitos e Justiça Global, que pesquisa o tema desde 2016. O levantamento foi divulgado nesta quarta, dia 7 de outubro.


A porcentagem de

vítimas mulheres aumenta

 mais ainda quando a pesquisa separa apenas os casos envolvendo candidatas e candidatos. Dos 134 episódios de violência política durante o primeiro turno, 102 foram dirigidos a pessoas que disputavam o pleito. Desse total, 60 eram mulheres, quase 59% do total.


Para a coordenadora do Setor de Incidência da Terra de Direitos, Gisele Barbieri, “os dados trazem importantes achados para identificar os ambientes em que agentes políticos estão mais vulneráveis e pensar medidas de proteção. Quando eleitas, essas pessoas passam a ser vítimas de violências nos seus locais de atuação, seja no Parlamento ou no Executivo”, afirma.


Machismo e misoginia se misturam nos casos de violência política


A pesquisa mostra que a violência política é marcada pela discriminação de gênero e raça.

Quando se considera o universo completo de 70 casos de violência política contra mulheres, 45 casos envolveram machismo ou misoginia, nove envolveram racismo e cinco envolveram transfobia. Mulheres pretas foram vítimas de 25% dos casos de violência política medidos nesse primeiro turno.


A ameaça foi o tipo de violência política mais recorrente no período, com 64 casos registrados. Na sequência, aparecem 33 episódios de ofensa e 19 de agressão física. Também foram registrados 11 atentados, cinco casos de criminalização e dois assassinatos.


Mais da metade dos casos (71 ocorrências) aconteceu nas ruas, durante atividades públicas de campanha. O ambiente virtual concentrou 31,3% dos episódios.


Além disso, apenas candidatas sofreram ameaças de violência sexual. Em todos os sete casos, as vítimas eram mulheres.


“Enquanto os homens são atacados por sua atuação política, mulheres, pessoas negras e pessoas trans enfrentam também o racismo, o machismo e a transfobia que estruturam a sociedade brasileira”, afirmou em nota Glaucia Marinho, diretora-executiva da Justiça Global.


Policiais e outros agentes públicos foram a maioria dos autores


Em quase 20% dos casos o autor identificado da violência política era um agente público, incluindo parlamentares e forças de segurança.

Até o encerramento da coleta de dados pelas organizações autoras da pesquisa, nenhum dos 134 episódios havia resultado em alguma punição efetiva, limitando-se a medidas cautelares de urgência determinadas pela Justiça Eleitoral.


A região Nordeste liderou o número de casos (48), seguido pelo Sudeste (38). Entre os estados, São Paulo lidera com 16 casos, seguido por Rio Grande do Norte (13), Minas Gerais (12) e Rio Grande do Sul (10).


A presença de policiais entre os autores de violência política já havia sido detectada também em

levantamento

 realizado pela

Agência Pública

 durante o primeiro turno.

 El fracaso de las Naciones Unidas para detenerlo y la inacción de la mayoría de los estadounidenses y europeos nos hacen a todos cómplices del crimen, porque

qui tacet consentire videtur

. Si solo somos

voyeurs

de esta masacre en curso, tenemos, como mínimo, responsabilidad moral. Por Alfred de Zayas 


En los últimos 30 años, Norman Finkelstein nos ha brindado muchos libros brillantes, entre ellos

Método y locura, Acuso, Saber demasiado,

Gaza

,

Más allá de la desfachatez

y

La industria del Holocausto.


Este libro de más de 400 páginas documenta el colapso civilizatorio de las clases dominantes en Occidente, la traición a todos los valores humanistas, el rechazo demasiado público por parte de Israel del derecho internacional y la moral, con la complicidad,

entre otros

, de Estados Unidos, Reino Unido, Francia, Alemania y la Unión Europea.


Todo esto se ve acompañado por la cacofonía de los medios de comunicación convencionales orwellianos, que difunden noticias falsas, historia falsa y leyes falsas, especialmente con respecto a los palestinos como pueblo, a quienes se les representa erróneamente como “terroristas”, cuando poseen el derecho, reconocido en el derecho internacional, a resistir la colonización y la ocupación.

[2]


Nelson Mandela también fue tildado de «terrorista», pero fue fundamental en la lucha por la liberación de su pueblo. Hoy todos reconocen que el fin del apartheid en Sudáfrica era algo que debió haberse hecho hace mucho tiempo. ¿Cuándo veremos el fin del apartheid en Israel y los Territorios Ocupados? Esto es lo que Jimmy Carter exigió en su libro

Palestina: Paz, no apartheid

.

[3]


Los políticos occidentales y los principales medios de comunicación han invertido los papeles y han culpado a la víctima de su desgracia. Israel es el terrorista que practica el terrorismo de Estado y coloca trampas explosivas en los buscapersonas, como demostró de forma obscena el primer ministro israelí Benjamin Netanyahu durante su diatriba en la Asamblea General de la ONU el 24 de septiembre de 2026.

[4]


Israel nació del terrorismo

[5]

 contra británicos y palestinos, ha sido un Estado agresor desde su creación, en un sentido muy real un

Estado fallido

, porque no ha aprendido a vivir en paz con sus vecinos.


Israel ha atacado Líbano, Siria, Irak, Irán, Egipto, etc. En una infame operación de falsa bandera, incluso atacó el buque de inteligencia de la Armada de los Estados Unidos USS

Liberty

[6]

 en junio de 1967, matando a 34 marineros estadounidenses, en un intento fallido de involucrar a los Estados Unidos en la guerra de agresión de Israel.


Israel ha sido un estado paria desde su creación en 1948, e incluso antes.


El genocidio de Gaza no es más que una continuación de la intención criminal de establecer un «Gran Israel» anacrónico e imperialista en medio del mundo árabe y musulmán.


[Fuente:

cartooningforpeace.org

]


Sin duda, los gobiernos de Israel, Estados Unidos y la UE están moralmente en bancarrota.

[7]


Lamentablemente, la

percepción

de la realidad es más determinante que la realidad misma. Dado que nuestras acciones están condicionadas por la información de la que disponemos, nuestro juicio se ve influenciado —e incluso subvertido— por las narrativas odiosas que recibimos de los principales medios de comunicación, y nuestras opiniones se distorsionan por el incesante discurso de odio y la propaganda contra los palestinos. Esto constituye una incitación al odio y a la violencia, en contravención del artículo 20 del Pacto Internacional de Derechos Civiles y Políticos.

[8]


Los principales medios de comunicación difunden la versión israelí y suprimen las opiniones disidentes. No solo nos mienten, sino que nos privan de información crucial que cambia radicalmente la situación.


El público es manipulado, pero muchos se dejan manipular. Como escribió Julio César en

De Bello Civili (II, 27, 2): «quae volumus, ea credimus libenter»

(Creemos lo que queremos creer). O peor aún, como decían los romanos …

Part One: The Bolshevik Counterrevolution

Lenin: Butcher of the Working Class

Timeline: A Revolution Derailed

The USSR: Force for Global Counterrevolution, Accomplice of Fascism

The Relevance of the Communist Counterrevolution

Part Two: Restless Specters of the Anarchist Dead

Golos Truda, The Voice of Labor

Since the mid-19th century, anarchists have maintained that the key to liberation is not to seize the state but to abolish it. From Paris to St. Petersburg, from Barcelona to Beijing, one generation of revolutionaries after another has had to learn this lesson the hard way. Shuffling politicians in and out of power changes nothing. What matters are the instruments of rule — the police, the military, the courts, the prison system, the bureaucracy. Whether it is a king, a dictator, or a Congress that directs these instruments, the experience on the receiving end remains roughly the same.

This explains why the outcome of the Egyptian revolution of 2011–2013 was not all that different from the outcome of the Russian Revolution of 1917–1921 or the French Revolution of 1848–1851. In each case, as soon as the people who made the revolution stopped attempting to carry out social change directly and shifted to investing their hopes in political representatives, power consolidated in the hands of a new autocracy. Whether the new tyrants hailed from the military, the aristocracy, or the underclass, whether they promised to restore order or to incarnate the power of the proletariat, the end result was roughly the same.

Government itself is a class relation. You can’t abolish class society without abolishing the asymmetry between ruler and ruled . The first condition for any government is that it must achieve a monopoly on coercive force. In struggling to achieve this monopoly, fascist despotisms, communist dictatorships, and liberal democracies come to resemble each other. And in order to achieve it, even the most ostensibly radical party must ultimately collude with other power players. This explains why the Bolsheviks employed tsarist officers and counterinsurgency methods, why they repeatedly took the side of the petite bourgeoisie against anarchists, first in Russia and later in Spain and elsewhere. History gives the lie to the old alibi that Bolshevik repression was necessary to abolish capitalism. The problem with Bolshevism was not that it used brutal force to push through a revolutionary agenda, but that it used brutal force to crush it.

It’s not particularly popular to acknowledge any of this today, when the flag of the Soviet Union has become a dim, receding screen onto which people can project whatever they wish. A generation that grew up after the fall of the Soviet Union has renewed the pipe dream that the state could solve all our problems if the right people were in charge. title: TEV-DEM condemns racist provocation in Hesekê
content:
Following a demonstration featuring anti-Kurdish demands in Hesekê, the Democratic Society Movement (TEV-DEM) warned against attempts to fuel ethnic tensions in the multi-ethnic city. At Friday’s rally in the predominantly Arab neighborhood of Xiwêran (Ghweiran), around 200 people called, among other things, for Kurds to be removed from institutions in Hesekê province.


During the demonstration, in which a particularly large number of children and young people participated, slogans were also chanted against Kurdish national symbols and flags. Kurdish flags were also reportedly burned following Friday prayers. In a statement on Sunday, TEV-DEM described the action as a racist provocation by a limited group and explicitly rejected attempts to portray it as reflecting the views or demands of the Arab population.


“Limited to a particular group”


According to TEV-DEM, the slogans voiced during the demonstration were aimed at inciting racism against the Kurdish population and other sections of society. The position expressed there was limited to a particular group, TEV-DEM stated. “Some of the rhetoric directly targeted the legitimate national and political rights of the Kurds. At the same time, rhetoric was used that fueled social discord and thereby served the enemies of Syria.”


TEV-DEM emphasized that the anti-Kurdish demands must not be attributed to the Arab population of Hesekê. The movement also rejected attempts to portray the provocation as an ethnic conflict between Kurds and Arabs.


Call for an investigation into the incidents


TEV-DEM called on the relevant authorities to launch a transparent and responsible investigation into the incidents, demanding that those who spread hatred and racist incitement be held accountable. At the same time, the movement warned against allowing Hesekê province to become a scene of ethnic conflict.


TEV-DEM said that Kurds, Arabs, Syriacs and other communities should not allow hate speech to turn them against one another but should instead remain committed to dialogue and peaceful coexistence.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Nobel Peace Prize Awarded to Jurist Who Led UN Inquiry Into Genocide in Gaza
content:
South African human rights lawyer Navanethem “Navi” Pillay began her career defending anti-apartheid activists.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, the South African jurist who led the United Nations commission of inquiry that concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Pillay’s long career in international human rights law includes work as a defense attorney for anti-apartheid activists, president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, a former judge at the International Criminal Court and the U.N.’s high commissioner for human rights from 2008 to 2014.

“Everybody in the human rights movement reveres Navi Pillay,” says war crimes prosecutor Reed Brody, who calls the award “a stinging rebuke to Donald Trump.” Brody, a member of the United Nations Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua, also comments on the Trump administration’s decision to deport a Nicaraguan opposition activist, Jeffrey Jarquín, from the United States, where he was in the process of seeking asylum. Upon his return to Nicaragua, Jarquín was immediately imprisoned at the same facility in which he was once tortured.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee has announced the winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. This is the chair of the Nobel Committee speaking in Oslo this morning.

JØRGEN WATNE FRYDNES: The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 goes to a person who, with exceptional courage and integrity, has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order. This year’s laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted. The Norwegian Nobel Committee has decided to award the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

AMY GOODMAN: The South African human rights lawyer and international jurist Navi Pillay has been the United Nations high commissioner for human rights and a judge at both the International Criminal Court and at an international tribunal investigating the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. Most recently, she led the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry that concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

Navi Pillay is now 85 years old. She was born into an Indian Tamil family in apartheid South Africa. The first woman to start a law practice in Natal, South Africa, in 1967, she began her legal career defending anti-apartheid activists, including Nelson Mandela, exposing torture and helping establish key rights for prisoners on Robben Island. The Nobel Committee also praised her work in South Africa.

JØRGEN WATNE FRYDNES: A common thread runs from her early work, defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid, to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time.

AMY GOODMAN: Navi Pillay was in Nuremberg, Germany, at an annual conference of human rights lawyers and judges when she got the news this morning.

NAVI PILLAY: Thank you very much. Thank you very much. If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump. … The last thing I did is the delivery of the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide.

AMY GOODMAN: Meanwhile, Israel’s Foreign Ministry took to X to denounce the awarding of the Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay, calling it a, quote, “grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice,” unquote.

This is Navi Pillay speaking to Reuters last year about her genocide findings as the chair of the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territories.

NAVI PILLAY: Genocide is occurring in Gaza. We haven’t gone into Palestine yet. We will, because this is a permanent commission. And we named the three individuals that we felt were responsible. And we said — and the one is the prime minister, the other the president, and the third is the former minister of defense. And we said that since they acted as agents of the state, then the state of Israel is responsible. …

Today, we witness in real time how the promise of “never again” is broken and tested in the eyes of the world. The ongoing genocide in Gaza is a moral …

author: Ariana Figueroa
title: Immigrants From Ukraine and Sudan Could Soon Lose Their Protected Status
content:
The Trump administration has moved to eliminate legal protections for more than 1 million immigrants that have TPS.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

More than 100,000 Ukrainians and roughly 2,000 Sudanese immigrants are bracing for the possibility they’ll lose their humanitarian protections by Monday.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has not indicated if he will renew protections for Ukrainians, who first received Temporary Protected Status after Russia invaded their country in 2022, and for Sudanese nationals, who were granted the designation several times, most recently in 2022, because of an ongoing civil war.

The Trump administration has moved to eliminate legal protections for more than 1 million immigrants that have TPS. Of the 17 countries with the designation at the start of the second Trump administration, the only remaining protections are for Ukraine and Sudan, which are set to end on Monday, and Lebanon, which is set to expire Nov. 27.

Mullin is supposed to declare his decision at least 60 days before a TPS designation expires, but he’s made no announcement.

The lack of an announcement would put Ukrainian and Sudanese TPS holders in the same situation as 200,000 Salvadorians, who are still in limbo after DHS did not renew protections set to expire on Sept. 9.

If no decision is made, an automatic six-month extension kicks in. DHS has not confirmed whether the extension is in place, only that Salvadorians have deportation protections and work authorization, for now.

DHS did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment about TPS extension for Ukraine or Sudan.

TPS is granted when a person hails from a country deemed too dangerous to return to because of conflict, natural disaster or another destabilizing event. The Trump administration has sought to wind the program down, especially after the U.S. Supreme Court this summer determined that decisions by the executive branch regarding TPS designations could not be challenged in court.

Immigration advocates say the rationale for providing TPS to Ukrainians has not changed.

“With the war in Ukraine still ongoing and conditions remaining unsafe, the administration should extend TPS for Ukrainians,” Jennie Murray, president and CEO of the advocacy group National Immigration Forum, said in a statement. “Forcing people to return to Ukraine in these circumstances is dangerous and a departure from longstanding U.S. policy.”

If Mullin ends TPS for Ukraine, it wouldn’t be the first time Ukrainians have lost humanitarian protections under the second Trump administration.

Last year, the Trump administration moved to end new applicants for a humanitarian program created by the Biden administration that allowed more than 220,000 Ukrainians to enter the U.S.

The State Department has a do-not-travel advisory, its highest advisory level, for Ukraine and Sudan.

Fraught relations between President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy further complicate the issue as Monday’s deadline approaches.

Trump has grown frustrated with the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war, and has blamed Ukraine for a spike in oil prices, ignoring the effect of his war in Iran.

On Oct. 9, Trump moved to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Zelenskyy called the decision “a weak decision by strong partners,” according to The Associated Press.

On Oct. 10, Trump told reporters that Ukraine should “get a new leader.”

In an interview with NPR, Zelenskyy said the Trump administration said unless Ukraine stops long-range drone strikes on oil refineries in Russia, it could cut off U.S. intelligence-sharing with Ukraine.

The two leaders have clashed in the past.

In February 2025, during a visit to the White House, the president got into a heated exchange with Zelenskyy, appearing to break with Ukraine and its resistance to Russia’s invasion.

Trump’s relationship with Ukraine was also the center of his first impeachment, after a U.S. House inquiry found the president threatened to withhold military aid unless Ukraine investigated his political opponent at the time, Joe Biden.

The U.S. Senate acquitted Trump in an impeachment trial.

There is a bipartisan congressional push to extend protections for Ukrainians at least until the end of 2029.

author: David Swanson
title: The One Big Peace Conference and Open Borders
content:
Nonviolent Activism, What to do, Why End War, World

By David Swanson, World BEYOND War, October 16, 2026

Approximately once a day for forever, so approximately 365 times a year, someone proposes to me the same good idea. Hey, they suggest, I’d like to organize one big peace conference and create one big peace movement to unite everyone and be stronger instead of fractured.

I have several answers. First and foremost is: hell yeah, great idea, do it! do it! do it!

Another answer is: there are reasons the 364 other people who’ve said this to me this year have not actually done it, just like the 365 who thought of it last year. It costs lots of money. It’s harder to get people to a conference than to a rally or a protest. There are language barriers. Whoever is in charge of organizing it will be assumed by others to not be totally welcoming of their views. There will be at least some truth to that, since no two people completely agree on everything. If you have this one big conference for everyone in a physical location, as 90 percent of you with this idea want, it will be closer and easier to get to for some people than for others. Maybe we should attempt a regional one for some people. Etc. Etc.

But once a year, I like to focus on a different answer, this one: I don’t have time to do yours for you because I’m already doing it.

In 2014, a bunch of us created World BEYOND War to be one big global peace movement based only on Earth and nowhere more specific, to oppose every side of every war, to oppose every manufacturing of every weapon, to oppose every scrap of war propaganda and war culture no matter its origin, to abolish the entire war business in toto as a global nonviolent educational and activist movement collectively run by a global board. We now have a large and growing staff (14) and board (17) and advisory board (19) and list of active chapters (56) and affiliates (125) engaged in opposing war and promoting peace night-and-day, year-in and year-out. We’re not yet nearly what we need to be, but we are a good step forward from “Hey, I’ve got an idea!” And we have an annual conference online for everyone.

Of course, no conference will meet exactly the detailed vision of any single person. But you’re all invited to make this one yours. It is the reason I can’t stop and start over with your idea for one, so why not at least check it out? It’s a gathering and strategizing bonanza with dedicated activists from locations in dozens of countries, plotting as a global movement to abolish the most horrible thing humanity does to itself. Want to come?

Each year, we focus on a particular theme closely tied to ending all war. This year’s conference, which is coming up soon on October 23-25 on Zoom (Register here) is looking at borders, including how wars form them, what they do and do not prevent, how borders are militarized against the victims of war transforming them into enemies in a new sort of war, and how borders creep inward militarizing whole societies.

We’ll be considering the prospects for a world beyond war and borders. What would that mean? What would it look like? What steps are already being taken to get there?

The mythical world of “open borders” that rightwing politicians falsely accuse liberal politicians of favoring: what is that world in the words of people who actually do favor it, and why is it not frightening so much as enticing? This conference will include panel discussions, breakout rooms where we can all share, artistic performances, and the growing solidarity and power of one big growing peace movement. You should come.

If you select to make a recurring contribution of at least $15 per month, you may select a thank-you gift. We thank our recurring donors on our website.

author: Nadia Salem
title: ‘Revolution, the dirty word’: On Lara Baladi’s Z for Zarafa
content:
What happens after revolution? How do we remember, if we do at all?


In her exhibition, Z for Zarafa, which opened at Gypsum Gallery at the start of June and closed on September 23, Lara Baladi takes us through a scavenger hunt of moments, leading us into an archive of revolution, specifically looked at from an aftermath vantage point of movement, migration, displacement and the ultimate wrestling for freedom.


The exhibition acts as a physical installation of aspects of an online database,

Anatomy of Revolution

, which is a project exploring the various iconography and language of resistance movements. The database

consolidates

 research, visual, written and audio material from past and present global struggles, which Baladi gathered between 2011 and 2021 as part of her project,

Vox Populi, Tahrir Archives

. The body of data, a vast space of references, is organized into an abecedary using the Arabic alphabet, designed to work as “an educational primer of struggles for freedom.”


The exhibition, a multi-year effort through a wide network of collaborations, brought together the works of editors, writers and visual artists reflecting on experiences of migration and exile, alongside the works of refugee women in Cairo, blacksmiths in Imbaba, antiquaries in downtown Cairo, embroiderers in Islamic Cairo and potters in Fayoum, among others.


The opening day marked the launch of the first edition of The Anatomist, a publication “befriending” themes of “displacement, borders, exile and return” through commissioned articles and testimonies, a “companion” to the exhibition.


Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi.


In the website abecedary, if we jump to the letter Z, we find the story of a giraffe named Zarafa. She was a diplomatic gift sent from Mohamed Ali Pasha to King Charles X in 1826. She was captured by hunters in Sennar, Sudan before being taken to France. Destined for a life of spectacle, she, along with her handler Hassan al-Berbery, made the arduous journey to Paris, crossing the sea through Alexandria and Marseille, to satisfy a cosmetic political urge: first by camel, then aboard a felucca, before embarking a ship and then completing a 900 km journey on foot. Once in Marseille, she had to be hidden out of fear of her premature discovery, so the walk to Paris was completed at night with her head and eyes covered. It took 32 days. She would be the first giraffe in France.


Once Zarafa arrived at the destination at the Jardins des Plantes in Paris, she sparked a cultural and fashion frenzy. People would line up to see her, feed her petals, celebrate her, even dress like her. She lived the rest of her life for the next 18 years confined in the beautiful yet estranging garden, available to the public for entertainment.


“

Forced out of her home in Sudan and into an estranged existence in France

,” Zarafa, or Zoo-Zoo as her handler would call her, becomes a metaphor for migration. The story and image of Zarafa and how it generated a cultural frenzy are our entry point to the exhibition, capturing the transformation, or recognition, of an image becoming a symbol that garners a collective shared meaning and response.


This shift in meaning is examined through the exhibition’s main reflection on migration and return; we start to explore stories of movement and the political and personal dimensions of cultural exchange before the physical experience takes us through historical, present and personal stories of migration and displacement. These confounded layers of movement, exchange, migration and displacement lead us into a portal to Baladi’s data on struggles for freedom, of which Zarafa is an excerpt.


At the exhibition’s entrance, we are faced with For Glory of the Wind and Water, a tapestry holding moments woven through fabric, depicting tragedies which have seared through minds and into the public consciousness, like the viral image of Aylan Kurdi, the three-year-old Syrian toddler who was found dead on a Turkish beach in 2015. He, his five-year-old brother and their mother drowned in the Mediterranean minutes into the dangerous journey of trying to escape from Syria to Greece. In the tapestry, we also see images selected by Baladi, like Dorothea Lange’s

Migrant Mother

, a photo which became a global symbol of the Great Depression, taken in 1936 of a farmworker and her children at a pea picker camp in California. Zarafa appears in the tapestry in illustrations of her travels by …

author: Anooradha Iyer Siddiqi
title: Reading List: Anooradha Iyer Siddiqi
content:
We are taught to think of a refugee camp as an object produced in an instant, only in response to an emergency — one brought on, perhaps, by those seeking refuge. We are taught that refugee environments are provisional and abject, moreover, to be naturalized as such within the African landscape —

as

 the African landscape. We are taught to misread migrant spaces as lacking history or architectural expression. To counter these misdirections,

Architecture of Migration: The Dadaab Refugee Camps and Humanitarian Settlement

 looks closely at the complex settlements, ecologies, domesticities, archives, and material aesthetics. In Ifo, Dagahaley, and Hagadera camps, established in 1991 by the Kenyan government and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees at Dadaab, Kenya, in lands shared with Somalia and Ethiopia, the book finds African, Muslim, and Afro-Asian aesthetic worlds and a historical repository of partition, sedentarization, and migration. Dadaab forms a material afterlife of events long unfolding, through colonial and postcolonial time and space, and in multiple registers, aesthetic as well as social.

My book is grounded in 14 years of feminist and critical collective practice and research (see

Cohabitations

,

Dadaab Commons

,

Feminist Architectural Histories of Migration

,

Insurgent Domesticities

, and

Settlement

). While researching in dozens of archives and libraries in Africa, Asia, and Europe, and interviewing hundreds of women practicing architecture and art, representing governments, cultural institutions, and nongovernmental agencies, or living life in refugee camps, I read many books! If the anticolonial thought in Frantz Fanon’s

Black Skin, White Masks

 and Walter Rodney’s

How Europe Underdeveloped Africa

 anchored my work, its everyday tugs and buoying came from feminists.

Ifo camp Chairlady Isnina Ali Rage. Photo by author, 2011.

My study of the handcrafted acacia camp environments and interviews with many of their builders — including Ifo Chairlady Isnina Ali Rage and shopowner Shamso Abdullahi Farah, and Dagahaley farmer Maganai Saddiq Hassan — gave shape to a consciousness rooted in the social and ecological worldmaking of African, Muslim, and Global South feminists. Let me begin with three. Sylvia Tamale not only insists on decolonizing master narratives that suppress multiplicity in

Decolonization and Afro-Feminism

, but through her years of activism in Uganda and beyond, plants the working and thinking of African feminists on the ground, in the natural environment. This perspective is hardly limited to African feminists, as Radha D’Souza demonstrates in the

Court for Intergenerational Climate Crimes

 — based on her book

What’s Wrong with Rights?: Social Movements, Law and Liberal Imaginations

 — which foregrounds the workhorse labor and the place of the indigo plant (Comrade Indigo) within majority-world feminist intellectual commitment; she dispenses with reductive “West versus Rest” critiques through the perspectives of European underground and Third World intellectuals in the co-edited

Decolonizing Knowledge: Looking Back, Moving Forward

 (

open access

). Further articulating the vitality of social difference to inform constructions of knowledge, Saba Mahmood argues that those constructions must assert against universalizing epistemes, secular as well as religious, in her foundational work on Cairo’s women,

Politics of Piety: The Islamic Revival and the Feminist Subject

.

Store and shelters designed and built by Shamso Abdullahi Farah, Ifo camp. Photo by author, 2011.

From there, global Black feminisms were my north star. Yvonne Adhiambo Owuor’s

Dust

 dwelt within the landscapes of Kenya’s Northeast, the erstwhile colonial “frontier” constituted of migratory lifeways and marabou storks; her habitations haunt my book’s histories of land, emergency territory, and sedentarized pastoralists.

Lose Your Mother: A Journey Along the Atlantic Slave Route

, Saidiya Hartman’s attempt to fill in the blank slate of the historical record and her own life, helped me think with the stories of enslaved children freed from Indian Ocean

dhows

, raised near Bombay, and resettled near Mombasa: the negotiation between rescuer and rescued in the East African abolitionist settlement of Freretown that forms Dadaab’s prehistory. My book stands on the shoulders of Mabel O. Wilson’s work on: (1) spatial agency, as rooted in the bodies of builders and the physical labor …

title: Ilya Kharkow - How to Ruin Statistics
content:
Author

: Ilya Kharkow

Title

: How to Ruin Statistics

Subtitle

: A Lesson from Ukraine

Source

: https://voidnetwork.gr/2026/07/07/how-to-ruin-statistics-a-lesson-from-ukraine-by-ilya-kharkow/


“Statistics likes to talk about people in large numbers, because that way it can’t see their faces.”


EXCAVATOR


 No one looks at an excavator and thinks:


 “What a shame it’s not destroying anything right now.”


 But the moment I refused to take part in a war, people suddenly appeared who were convinced I was wasting my life.


LANGUAGE


 I’m tired of having to justify the fact that I was born in Ukraine and consider Russian my native language. I grew up in a Russian-speaking mining town in eastern Ukraine. It wasn’t a political statement. It was my life.


 Before becoming president, Ukraine’s current president played a president in the popular Ukrainian TV series

Servant of the People

. The show was in Russian. If most Ukrainians had spoken Ukrainian back then, the show probably would have been in Ukrainian too. But for some reason it wasn’t. Neither were most of the films, music, books, TV programs, and everyday conversations I grew up with.


 Some people see language as proof of loyalty. I see it as a tool. A hammer doesn’t become guilty because someone used it to hit another person. Language doesn’t either.


DUTY


 Talk of duty begins precisely where volunteers run out.


 No one asks a hammer whether it wants to drive nails or crack skulls. Its value is measured solely by its usefulness. Conversations about a man’s duty to his country often work the same way.


 If I am expected to pretend to be a tool, then let me be neither a hammer nor a rifle. I’d rather be somebody’s vibrator.


UNITY


 On the first day of the war, I boarded a bus from Kyiv to Lviv. Back then, every missile seemed to be flying not just toward the city, but directly at you. At least that’s how it felt.


 Somewhere along the way came the news that men were no longer allowed to leave the country. A strange feeling. That morning you had still been a person. By evening, you had become a prohibited category.


 Then soldiers pulled me off the bus. They forced me to sign a document stating that I was volunteering for military service. Later, friends explained that such a thing couldn’t possibly have happened. Later, women on the street politely reminded me that all men were expected to report to the draft office. Later, taxi drivers stopped asking for my destination and started asking: “The draft office?”


 TV talked about national unity. In reality, the world was losing its mind faster than a morning erection appears. I’ve already used some of these stories in my fiction. The rest are still too dangerous to publish.


 Everyone kept saying the war would be over in a few days. Four years have passed. No, the last missile won’t change anything. Some wars end before they begin. Others continue long after the ceasefire.


BORDERS


 There it is again: another well-fed, comfortable person talking about the importance of borders. It’s strange hearing that from people who cross dozens of invisible borders every day.


 The border between work and home.


 The border between a friend and a lover.


 The border between a child and an adult.


 The border between the person you were a year ago and the person you are today.


 Everything good in my life began with breaking someone’s rules. So whenever I hear that borders are sacred, I remember that love, emigration, and growing up begin with crossing them.


NATURE


 I’m tired of hearing that sex between men is unnatural. That we should look to nature for guidance. Fine. Let’s take a look at what nature actually has to offer.


 As a child from a broken home, it pains me to write this, but nature is not particularly sentimental. A cuckoo chick dropped into another bird’s nest throws the other chicks out to monopolize the attention of its foster parents. Nobody calls that unnatural.


 I’ve been on many dates. Some of them were terrible, but none of my partners ever tried to eat me afterward, as female praying mantises and some spiders do.


 Ducks evolved complex reproductive anatomy to protect themselves from gang rape.


 Maybe we shouldn’t look to nature for moral guidance in every situation. Maybe we should just make love.


 If morality is determined by nature, then infanticide, cannibalism, and group violence must also be considered natural.


 Fortunately, people usually build ethics not …

author: Harriet Williamson
title: Anti-Migrant, Anti-Muslim Extremists Drive UK Terror Threat Level Increase
content:
Anti-migrant and anti-Muslim extremists are becoming increasingly likely to attempt terrorist attacks against mosques and asylum seeker accommodation, Britain’s spy chief has warned.


MI5 director general Sir Ken McCallum said cases where anti-immigration and anti-Muslim views had tipped into “terrorist intent” were the “most marked trend” of the past year. 


In comments made as part of

his annual threat update

delivered on Tuesday, McCallum also said the recent upgrade of the UK terrorism level to “severe” (which means an attack is highly likely) was “driven in significant part by extreme rightwing terrorism”. 


The MI5 boss noted the case of a teenager who

planned to set fire to Inverclyde Muslim Centre

 in a racially-motivated terror attack, and described the demographics most likely to be drawn into extreme rightwing terrorism as skewing young and “driven by the internet”.


One mosque in Britain is

attacked every five days

, according to data released in July by the British Muslim Trust, the government’s partner for monitoring anti-Muslim hatred. It had tracked and verified 78 attacks and incidents at Muslim places of worship in the last year. 


The UK has seen a spate of protests and violent disorder outside hotels and addresses  believed to house asylum seekers since the Southport riots in the summer of 2024. 


August saw

attacks on addresses believed to house asylum seekers

 in Thetford, Norfolk, with a senior police officer

 telling the i Paper

 that such disorder is becoming harder to predict due to a “growing narrative” that all asylum seekers are a threat.


Last month,

anti-migrant protesters targeted

 the Marriott in Portsmouth, believing migrants were inside. In reality, a visiting Pakistani cricket team was staying at the hotel. 


McCallum’s wide-ranging speech on threats to UK national security included a warning about the risks posed by AI’s potential to produce new bioweapons, along with individually tailored propaganda and radicalising material. 


He named Russia as “aggressor number one” and the most serious foreign state threat to UK security.

author: Mag
title: Migrationspakt und GEAS: Neuer Anlauf in der EU-Flüchtlingspolitik (???)
content:
Dossier


„… Die EU hadert und ringt spätestens seit der Flüchtlingskrise von 2015 mit ihren Regeln für Asyl und Migration. (…) Inzwischen hat sich die Diskussion verlagert. Wichtige Akteure wie

Bundesinnenminister Horst Seehofer (CSU) richten ihr Augenmerk stärker auf die EU-Außengrenzen

. Die Idee: Die Menschen werden schon dort einem Asylverfahren beziehungsweise einer sogenannten Vorprüfung unterzogen, die Anträge würden in beschleunigter Weise bearbeitet. Abgelehnte Bewerber würden direkt abgeschoben. Mit Blick auf die Aufnahme der übrigen Menschen, also der Schutzberechtigten, sind zudem schon lang Alternativen im Gespräch, etwa dass aufnahmeunwillige Staaten wie Ungarn Geld bezahlen. Entwicklungsländer wiederum könnten auf EU-Zahlungen hoffen, damit sie ihre Bürger schneller wieder zurücknehmen und deren Perspektiven verbessern…“


Beitrag von Phillipp Saure vom 19. Juni 2020 im Migazin


, siehe dazu nachfolgend:


GEAS-Verschärfungswelle der EU: Rückführungsverordnung mit Return-Hubs in Afrika, Abschiebungen ohne Asylverfahren und bald die Aussetzung des Rechts auf Asyl?


[GEAS-Verschärfungswelle der EU] 38 Organisationen fordern: Bundesregierung muss im Europäischen Rat die Aussetzung des Asylrechts in der EU verhindern


„

Vor der Tagung des Europäischen Rats am 15. und 16. Oktober warnen 38 Organisationen, darunter PRO ASYL eindringlich davor, das Recht auf Asyl in bestimmten Situationen auszusetzen. Gemeinsam appellieren sie an die Bundesregierung, den diskutierten Vorschlägen entschieden entgegenzutreten und auf europäischer Ebene für den Schutz des individuellen Asylrechts einzustehen: „Eine von der EU genehmigte Aussetzung des Asylrechts wäre ein folgenschwerer Bruch mit den europäischen Grundrechten.“

Erstmals wird der Europäische Rat über Ideen diskutieren, wonach das Asylrecht vorübergehend ausgesetzt werden kann, wenn zum Beispiel sehr viele Menschen auf einmal an einer Grenze ankommen und vermutet wird, dass ihre Ankunft von einem Drittstaat instrumentalisiert werden könnte. Das würde bedeuten: Schutzsuchende könnten an europäischen Grenzen zurückgewiesen werden, ohne dass überhaupt geprüft wird, ob ihnen Verfolgung, Krieg, Folter oder andere schwere Menschenrechtsverletzungen drohen

…“ gemeinsame

Pressemitteilung vom 14.10.2026 bei Pro Asyl

 


Weniger Asylsuchende, noch weniger Schutz: GEAS verschärft den Trend


„

Die Zahl der Asylerstanträge ist im ersten Halbjahr 2026 erneut gesunken, während die Schutzquote weiterhin erschreckend niedrig ist. Das reformierte GEAS verstärkt diese Tendenz, wie erste Zahlen zeigen. PRO ASYL befürchtet einen Einbruch der Schutzquote. Denn mehr beschleunigte Verfahren bedeuten auch: mehr Menschen, die durch das Raster fallen

…“

Meldung vom 02.10.2026 von Pro Asyl

 


Ein Fundament, auf das gebaut werden soll: Der Migrationspakt ist erst wenige Monate alt, doch die EU-Innenminister wollen es noch verschärfen. Sogar über die Aussetzung des Asylrechts wird nachgedacht


„Den ganzen Tag hatten die EU-Innenminister am Donnerstag in Luxemburg beraten, am Abend trat EU-Innenkommissar Magnus Brunner mit Jubelmeldungen vor die Presse. Es gebe ein „Rekordtief“ bei den Asylanträgen in Europa, die Zahl der irregulären Grenzübertritte sei in den vergangenen zwei Jahren um 55 Prozent gesunken, verkündete er strahlend. (…) „Das ist eine wirkliche Veränderung, die zeigt: Unsere Reformen funktionieren“, sagte der aus Österreich stammende Brunner. Mit den Reformen meinte er das von ihm „Pakt“ genannte EU-Asylsystem Geas, das nach neunjährigen Verhandlungen am 12. Juni in Kraft getreten war. Aus Innenministersicht also alles in Ordnung? Von wegen. Der Pakt sei natürlich nur das „Fundament“, meinte Brunner. Und mit einem Fundament „hört man nicht auf, man baut darauf“. Und deshalb standen bei der Innenministerrunde gleich drei neue Reformen auf der Tagesordnung, mit denen die EU-Grenzen noch stärker geschützt werden sollen. Zum einen nahm die Runde die neue EU-Rückführungsverordnung formal an. Dieses neue Abschiebegesetz gibt unter anderem den Behörden weite Spielräume für Razzien in Privatwohnungen und anderen „relevanten Räumlichkeiten“ bei der Suche nach Ausreisepflichtigen. Abschiebehaft ist für mehr als 24 Monate möglich. Vor allem aber ermöglicht sie den EU-Staaten, nach eigenem Ermessen Abschiebezentren in Drittstaaten einzurichten. In die sollen Ausreisepflichtige gebracht werden können, wenn die EU sie nicht in ihre eigenen Länder abschieben kann. (…) …

author: Madhavi Madhu
title: Malaysian PM's meeting with Myanmar coup regime leader condemned
content:
Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing visited Malaysia on October 7–8 and met with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim in Putrajaya. Madhavi Madhu, a member of the Socialist Party of Malaysia (PSM) and a longstanding refugee rights activist, explains why this move has prompted concern and protests from human rights and refugee rights groups.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim should have maintained a stance toward Myanmar similar to his stance toward Israel, as both leaders fall into the same category: that of war criminals.

A protest was held on October 8 and a joint statement issued unequivocally rejecting and condemning the visit.

The protest was called by the Anti-Imperialist Coalition Movement (Gerakan Gabungan Anti-Imperialis, GEGAR) and the socialist student group AKSI and supported by local human rights NGOs such as Beyond Borders, Suara Rakyat Malaysia (SUARAM), Mandiri, Kuala Lumpur and Selangor Chinese Assembly Hall (KLSCAH) Youth, Malaysian Islamic Youth Movement (ABIM), and the Coalition for Clean and Fair Elections (BERSIH).

They urged the Malaysian government to stand in solidarity with the people of Myanmar and refuse all formal recognition of the junta leader. They also highlighted that this presidential-level reception for the Myanmar President violates the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Five-Point Consensus.

The joint statement demanded: The immediate cessation of violence in Myanmar and dialogue among all parties concerned; mediation by an ASEAN special envoy; humanitarian assistance through ASEAN mechanisms; and a visit by the ASEAN special envoy to meet with all parties concerned.

The Myanmar president stated again that the regime will only accept the deportation of "genuine citizens" of Myanmar (Rohingyans are not recognised by the regime as genuine citizens).

So while this diplomatic engagement was justified as an attempt to resolve the so-called "Rohingya issue", it has been reported that no Rohingyans have been sent back to Myanmar.

Nevertheless, the recent deportation of 1500 refugees to Myanmar and the planned deportation of another 5000 is a dangerous shortcut and a violation of the principle of non-refoulement — the international law rule that forbids returning people to a country where they face serious threats to their life or freedom.

The Malaysian Bar Association has sought the High Court's permission to challenge the government's repatriation plan.

It is important to be mindful that, apart from Rohingyan refugees seeking protection, there are other refugees from various countries in Malaysia.

A holistic, human rights-based approach is important, and a promised refugee right to work during the previous election is definitely a more dignified and humane solution for refugees and Malaysia.

The government could use readily available United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees expertise and services to manage refugees, while setting up the Dokumen Pendaftaran Pelarian (refugee registration documentation) with more transparency.

author: Majid Maleki Meighani
title: The Radicalism of Form and the Radicalism of Content
content:
The wave of high-school protests in France, which began in late September 2026 in the suburbs of Paris and spread to many other cities, has revived an old question on the radical left: is a riot left-wing simply because its form is radical? Drawing on the Marxist tradition, this article separates three levels of analysis: the social cause of a protest, the form the struggle takes, and its political direction. It argues that these do not necessarily coincide. The legitimacy of a demand does not guarantee the legitimacy of every form of action. The radicalism of a form of struggle does not guarantee the radicalism of its political content. And the political outcome of a movement is not necessarily what its first participants intended. The left’s criterion should be neither the intensity of images from the street nor even the form of action itself, but the capacity to convert scattered anger into organized social power. The article warns against two traps at once: glorifying disorder for its own sake, and accepting the frame in which the state reduces every protest to “urban violence.”

The current protests in France began with entirely material grievances: a shortage of teachers, overcrowded classrooms, decaying school buildings, mounting pressure to perform, and anxiety about a future that looks less secure to much of this generation than it did to the last. The first protests took shape in the Paris suburbs. According to reports, they were spontaneous, with no central organization or political leadership. In parts of the movement there were clashes with the police, property destruction and arson, and the state’s security response became one of the factors escalating the confrontation. The government has called the students’ demands legitimate while describing what is happening in the streets as “urban violence.”

Yet the movement has not stood still. In recent days, student organizations at both school and university level have called for convergence, and with the support of teachers’ associations and parts of the union movement, the protests have moved from the high schools to the universities and into a broader social arena. In this sense the movement is itself demonstrating the distinction at the heart of this article: the difference between an explosion of discontent and the building of collective power.

At such a moment, part of the radical left drifts toward a simple reading: the more violent the street, the more left-wing the movement. Another part, seeing broken glass and burned buildings, reduces the whole affair to “disorder.” Both readings share the same error. They equate the form of struggle with its political content, and so avoid the central question, which is the question of power.

Three Things That Are Not the Same

Any analysis of a social protest has to distinguish at least three levels.

The first is the **social cause**. What objective contradictions produced the protest? In France the answer is clear: a crisis of public services, austerity policy, and educational inequality.

The second is the form of struggle . How is the protest organized, and what means does it use? Riot, occupation, destruction of property, street fighting, strike, blockade, or civil disobedience.

The third is the political direction . Whose interests does the protest ultimately serve, and what relations of power does it change?

The common mistake is to slide from one level to another. Because the cause of a protest is legitimate, we conclude that every form it takes is also legitimate and effective. Because the form is radical, we conclude that its direction must be emancipatory. To clear the ground, three propositions should be set side by side:

The legitimacy of a demand does not guarantee the legitimacy of every form of action.

The radicalism of a form of struggle does not guarantee the radicalism of its political content.

And perhaps most important: the political outcome of a movement is not necessarily what its first participants intended.

The last proposition lifts the problem out of the moral register of “good violence versus bad violence.” The question is no longer whether the protesters are right to be angry. It is what their action does within the real network of social forces.

No Form Is Inherently Left-Wing

By “form” I mean the repertoire of tools and methods of action: riot, occupation, destruction, street fighting, strike, blockade, and civil disobedience. The essential point is that none of these …

author: Phil Wilson
title: Wisconsin Gubernatorial Candidate, Carlos LeMar Dixon, Joins the Class Struggle in Northampton, Massachusetts
content:
Northampton, Massachusetts masquerades as one of the most progressive cities in America – a place where police raided a homeless encampment and took away warm clothes on a cold, rainy “Columbus Day” weekend two years ago. In Northampton we manufacture armaments to reduce Gaza to rubble. We underfund our schools, attempt to build gaudy renewal projects to attract gentrification, but the city council convenes beneath an austere portrait of Frederick Douglas. We are a cauldron of pretense, indifference, hope and confusion – as American as apple pie. My wife, Shelly, and I have lived here among wonderful neighbors and friends for more than three decades, but like everywhere else we are cleaved into irreconcilable segments – rich and poor, working class and managerial class, college professors and tent city residents.

At 11PM on a Wednesday night I am walking fast down Prospect Street in Northampton, Massachusetts with our house guest, Carlos LeMar Dixon – a write-in candidate for Governor of Wisconsin. It’s a long story. Our pace might be brisk, but our discussion floats leisurely, expansively encompassing an array of topics from war and ecology to NBA basketball. We undoubtedly get a few double-takes from the occasional late night driver passing by – me: old, weathered and white, Carlos: long, lean and Black, almost a foot taller and young enough to be unnoticed if he stepped off of a pro basketball team bus.

The two of us, unlikely comrades at a glance, quickly discover that we share compatible visions of radical political possibility – our discussions seamlessly turn into plans. We talk about a visit tomorrow to a Northampton “homeless” encampment (I prefer the rejected designation, “homeless,” to the fashionable, “unhoused,” because the former seems to describe an existential condition, the latter a mere matter of circumstance, but this is a semantic trifle). Carlos has been homeless much of his adult life and I formerly worked as an outreach worker with a small number of clients who camped in the woods – thus, I defer to him. In fact, Carlos launched his Wisconsin gubernatorial candidacy from a Milwaukee shelter.

“We make maybe 50 peanut-butter sandwiches,” he says, “stuff some fruit and water bottles into a bag, and just listen. It’s not about us and what we want. It’s about them.” I nod. Carlos often talks about the “non-profit industrial complex” – the institutional shadow that moves with, breathes with, and shapes the institution of poverty. He warns me that a homeless encampment will be a battleground for control between politicians, police and various representatives of the agencies that oversee the industry of poverty. Our goal, if I understand Carlos accurately, is to find the unfiltered voices of the people living in the tent city adjacent to Texas Road by the Mill River.

Carlos and former Northampton City Councilmember, Quaverly Rothenberg, struck up a friendship on Instagram. Shelly and I don’t think twice when Quaverly asks us to host Carlos. Quaverly, too is a force, passionate and fast on her feet – a classically trained cellist and born iconoclast. The members of the entrenched, local political establishment regard Quaverly with the uneasy, frozen sort of contemplation that vampires reserve for baskets of garlic.

I have written a number of pieces arguing that the leftwing in the US is sorely lacking the input and leadership of poor and disenfranchised people. Carlos’ story fits almost too perfectly into my somewhat abstract political narrative. He remembers pointing (for a court investigator) at the spot where his grandmother struck him – he had just turned three. He recently considered suing his grandmother, until he realized that she had worked her whole adult life in the US Postal Service, and, despite becoming a supervisor, was still poor. “I just couldn’t do it,” he says.

He began his odyssey across the landscape of temporary foster placements at the age of twelve – nine different ones in a single year, followed by group homes and large institutions. I know the story, sort of. I lived in a foster home as an eleven year old myself, but my months of benign neglect taught me little about the larger system of trauma and abandonment. However, I also worked for three years in a group home in Hayward, California. I have seen my share of wounded kids passing through a makeshift system of overmatched bureaucrats and overwhelmed staff. Underpaid workers in the foster care system enter the lives of …

author: Monthly Review Press
title: The latest on Gabriel Rockhill’s “Who Paid the Pipers of Western Marxism?”
content:
Controversy, controversy…it’s no surprise that this book is selling very well. See more on this from

Bisharat Abbasi

, in his post: “

In Defence Of Gabriel Rockhill’s

Who Paid the Pipers of Western Marxism: Anti-Imperialist Marxism Versus The Imperial Theory Industry

.

“


DIGEST: Reviews, interviews, appearances


Marx Memorial Library

in London hosted a dual book launch for

Requiem for French Theory

 and

Who Paid the Pipers of Western Marxism?

with Gabriel Rockhill, Aymeric Monville, and Jennifer Ponce de León, who engaged in a discussion regarding the effects of imperialism on the production and dissemination of knowledge. Far from simply engaging in a critique of the faux radicalism of the prominent discourses within the imperial theory industry, the discussion was grounded in a reasoned defense of the vibrant international tradition of anti-imperialist Marxism. Topics included the imperial promotion of Western Marxism and postmodern French Theory, the international war of ideas, the failed efforts to discredit anti-imperialist Marxism, culturalism and identity politics vs. a materialist analysis of the colonial question, fascism past and present, the dialectics of actually existing socialism, and the current state of global class struggle in theory and practice.

Watch here

or below


The Left Chapter

, reviewed by Leo Schwarz:


“Shortly before his death, Herbert Marcuse wrote an essay on Rudolf Bahro’s book

The Alternative in Eastern Europe

. In the essay, Marcuse hailed Bahro’s ‘critique of actually existing socialism’ as ‘the most important contribution to Marxist theory and practice in decades.’ This statement was part of a coordinated campaign for the book and for Bahro that swept through the major media outlets of the Western world between 1977 and 1979–80. As we now know (or can know), a striking number of the key figures in this campaign maintained connections in the postwar decades to the Central Intelligence Agency or to various institutions and organizations that were either controlled, funded, or considered ‘friendly’ by the CIA or the U.S. State Department. In the first volume of his three-volume reconstruction of the ‘intellectual world war’ against actually existing socialism, Gabriel Rockhill examines the history and specific function of these networks of the ‘imperial theory industry’ that emerged after 1945, with his interest focused primarily on the Frankfurt School and the academic “Marxisms” of the Western world, which are usually categorized as ‘Western Marxism’…..”

 Read more….


Kaanan

,

 reviewed by Adel Samara


“…I was among those who criticized the Soviet system in its post-Stalin decades, and the lesson learned was that the greatest losers were the peripheral countries, especially the Arab nation, since the Soviets had long acted as a force restraining the imperialist beast. More importantly, this collapse was, in historical-materialist terms, a setback—an exception—because history fundamentally advances upward. Though our wounds were deep, the class enemy emerged victorious but also wounded, most notably by becoming the sole superpower, exposing its flaws and unleashing its brutality. In this brief context, I attempt to summarize Gabriel Rockhill’s book—a painstaking and rigorously documented scholarly work. Yet its timing is no less important than the work itself, for it constitutes a bold revolutionary confrontation that demonstrates the author’s profound communist commitment in an era when loyalty to communism has become rare and the fungi of internalized defeat have spread everywhere, filling the burrows with fleeing rats….”

author: Author and Editors
title: Who Gets to Turn Numbers into Evidence?
content:
Turning numbers into evidence is a form of labour – and in the Global South, that labour is unevenly distributed.


1. Who Gets to Question the Numbers?


By the end of 2018, India’s National Sample Survey Office had completed its 2017–18 Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) – the government’s own instrument for measuring employment. The report was not released. Weeks later, a version leaked to the press showed unemployment at 6.1%, its highest level in forty-five years. Two members of the National Statistical Commission, which had approved the report, resigned over its withholding.

1

 The immediate dispute was not over a mathematical error in the figure, but over whether the public would be allowed to see it.


The PLFS controversy showed how much political weight a number can carry. Numbers are central to public debate: debt ratios, growth rates, unemployment rates, poverty lines, price indices, and export values help decide whether an economy is ‘recovering’, whether workers are ‘employed’, and whether public spending is treated as ‘affordable’. But withholding a number is only one way to control its political meaning. Numbers can also obscure reality through the definitions, classifications, comparisons, and formats that make them appear neutral.


Unemployment rates are a good example of what numbers can reveal and obscure at the same time. An unemployment rate is never a simple head count of the jobless. It is a ratio between those classified as unemployed and those counted as part of the active labour force. That ratio depends on definitional boundaries: who qualifies as employed, who is actively seeking work, who has stopped searching, who is immediately available to work, and which forms of informal or unpaid labour fall outside the metric.


The rate can fall because employment has genuinely expanded, but it can also fall because discouraged jobseekers stopped searching, because precarious informal work is counted as employment, or because underemployment has been swept into a different statistical bucket. On its own, the number cannot tell us which underlying social process it records.


These examples point to a deeply political problem. Accuracy is only part of it. The deeper question is who has the power to interrogate a number. Who can probe its definitions? Who has the means to audit the denominator, distinguish a count from a rate or an index, or tell a nominal value from a real one? Who can trace a polished indicator back to the realities of labour and class, gender and region, debt and the world market?


These questions have real-world implications that affect the lives of billions. International Monetary Fund (IMF) surveillance and its formally voluntary data-dissemination standards shape the formats through which states report economic data; World Bank lending has financed and shaped the development of national statistical systems; the United Nations’ System of National Accounts defines the international standards for measuring gross domestic product (GDP); and sovereign credit ratings from Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch influence borrowing costs through methodologies whose final judgements are not fully open to public scrutiny.

2


This concentration of statistical authority leaves researchers in the Global South in a bind. They may ask how sovereign debt constrains public spending, or how commodity prices bind national production to an unequal world market. But the data through which they must answer those questions are often organised elsewhere, sometimes by the very institutions and standards they seek to interrogate. The pattern is not new. Raúl Prebisch’s account of core–periphery terms of trade

3

 and Walter Rodney’s account of colonial economies organised for extraction

4

 point to an older problem: economic domination shapes not only the movement of commodities, labour, and capital, but also the terms through which those movements are counted, compared, and understood. The question today is how that older problem reappears in datasets, indicators, metadata, and institutional standards. Nor does the Global South confront this problem from a single standpoint. A finance ministry technocrat, a business lobby, and a union research department do not approach IMF numbers with the same interests. The question is therefore not only where statistical authority is located, but whose interests its categories and measures serve.


For researchers, movements, and public institutions that have long …

author: greensyndic
title: Speed Kills: Snuff Capitalist Acceleration - Jeff Shantz
content:
The elimination of jobs at the workplace now coincides with the elimination of former workers outside the workplace under snuff capitalism. And this elimination too must be done in accelerating rates. Time, as always, is money from capital’s perspective. From Anarcho-Syndicalist Review, 95, Fall 2026.

Whether we like it or not, capital is accelerationist. Speed up is built right into the very engine of capitalism. Capital’s drive for accumulation, in competition with other capital for profit, means that it must always go faster, must always accelerate exploitation and value extraction. This is the drive behind the ceaseless, permanent, push for technological advance, from motors to assembly lines to robots to computers, to AI, and beyond.

Speed is the means by which capital beats its competitors in extracting value. More surplus value in an ever-shorter period of time. Any worker knows the tyranny of the clock in the capitalist workplace. Marx suggests that this surplus value extraction is either absolute, the lengthening of the working say, so we work longer beyond the point that we produce the value equivalent to our wages or relative, narrowing the time it takes us to produce the equivalent of our wages. Relative surplus value is the logic of the speed up—using technology to get us producing more and faster. Both forms of extraction, though, dominate the worker’s lifetime. Denying us rest, breaks, mealtimes, or even bathroom breaks. Stealing our life times—time away from family, from loved ones, from ourselves.

Speed also, significantly, overcomes obstacles—first and foremost among them the slowness built into human labor by the physical and mental limits and frailties of our bodies. Technological acceleration is therefore about overcoming the human element in labor. It is about controlling us too, taking initiative away from us.

Reducing and then replacing our numbers, and our capacities to resist or control the labor process. Fundamentally it is about rendering our human labor irrelevant, while doing the same to the embodiment of that labor itself—us.

Capital has used speed to overcome the limitations posed by workers on value extraction and accumulation. But under current and emerging conditions of accelerating electronicization (AI and its ilk are exemplars), capital is accelerating, not with workers, but without us. The working class becomes an obstacle to be overcome, not only at work but increasingly outside of work. The living bodies of the working class slow down the circuits of capital in distribution (consumption) as well as in production. Capital moves quickly from stealing our life times to stealing our life itself.

The elimination of jobs at the workplace now coincides with the elimination of former workers outside the workplace under snuff capitalism. And this elimination too must be done in accelerating rates. Time, as always, is money from capital’s perspective.

From Social Services to Snuff Services

Those expelled from production and (simultaneously) from consumption are too costly for capital, too much of an obstacle to accumulation. As capital becomes more desperate it increasingly sees any supports that might sustain the unemployed, such as welfare, unemployment insurance, social housing, health care, as a transfer of wealth by the state away from capital and to the unproductive and unnecessary. They are, from capital’s perspective, expendable. They must be eliminated. This is the impetus, and organizing principle, of snuff capitalism.

Like production and consumption themselves, this elimination must be done quickly, at accelerating speeds. Every day the unneeded are kept around is an impediment to accumulation, a drain on capital.

This elimination must at least keep pace with the elimination of jobs, of workers from work, of consumers from consumption. Time, as always for capital, is money. First and foremost.

This is driving expansion of and innovation in snuff industries, innovation and expansion of murder infrastructures, innovation and transformation of capital’s states from neoliberal tools (of crisis) to democidal weapons (of extermination).

This is made to happen through the dual spheres of the state as usual, through law (legality) and force (police). Increasingly it will happen through what were once called social services—health care as assisted suicide and coercive detention, social assistance as death camp labor and medical experimentation.

One focus of democidal …

author: David S. D'Amato
title: Jalan Libertarian Menuju Egalitarianisme
content:
Oleh:

David S. D’Amato

. Teks aslinya berjudul “

The Libertarian Road to Egalitarianism

”. Diterjemahkan ke Bahasa Indonesia oleh Taratsa.


Sebuah studi terbaru dari

National Bureau of Economic Research

 yang dilakukan Emmanuel Saez dan Gabriel Zucman

 menemukan bahwa “

0,1% keluarga [di Amerika Serikat] yang berada di puncak distribusi kekayaan kini memiliki bagian kekayaan yang kira-kira sama dengan 90% keluarga yang berada di bagian terbawah.

” Lebih jauh, studi tersebut menunjukkan bahwa “pemulihan” ekonomi yang terus kita dengar ternyata belum sampai kepada kelas menengah. Hanya mereka yang berada di puncak piramida ekonomi yang benar-benar menikmati manfaatnya.


Ketika sebagian kecil penduduk menimbun begitu banyak kekayaan negara, para pakar kebijakan dan akademisi sibuk mencari pihak yang harus disalahkan sekaligus menawarkan berbagai solusi. Seperti yang bisa diduga, pasar bebas kemudian menjadi sasaran kritik sebagai sumber semakin lebarnya ketimpangan kekayaan dan pendapatan. Sebagai pendukung deregulasi dan pasar bebas, kaum libertarian sering dituduh hidup dalam dunia fantasi dan menutup mata terhadap persoalan ketimpangan.


Kami, kaum libertarian, sebenarnya ikut memperburuk keadaan. Ketika persoalan ini tak terhindarkan muncul, terlalu banyak dari kami justru terlihat gelisah dan bersikap defensif dengan bersikeras bahwa ketimpangan

sama sekali bukan

 masalah, bahwa yang seharusnya kita lihat adalah standar hidup atau ukuran lainnya. “Kapitalisme sangat baik bagi orang miskin—sumpah!” Kaum libertarian harus menerima kenyataan yang pahit bahwa ketimpangan memang merupakan persoalan yang sangat besar.


Namun, kita tidak perlu memandang ketimpangan sebagai titik lemah dalam argumen kita mengenai kebebasan ekonomi, atau sebagai persoalan yang tidak mungkin kita menangkan. Hubungan ekonomi yang ada saat ini bukanlah hasil dari kebebasan pertukaran maupun kepemilikan pribadi yang sah. Justru kaum libertarian berada pada posisi yang kuat dalam persoalan ketimpangan. Kebebasan dan kesetaraan pada kenyataannya saling melengkapi dan memperkuat satu sama lain; yang pertama secara alamiah menghasilkan yang kedua.


Kaum anarkis individualis seperti Lysander Spooner berpendapat bahwa “ekstrem dalam kekayaan maupun kemiskinan” merupakan hasil dari “legislasi positif”, yakni ketika hukum-hukum arbitrer menggantikan hukum alam dan “menciptakan monopoli serta privilese”. Dalam kapitalisme, menurut Spooner, pemilik modal memperoleh kekuasaan khusus dalam perekonomian—kekuasaan yang tidak ada hubungannya dengan kebebasan sederhana untuk memproduksi, bertukar, dan berkompetisi. Jika dilihat secara menyeluruh, intervensi negara pada akhirnya menguntungkan orang-orang kaya dan mereka yang memiliki koneksi politik, yakni elite ekonomi yang mempunyai akses khusus kepada mereka yang membuat dan menjalankan aturan yang harus kita semua patuhi.


Intervensi-intervensi tersebut memang tidak selalu sempurna, dan sistem kapitalisme monopoli di negara ini tentu dilapisi dengan berbagai kebijakan yang secara formal dimaksudkan untuk melindungi pekerja, konsumen, dan masyarakat miskin. Namun, tidak satu pun kebijakan tersebut mengubah tujuan mendasar intervensi negara: merampas hak para pemilik yang sah dan menempatkan massa masyarakat dalam posisi bergantung pada para pemberi kerja. Singkatnya, tujuan historis negara adalah perang kelas yang permanen, yakni penggunaan kekuasaan negara untuk melindungi sebuah kelas bangsawan sosial-ekonomi.


Karena itu, kaum kiri sebenarnya cukup tepat dalam persoalan ketimpangan, meskipun mereka cenderung keliru dalam memahami kebebasan, hak-hak individual, dan pasar. Kaum anarkis pasar menghendaki

keduanya

, kebebasan dan kesetaraan, dengan memperjuangkan masyarakat tanpa negara yang menjadikan kesetaraan dalam kebebasan dan otoritas sebagai hukum tertingginya.


Persaingan yang benar-benar terbuka merupakan kekuatan yang membubarkan sekaligus menyebarkan konsentrasi kekuasaan. Kaum libertarian seharusnya berhenti mencari-cari alasan untuk membenarkan ketimpangan yang luar biasa besar saat ini, seolah-olah kita sampai pada kondisi ini melalui

laissez-faire

 dan kedaulatan individu.


Seluruh hasil publikasi didanai sepenuhnya oleh donasi. Jika kalian menyukai karya-karya kami, kalian dapat berkontribusi dengan berdonasi. Temukan petunjuk tentang cara melakukannya di halaman Dukung C4SS:

https://c4ss.org/dukung-c4ss.

Anthropologists have yet to give up their calipers

Secret history, or shaky historiography?

Occult Features of Occult Features

I have been sitting on this review for quite a while. This short book comes up quite often when combing through anarchist literature on occultism (and vice-versa). With the release of more than a million documents from the Epstein files bringing new relevancy to the issue of conspiracy theories, I think the most fortuitous time to publish it has come. Or went, because I again sat on this review for many months.

Occult Features of Anarchism, by Erica Lagalisse, concerns the alleged roots of classical anarchism (and the wider radical milieu) in Western esotericism and in particular, the late antique Corpus Hermeticum. This is combined with an anthropological analysis of conspiracy theories, loosely (indeed, very loosely) connected through the Masonic tradition.

Lagalisse begins Occult Features with two pastiches in her activist and fieldwork. First, she recounts dissuading a fellow activist from accepting an antisemitic conspiracy theory during an EZLN event in Montreal (pg. 3). Then, she observes Montreal anarchists marginalizing an Indigenous Mexican woman named Magdalena – on a speaking tour organized by the EZLN – due to a combination of gendered and racial prejudice (pg. 6). These events left her deeply changed, and her research interests shifted to the influence of theosophy and Freemasonry on classical anarchism (pg. 8). Through this analysis, she hopes to “illustrat[e] the cosmology of classical anarchism” and thus complicate anarchism's alleged relation to secularity (pg. 11). For Lagalisse, this sort of analysis is central to “a decolonized anarchism that properly challenges gendered power”, in which the modes in which the modern colonial state privatizes religion and gender – while reproducing its own cosmology and patriarchal structure – are studied (pg. 12). Thus her focus on esotericism: “any inquiry into the gender of the modern revolutionary left that digs farther back in history than the union movements of the masculine wageworking proletarian [...] necessarily stumbles upon the institution of Freemasonry, among other clandestine fraternities” (pg. 8).

Her first premise is that anarchism, like all Western political theory, is innately tied up with theology, following from Schmitt and Sahlins – particularly, the dialectic between the immanence and transcendence of God. Utopian socialism, anarchism, and Marxism rely on a “cosmology that is incipient in the Middle Ages, changing and crystallizing in the Renaissance, and gradually given a scientific makeover throughout the Enlightenment and up to the twentieth century” (pg. 18). A crucial point for Lagalisse here is the “shift from the spontaneous millenarian movement to the organized heretical one” which is related to the “dissemination of diverse mystical doctrines” that began in Europe during the Crusades – the Corpus Hermeticum is a “largely unrecognized” source of modern leftist politics (pg …
