author: Rodrigo Acuña
title: Cubans See Hope in Reforms But Worry Over How the US May Thwart Them
content:
Residents of Havana discuss the obstacles facing the revival of the Cuban economy amid the US fuel blockade.

Residents of Havana discuss the obstacles facing the revival of the Cuban economy amid the US fuel blockade.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Last month, Cuban Prime Minister Manuel Marrero Cruz declared that 158 new economic and social measures, out of an original package of 176 approved in July by the Cuba’s National Assembly, were being implemented and backed by 197 legal decrees. The measures include allowing private business to import medicines and other goods, loosening restrictions on private tourism, and authorising privately owned banks — under Central Bank supervision — on a regulatory basis equivalent to state banks. Adding to these measures, the National Assembly for the first time permitted foreign capital to invest directly in Cuban private businesses instead of having to operate exclusively through state-controlled structures. Private companies also will no longer be restricted to a maximum of 100 employees.

According to Daniel Torralbas, a London-based Cuban economist, the National Assembly’s new measures are “the most profound economic reform programme … since the 1959 revolution.” Headed by Fidel Castro, the government in Havana between the mid and late 1960s nationalized a vast array of U.S.-owned businesses that controlled major shares in key industries such as public utilities, mining, railways and infrastructure, and land and agriculture.

Mauricio Alonso, a 68-year-old former nuclear engineer who lives in Havana and now runs an Airbnb rental, is embracing the government’s new economic measures.

“On a personal level this is going to benefit me,” says Alonso, “because it’s going to allow, for example, me — since I’m self-employed — to partner with foreigners, to team up, to be part of a larger organization, and to carry out actions with my lodging business, and so on.” Working with travel agencies, in Alonso’s view, will now be made easier with the lifting of restrictions. “If I qualify, if I get accredited as such,” says Alonso, “I can carry out the work of a tour guide without any kind of problem.”

During the 1980s, Alonso worked at the Central Electronuclear de Juraguá, near the city of Cienfuegos, which was being built with the aid of the Soviet Union to become Cuba’s first nuclear power station. Alonso says that, “when the Soviet Union collapsed in late 1991, work on the plant came to a halt in 1992.” Although Alonso continued working in the nuclear sector until 1995, he “realized that the project couldn’t go on — due in part to [the] intense pressure from the U.S. government.” At that point, he decided to “switch to the private sector and start renting out rooms” after inheriting a large apartment from his mother.

Had Cuba’s nuclear power station become operational, it is doubtful the island would be facing its current energy crisis.

Despite a small recovery between 2021 and 2022, after Cuba’s GDP in 2020 contracted by 10.9 percent as COVID-19 effectively shut down international tourism, the island’s economic crisis has been worsened by the Trump administration’s fuel embargo. When U.S. President Donald Trump began to take action against Venezuela’s oil shipments to Cuba in 2025, which approximated 26,500 barrels per day, Cubans saw a serious reduction of fuel on the island. On January 29, the Trump administration formalized the oil sanctions on Cuba by signing Executive Order 14380, which did not simply add another sanction on the island, but instead, created a mechanism to penalize third countries that supply oil to Cuba. Should a country provide crude oil or petroleum products, then the United States government can impose further tariffs on that country’s goods entering the U.S.

For Amalia Díaz Pérez, a 21-years old recent graduate in philosophy from the University of Havana, the Trump administration’s oil embargo disrupted her final year of study. Speaking to Truthout, she said:

The total blockade of fuel imports — with only one ship arriving in nine months — caused public transportation to disappear and reduced daily electricity availability to a minimum. Consequently, my study conditions and most of my daily recreational activities were affected. Compounding this situation, household chores became increasingly difficult due to the strain of the nationwide fuel shortage placed on water and …

author: anred
title: Flávio Bolsonaro y Lula van a segunda vuelta en Brasil
content:
Con casi el 100% de las mesas escrutadas, Flávio Bolsonaro se impone con el 47,05% de los votos y suma en total 56.082.216 votos. Este resultado no le alcanza para ganar la presidencias, por lo que se disputará una segunda vuelta con el actual presidente Lula Da Silva que consiguió 45,14% de los votos, que equivalen a 53.799.870. Las elecciones se dan en un contexto de extrema polarización, incertidumbre e injerencia del imperialismo yanqui. El resultado de las elecciones brasileñas tiene un especial peso en la balanza de las fuerzas políticas en Latino América. Tanto por el tamaño de la economía de Brasil como por la polarización entre el actual presidente Lula y el hijo de Bolsonaro subordinado al alineamiento del continente a Trump, el Escudo de las Américas y su doctrina de seguridad Donroe.

Por La Izquierda Diario.


Distintos analistas sostienen que el voto indeciso fue el que sorprendió en esta primera vuelta al volcarse a favor de Flavio Bolsonaro, que quedó dos puntos arriba de Lula. Este resultado refleja lo que las encuestas captaron días antes, una mejora de Bolsonaro quien capitalizó el voto útil de otras fuerzas conservadoras.


La presión del imperialismo parece haber surtido efecto como en la Argentina en las elecciones intermedias de 2027. Allí con el respaldo de dinero y la amenaza de retirar el apoyo y hundir las finanzas del Estado, de la mano del Secretario del Tesoro yanqui Scott Bessent. En Brasil, la amenaza se materializó con el cierre de consulados y la embajada por una supuesta cuestión de seguridad que la Policía Federal investigó y descartó. Además, está el antecedente de Venezuela y todas las acciones de presión con aranceles, y otras presiones diplomáticas sobre el gobierno de Lula.


Por otro lado, en todos estos años de gobierno petista no se cambió la estructura de la nación dependiente del imperialismo, así como tampoco se resolvieron las diferencias sociales, el racismo ni la concentración de tierras en manos de los latifundistas. Los salarios bajos y las familias endeudadas demuestran eso. No es solo el grave tema de las apuestas on line, son los ingresos de las familias, cada vez peores.


Cronología de este domingo 4 de octubre


22:41


«Brasil quiere un cambio»


Después del triunfo en primera vuelta, el candidato opositor Flávio Bolsonaro habló desde su bunker en Brasilia y aseguró que «Brasil quiere un cambio», sin hacer mención a la fallida presidencia de su padre.


También afirmó que este resultado muestra el fin del PT (Partido dos Trabalhadores) y dijo estar muy contento con los resultados regionales.


22:25


Un resultado inesperado


A poco de conocerse los resultados oficiales, Lula habló dió un discurso diciendo que el resultado lo había sorprendido y hasta aseguró que había confiado en que ganaba en primera vuelta.


Pensando en el próximo round, le dijo a sus seguidores que en la segunda vuelta «mostraremos la verdadera foto de Brasil.» También afirmó que su campaña se centrará en convencer a todos los que se ausentaron de las urnas de la importancia de ir a votar.


22:01


Segunda vuelta confirmada


Con casi el 100% de las mesas escrutadas, Flavio Bolsonaro se impone con el 47,05% de los votos y suma en total 56.082.216 votos. Este resultado no le alcanza para ganar la presidencia, por lo que se disputará una segunda vuelta con el actual presidente Lula Da Silva que consiguió 45,14% de los votos, que equivalen a 53.799.870.


Muy lejos se ubica el tercer candidato, Augusto Cury, con algo menos del 3%. Cury adelantó que no apoyará a ningún candidato en la segunda vuelta.


20:30


El Partido Liberal acumula gobernadores


Según resultados proyectados, los candidatos del partido de Bolsonaro fueron electos en Rio Grande do Sul, Rondonia, Roraima y Santa Catarina, donde reelige. Además, disputa en una segunda vuelta los estados de Paraná y Rio de Janeiro, donde actualmente gobierna, para un posible total de 6 estados.


San Pablo, el distrito electoral con mas peso y centro económico más importante del país, queda en manos del mismo gobernador de la ultraderecha, Tarcísio de Freitas, que no es del partido del Bolsonaro PL, sino de otro de la derecha, República. title: The Encampment Movement against Evictions and Gentrification : A Report from Madrid and Barcelona
content:
On September 23, 2026, Spanish authorities violently evicted Maricarmen Abascal, a disabled 87-year-old woman, from her home in Madrid following her long judicial struggle with a real estate company named Urbagestión. She had lived there for 70 years, but could not afford the latest rent increases. In response, 10,000 people took the streets in protest that day. Three days later, a much larger demonstration established an encampment in the Puerta del Sol square, which had been the site of the

15-M movement

 in 2011, itself the trigger for the

Occupy

 movement in the United States.


Maricarmen Abascal passed away on October 7 as a consequence of the stress resulting from the eviction. Protesters have continued to occupy the squares in many cities across the Iberian Peninsula. A general strike has been called for November 11.


Here, our correspondents in Madrid and Barcelona offer a view from within the movement against evictions and gentrification that has spread across Spain and Catalunya.


Anti-fascists gather to defend the housing encampment in Madrid’s Plaza del Sol, 2026.


The housing movement in Spain has a long and complex history. For any period that we might choose as a point of departure, there always exists a prior precedent that could serve just as well—so where we begin depends on how we wish to make sense of what is happening today, how we wish to narrate this story that is still being written in the streets. What follows, then, is an attempt, however insufficient and incomplete, to tell this story, in hopes that you can learn or be inspired by something from it and, in this way, become part of this story and build upon it wherever you live.


We could perhaps begin with the

15-M movement

, which erupted a decade and a half ago as part of the sequence of uprisings that unfolded across the globe in 2011. Encampments spread across Spain much as they have today, full of people clamoring for “

real democracy

.”


Whereas elsewhere, repression often put these movements to an unresolved end, in Spain, this movement culminated with the formation of several far-left political parties, including Podemos, as well as strong municipalist movements in Madrid, Barcelona, and other cities. Today, these parties lie in ruins, while the municipalists have largely lost whatever power they once held. Ultimately, much like

Occupy Wall Street

 and the Arab Spring, the true legacy of this sequence remains ambiguous, contested, and open to interpretation. Perhaps the 15-M movement is not the beginning of the story we’re telling, but simply the ruins from which the current one is being told.


Riot police are covered in eggs and paint while attempting to evict a building in Barcelona, 2021.


The movement that is now swelling across Spain emerged as a result of strong and stable union-style organizations that operate apart from the official institutional structures that are otherwise so present and influential in political life here. These organizations were built to tackle the housing crisis using horizontal and grassroots power, while simultaneously driving widespread and popular mobilizations like those we are witnessing today. These unions are novel in that they don’t involve questions of work directly, but rather address the conditions in which we live. The movement’s most significant antecedents lie in the creation of organizations such as the PAH (Platform for People Affected by Mortgages), the first chapter of which was founded in Barcelona in 2009. Like the more recently created housing organizations, the PAH groups practice what we call “social unionism.”


The premise is simple: an individual problem like a person facing the threat of losing their home is transformed into a collective issue addressed through shared political action. A variety of union-style tactics soon began to emerge, leading to the halting of many imminent evictions.


A group of thirty or so people assembles in front of an apartment in the historic city center as the sun is rising. People cling to one another tightly, locked arm in arm, crowding in front of the door of the building’s entrance while several vans of riot police pull up and park nearby as scheduled. There’s an announcement from a police loudspeaker to the effect that people must disperse, but no one does. Eventually, the cops move in, struggling to pull each person away one by one, until finally everyone has been cleared. In the end, the eviction is successful, but it …

author: Deaglan Godwin
title: NSW Socialists launch campaign with a bang!
content:
“Our message is clear: the working class isn’t going to take this shit lying down anymore”, roared Ryan Chapman, NSW Socialists candidate for the seat of Wollongong, at the launch of the party’s 2027 state election campaign.

The 300-strong crowd burst out in applause. The venue, Ashfield Town Hall, was packed to capacity.

The speakers, three of the party’s six lower-house candidates, reflected Australia’s modern, multicultural working class. The first speaker, Alma Torlakovic, candidate for the Western Sydney seat of Granville, spoke movingly of her childhood in war-torn Bosnia and Croatia. Shovan Bhattarai, candidate for the inner-west seat of Newtown, humorously described the multicultural lunchtimes at her Western Sydney primary school. Chapman spoke of growing up working class on the South Coast and joining the navy as his only option.

The housing crisis was a recurring theme. Chapman spoke about the campaign to defend the Bellambi housing estate north of Wollongong. Labor MP for the area and state planning minister Paul Scully wants to knock down the estate because it is on prized beachfront property. After detailing the eye-watering average rent rises in the inner-west, Bhattarai explained the party’s housing policy of slashing rents by 35 percent, implementing a rent freeze and building 150,000 new public housing units.

Housing is a clear example of how the NSW Labor government screws over workers to protect the profits of the rich. Labor is happy to take workers’ votes, but once in government, the party, in Torlakovic’s words, “treat Western Sydney like garbage”. The crowd was full of boos and cries of “shame” at any mention of federal or state Labor politicians.

“We are the party for the millions of people who make this city run”, declared Bhattarai. This unashamed emphasis on class politics is a refreshing antidote to a mainstream politics filled with either middle-of-the-road progressivism or vitriolic far-right bile.

After the speeches, people stuck around for food, drinks and campaign strategising. New volunteers met the campaign managers in their electorates, and people signed up for the numerous party activities planned for the coming weeks. The launch kicked off a frenetic fortnight of activity. Party activists hope this will help firmly establish the party among prospective voters and meet more people who will join the movement.

While we may not be backed by billionaires or the mainstream media, the socialist movement has always been fuelled by endless enthusiasm and dedication combined with a radical vision of a better world. If you want to be a part of that, get involved with the campaign today.

author: Javier Moreno Zacarés
title: Fifteen Years Later
content:
Fifteen years after the indignados occupied the Puerta del Sol, Madrid’s central plaza is once again the locus of a mass movement that has brought Spain to a political impasse. How are we back here again? The immediate trigger was the eviction of an elderly tenant. Maricarmen Abascal, who had occupied her rent-capped apartment in central Madrid since 1956, was expelled from her home on 23 September after the investment fund Urbagestión acquired the property and exploited a legal loophole to quintuple her rent. Maricarmen’s age and vulnerability – the 87-year-old was removed on a hospital bed and has since died – made it a particularly egregious breach of the moral economy. The case struck a nerve, prompting a political storm; the government has now announced a snap election. As protests spread nationwide, the encampment at Puerta del Sol consolidated under the leadership of the Sindicato de Inquilinas, Madrid’s tenant union. Media outlets are reporting on the motions passed at the open-air general assembly. One decision has been of particular public interest: a general strike for the right to housing, announced for 11 November, a few weeks before the election.

The political elite faces a reckoning. At the outset of the current parliamentary term in 2023, the progressive coalition headed by Sánchez’s centre-left Socialist Party (PSOE) placed housing at the top of the agenda. The promises were ambitious: the provision of mass social housing, the imposition of rent controls, the reassertion of the public interest against rentier logics. Yet these commitments yielded little. This was partly due to the obstruction of the right, both in parliament and in the regional governments under its control. But a share of the blame lies in the ambivalence of the Socialist Party itself, whose ministers have repeatedly expressed discomfort with what they regard as excessive regulation of housing. The junior coalition partner Sumar, a nebulous alliance of progressive parties, has proven feeble in holding the Socialists to account. They are now also a target of the protests, who charge the entire governing alliance of complicity with the rentiers. Amid the fury in the streets, Sumar’s cabinet members hastened to pressure the Socialist housing minister, Isabel Rodríguez – herself a landlord who owns multiple properties – to approve emergency measures to block evictions and institute permanent rolling contracts, both key demands of the tenant unions. Last Friday, both measures were struck down in parliament, to the anger of the masses gathered outside.

That a recalcitrant right-wing opposition – comprising the conservative People’s Party (PP) and the far-right Vox – would block the measures was entirely predictable. What was less so was that the deciding vote would be cast by an ally of the government: the centre-right Junts, party of the Catalan-nationalist bourgeoisie. The vote revealed a peculiarity of the Spanish conjuncture. Though the right-wing bloc is the largest in parliament, it is divided along nationalist lines, fractures the government has exploited – drawing support from the Catalan right to keep the Spanish unionist right out of power. It was always an unstable arrangement, premised on nation trumping class. On the housing question, the plurinational right voted in alignment with its shared interests (Junts has the largest proportion of landlords in parliament).

The Spanish right now enjoys a comfortable lead in the polls, which point to a PP–Vox coalition if elections were held tomorrow. But the wind is blowing in an uncomfortable direction for them. Over the past week, public opinion has swung massively in favour of regulating house prices, even among a slim majority of right-wing voters. In a matter of days, the protests have shifted the national conversation away from the right’s preferred talking points of crime and migration, overwriting a summer of hysteria around the border crisis in Ceuta. They have also deflected attention from the corruption scandals afflicting PSOE: only last June, a former minister in Sánchez’s cabinet was sentenced to twenty-four years in prison for influence-peddling related to substandard Covid-19 face masks. Ever the survivor, Sánchez has seized the moment with a characteristically audacious move. He has framed the election on 29 November as a plebiscite on the housing question, shifting the blame for it onto the right and boldly appealing to the electorate to ‘subdue the elites’ …

title: «12 de Octubre, nada que celebrar»: pueblos originarios marchan contra los desalojos y la extranjerización de la tierra
content:
Marcha del Contrafestejo del 12 de octubre de 2024. Foto: archivo Nicolás Parodi / Página 12


Bajo la consigna “¡Nada que celebrar, muchas luchas que sostener!”, la Organización de Comunidades y Pueblos Originarios (ORCOPO) convocó a una marcha y contrafestejo para este lunes 12 de octubre, a las 18, en Plaza de los Dos Congresos. La jornada de lucha denunciará el avance de los desalojos, la criminalización de las comunidades indígenas, la extranjerización de la tierra, los proyectos extractivistas, la entrega, el saqueo y el despojo, en un escenario de creciente conflictividad territorial luego del reciente fallo de la Corte Suprema. La convocatoria se da en el marco de la confirmación judicial del desalojo de la Lof Inalef, en Río Negro, y una nueva amenaza contra la Lof Melo, en Neuquén. Ambos casos se suman a otros conflictos territoriales que atraviesan comunidades originarias en distintas regiones del país y que, para las organizaciones indígenas, evidencian una ofensiva sobre sus territorios en paralelo con el desmantelamiento de herramientas de protección y la reactivación de la derogación de la Ley de Tierras Rurales. También exigen justicia por Rafael Nahuel y libertad para quienes permanecen detenidos por luchar.

Por ANRed.

title: Çelik: No budget’ for students’ demands, yet 7.4 billion TL transferred to foundations
content:
As universities begin the autumn semester of the 2026–2027 academic year, a student at Istanbul Technical University (ITÜ) was expelled from a dormitory run by the Credit and Dormitories Institution (KYK) on the grounds that they had failed to pass the preparatory year in a single semester. With nowhere to stay, the student was forced to take refuge in the university library for days. They are now trying to continue their education while working to support themselves.


The experience of the ITÜ student is one example of the problems faced by thousands of students who are forced to work to continue their education, only to be labelled academically unsuccessful as a result and deprived of their right to housing.


Being a university student in Turkey is increasingly becoming less an educational experience and more a struggle for survival. The monthly scholarship or student loan of 4,000 TL (some 73 euros) provided to undergraduate students by the Ministry of Youth and Sports is not even enough to cover their basic needs, particularly in the face of rental prices and living costs in major cities.


Students forced working while studying


Rapidly rising rents for private dormitories and apartments in major cities have made KYK dormitories virtually the only housing option for students. Unable to receive sufficient financial support from their families due to the deepening economic crisis, students are forced to work in insecure and harsh conditions to make ends meet. When they cannot devote enough time to their studies as a result, the system labels them “unsuccessful”. This “failure” is then punished by depriving them of one of the most fundamental human rights: the right to housing.


ANF spoke with Senem Çelik of the

We Cannot Afford to Live Movement

, which has been working for days to bring the expulsion of an ITÜ student from a KYK dormitory to public attention, about the housing crisis and poverty experienced by students.


Referring to the mother who appealed for help on Instagram for her son, who had been expelled from his dormitory, saying, 'I don’t want my son to be left on the street. He hadn’t slept for two days, and neither have I,' Senem Çelik described what had happened: “Recently, we heard the desperate plea of a mother who explained that her child had been expelled from the dormitory for having to repeat a year. A fellow student at ITÜ has been trying to get through each day and continue their education since the semester began, sometimes staying in the library and sometimes at friends’ homes. The reason our fellow students have had to continue their education this way is that they have been forced to work while studying, which in turn has meant having to repeat the year.”


Stating that the

We Cannot Afford to Live Movemen

t has been working for years to bring the housing crisis facing young people to public attention and secure concrete gains for students, Senem Çelik said the housing problem could not be explained solely through economic indicators. She pointed out that the way university bureaucracies operate, treating students as secondary concerns, and their proposed solutions, which run counter to the ordinary realities of life, further deepen the injustices students experience.


Çelik said university students face not only housing difficulties and poverty but also declining educational quality, the failure of democratic mechanisms within universities to function, sexism in academia and harassment. She added that these problems cannot be considered separately from the deep poverty and the condition of being “excluded from citizenship” experienced by broad sections of society.


Senem Çelik said: “For example, struggles against the injustices experienced by students affected by earthquakes require us to connect with all citizens whose needs are ignored for the sake of profit and to support their struggles. Campaigns against poor living conditions in student dormitories bring together all students who cannot afford to heat their homes with natural gas or even pay for their meals.”


She added: “Alongside the exclusion of the public from all mechanisms of governance and oversight, students at universities, which should be centres of science and free thought, are increasingly being excluded from all decision-making and oversight mechanisms as universities are privatised and run like companies. Students do not even have a say in matters concerning their own living spaces in the dormitories …

title: İzmir halkından EÜ’deki köpeklerin toplatılmasına tepki
content:
İzmir - Ege Üniversitesi Hayvan Hakları Topluluğu ve İzmir Yaşam Hakkı Savunucuları, dün gece Ege Üniversitesi Hayvan Hakları Topluluğu tarafından öğrencilerin beslediği eğitim alanındaki köpeklerin polis zoruyla toplatılmasına tepki göstermek için Bornova’da yürüyüş ve basın açıklaması düzenledi. Bornova Cumhuriyet Meydanı’ndan Küçükpark Meydanı’na yürüyen İzmirliler burada basın açıklaması gerçekleştirdi. Basın metnini Melodi Zengin okudu.

Ege Üniversitesi’nde 2022 yılında rektörlük tarafından Hayvan Hakları Topluluğu’na tahsis edilen, yaklaşık 160 köpeğin padoklar içinde öğrenciler tarafından bakıldığı yaşam alanına gece 00.00 sıralarında Bornova Belediyesi ve çevik kuvvet eşliğinde baskın yapılarak köpeklere el konulduğunu belirten Zengin, “Buna karşı çıkan öğrenciler ve hak savunucuları polis tarafından darp edildi, biber gazı sıkıldı, alanda darptan dolayı yaralananlar oldu ve bu işkence gözükmesin diye alandaki tüm elektrik kesildi. Bu alan, kampüsteki köpeklerin öğrencilerin harçlıklarından artırdıkları paralarla tedavi ettirdikleri, besledikleri, ilgilendikleri; çoğu öğrencinin de mezun olduktan sonra alandan bir köpeği sahiplenip memleketine götürdüğü bir alandı” dedi.

AKP’li kayyım rektör Musa Alcı’nın yaklaşık 6 ay önce Cumhurbaşkanı kararnamesiyle Ege Üniversitesi’ne rektör olarak atandığını belirten Zengin, “İlk icraatı okula eylem yasağı koymak olduktan sonra ikinci icraatı da gece yarısı çevik kuvvet eşliğinde yaşam alanından köpek toplatmak oldu. Musa Alcı’nın şikayeti üzerine boşaltılan alanın özel yurt inşaatı için kullanılacağına dair söylemleri duymaktayız. Musa Alcı bu üniversiteye rektör olmadan önce AKP’ye secde ederken bu köpekler bu kampüsteydi” diye konuştu.

Köpeklerin çoğunun çipli olduğunu ve alanın topluluğa Ege Üniversitesi Rektörlüğü tarafından tahsis edildiğini vurgulayan Zengin, “Yasa dışı hiçbir şey yoktu. Buna rağmen öğrencilerin yıllardır emek vererek kurduğu yaşam alanı, gece yarısı baskınıyla dağıtıldı. Dün gece Ege Üniversitesi öğrencileri ve hak savunucuları olarak eşi benzeri görülmemiş bir direniş sergiledik. Yaptıkları işkence belgelenemesin diye bölgedeki tüm elektriği kestiler. Hayvanlara ve hak savunucularına işkence ettiler. Ege Üniversitesi KYK yurdunda kalan öğrenciler, yurtlarının içinden bize ışık tutarak bu işkencenin belgelenmesini sağladılar” ifadelerini kullandı.

Onca itiraza ve görüşme talebine rağmen öğrenciler ve hak savunucularının darbedilerek köpeklerin Ege Üniversitesi’nden çalındığını belirten Zengin, “Şu an akıbetlerini bilmiyoruz. Toplama araçlarının önlerine yattık, hesap sorduk. Gecenin birinde, polis şiddetine, darp edilmeye ve biber gazına rağmen yaşamdan yana tavrımızı koyduk ve bir adım geri atmadık. Bugün Bornova Hükümet Konağı’nın önünden Bornova Belediyesi’ne yürüdük. Çünkü açıkça gördük ki mesele hayvanların yaşam hakkı olduğunda en muhalifinden en sağcısına kadar aynı düzenin aktörleri el ele durabiliyor” dedi.

‘Yasayı uygulamayacağız’ sözünü veren Bornova Belediye Başkanı Ömer Eşki’nin belediyesinin, çevik kuvvet eşliğinde öğrencilere ve hak savunucularına yönelik şiddetin yaşandığı operasyonun parçası olduğunu belirten Zengin, şunları söyledi: “Ömer Eşki ise çıkıp tek bir açıklama dahi yapmadı. Hayvanların yaşam hakkını savunduğunu söyleyenlerle bu hakkı ortadan kaldıran politikaları uygulayanlar arasındaki fark, işte tam da burada ortaya çıkıyor. Sözlerinizin değil, eylemlerinizin hesabını vereceksiniz. İçişleri Bakanı Mustafa Çiftçi, her geçen gün yeni bir oran paylaşarak köpeklerin toplatıldığını söylüyordu. Son açıklamasında İzmir’i de hedef gösterdi. Ardından İstanbul’da selden etkilenen kedilerle videolar paylaşarak hayvan sevgisinden bahsetti. Siz kimi kandırıyorsunuz? Önce kısırlaştır, aşıla, yerinde yaşat politikasını ortadan kaldırdınız; yerine katliam yasasını getirdiniz.”

Tüm karşı duruşlara rağmen nefret pompalayarak, halkın vergilerini trollere akıtarak Türkiye tarihinin en kanlı hayvan düşmanı yasalarından birini çıkaran AKP iktidarının ve bu yasayı uygulayan yerel yönetimlerin sorumlu olduğunu vurgulayan Zengin, “Hayvanlara eziyet ve işkence pahasına yürütülen bu politikaların, yasanın ötesine geçen uygulamalarla hayvanlara ve hayvanların yaşam hakkını savunanlara yöneltilen şiddetin hesabını soracağız. Bornova Belediyesi de bu sorumluluktan kaçamayacak. Emri verenlerden de uygulayanlardan da hesap soracağız” ifadelerini kullandı.

Dün gece yaşananların unutulmasına asla izin vermeyeceklerini söyleyen Zengin …

author: Daniel Hunter
title: How Vermont shut down ICE
content:
This article

How Vermont shut down ICE

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


After Operation Metro Surge, the Trump administration moved to rein in the Bovino-style spectacle with its made-for-TV arrests. In an attempt to avoid another public outcry, Immigration and Customs Enforcement has quietly settled into a new rhythm.


Arrests have still increased month after month, reaching

a record high

 of roughly 51,000 people taken into ICE custody in August. This is part of a new surge — carried out in hospitals, courthouses and airports — with an intent to stay off the nightly news. As

The


New York Times


reported

, this phase is “captured mostly by grainy security camera footage, through cracked blinds and from behind closed doors.” 


This phase is also backed by a dragnet of data. At airports, ICE has been

running name matches with TSA to detain people

 at check-in counters and gates. It has found a backdoor into the country’s license-plate cameras: Records show local and state police

ran more than 4,000 immigration-related searches

 on Flock’s camera network in a single year. (Yet another reason

Flock cameras should not exist

.)


Perhaps surprisingly, much of the tech infrastructure driving ICE’s new surge is headquartered in … Vermont. The town of Williston, outside Burlington, is home to both ICE’s

Law Enforcement Support Center

, which houses the agency’s national tip line, and ICE’s National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center, or NCATC, its social-media surveillance hub. 


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


As ICE tries a new approach, this new phase of resisting ICE requires moving to more offense — and the people of Vermont are offering us some clear lessons. 


Vermont resistance


Resistance started with the fight over flights. Early in Trump’s second term, activists

documented

 ICE moving detainees onto commercial flights out of Burlington’s airport — more than 450 people as of mid-July 2025, by their count. They showed up in airports as witnesses and disruptors, sometimes aided by empowered flight attendants. They forced an ICE retreat: organizers say

ICE hasn’t moved detainees through the airport in more than a year

.


More recently they’ve gone after the hard infrastructure. Sit-ins at the White Cap Business Park in Williston, where the NCATC facility is located, have led to arrests for allegedly blocking the entrance to the ICE offices, including

11 people in February and 13 in July.


After those arrests came some unusual twists, which speak volumes about the courage it takes to refuse unjust orders and to continue protesting in the face of repression.


Complicity and noncooperation


Responses to authoritarianism are as old as a time — many of the same dynamics from Vermont show up in the ancient story of Pharaoh and Moses.


Undeniably the most powerful person in his land, Pharaoh was the ultimate authoritarian. His big trick was taking beautiful work and turning it evil. Take the work of midwives, whose job is to usher life into the world — he turned that work into ugliness by ordering the Hebrew midwives to kill every newborn boy. 


But we all have a choice. And famously, several of the midwives refused. Their act of noncooperation with an unjust order is the reason Moses lived.


We are living through a moment when institution after institution is being turned toward evil. Some, like the Department of Justice, were already a mixed bag. But now it is being turned against the very logic of due process it claims to serve, as we’ve seen recently with the

criminal indictment of whistleblower Cassidy Hutchinson

. Other institutions, like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, are being perverted, with

great resistance from insiders

 who cling to the key values that these agencies were founded on.


Previous Coverage


The movement to defend the Minneapolis 15


In Vermont, the local prosecutor, Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George, faced her own choice. When asked to

bring charges

 against the protesters who held the sit-ins, she repeatedly declined, citing limited resources. That makes sense: No one was harmed, and the protesters have a strong necessity defense — the argument that they were preventing an even greater harm. Every minute that ICE isn’t taking part in abducting people is good for the country.


Then came a bizarre turn of …

title: Αντιφασιστική διαδήλωση, την Πέμπτη 15/10, 18.00 στη πλατεία Βασ. Γεωργίου, Πάτρα
content:
Αντιφασιστική διαδήλωση στην Πάτρα με αφορμή την δολοφονική επίθεση φασιστών σε μέλος του αντιφασιστικού κινήματος στην Ελευσίνα.


Καλέσματα/Αφίσες:


αναρχική ομάδα “δυσήνιος ίππος”


ΟΥΤΕ ΣΠΙΘΑΜΗ ΓΗΣ ΣΤΟΥΣ ΦΑΣΙΣΤΕΣ


ΤΣΑΚΙΣΤΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΦΑΣΙΣΤΕΣ ΣΕ ΚΑΘΕ ΓΕΙΤΟΝΙΑ


Αντιφασιστική διαδήλωση με αφορμή τη δολοφονική επίθεση φασιστών σε βάρος αντιφασίστα στην Ελευσίνα


Πέμπτη 15 Οκτωβρίου 18.00 Πλ. Γεωργίου


αντιφασιστες/αντιφασιστριες


Το μεσημέρι της Πέμπτης 8/10 στην Ελευσίνα δύο φασίστες στήνουν ενέδρα σε αντιφασίστα σύντροφο στη γειτονιά του. Εκείνος αντιστέκεται [ισοπεδώνοντας τον έναν]και έπειτα μαχαιρώνεται πισώπλατα από τον δεύτερο στα πόδια και στον κορμό. Ούτε απόπειρα ληστείας ήταν, ούτε “οπαδικό”, όπως ισχυρίστηκαν αρχικά οι θρασύδειλοι φασίστες στην κατάθεση τους στους μπάτσους και που στοχευμένα αναπαρήγαγαν ορισμένα καθεστωτικά μέσα για αποπολιτικοποίηση του γεγονότος [όπως είχαμε δει να γίνεται και στην περίπτωση της δολοφονίας του αντιφασίστα Παύλου Φύσσα] Αντιθέτως, ήταν μια προμελετημένη και στοχευμένη επίθεση απέναντι σε γνωστό για την πολιτική του ταυτότητα αντιφασίστα.


Ανέκαθεν ο ρόλος του φασισμού μέσα στον καπιταλισμό είναι συγκεκριμένος. Ως η πιο ολοκληρωτική μορφή του αστικού κράτους, ο φασισμός εξυπηρετεί την ανεμπόδιστη ροή του κεφαλαίου. Δεν είναι τυχαίος ο χρόνος στον οποίο οι φασίστες ξεπηδούν και προμοτάρονται από την κυριαρχία. Το καπιταλιστικό σύστημα βρίσκεται σε κρίση και γεννά πολέμους ώστε να ανακάμψει μέσα από την πολεμική βιομηχανία, ενώ η κοινωνική βάση εξαθλιώνεται και φτωχοποιείται αδιάκοπα. Η συνθήκη αυτή επιτάσσει περισσότερο από ποτέ πειθήνιους πολίτες, πρόθυμους να παραγκωνίσουν τα ταξικά τους συμφέροντα, να σφαγιάσουν και να σφαγιαστούν στο όνομα του έθνους. Όμως η εθνική ενότητα δεν είναι παρά η “συμφιλίωση” των καταπιεσμένων με τους καταπιεστές τους. Ο βασικός ρόλος των φασιστών, εξυπηρετώντας προτίστως τον ίδιο σκοπό με το κράτος, είναι να δημιουργούν εσωτερικούς εχθρούς (μετανάστριες, κουήρ άτομα και οποιαδήποτε κοινωνική ομάδα δεν εμπίπτει στα πρότυπα της “κανονικότητας”),να καταστέλλουν τα κοινωνικά κινήματα που προασπίζονται την αξιοπρέπεια και την ελευθερία και να αποπροσανατολίζουν την οργή της κοινωνικής βάσης απο τους πραγματικούς υπαίτιους -δηλαδή το κράτος και το κεφάλαιο- για την καθημερινή ταξική βία που αυτή δέχεται. Όσο κι αν προσπαθούν να παρουσιαστούν ως αντισυστημικοί, στην πραγματικότητα οι φασίστες κάνουν την πιο βρώμικη δουλειά του συστήματος.


Απέναντι στην επιχειρούμενη επέλαση του φασισμού, εμείς προτάσσουμε τον μαχητικό κοινωνικό αντιφασισμό. Ο αγώνας μας είναι δίκαιος και αναγκαίος. Απέναντι στην σαπίλα του φασισμού, του εθνικισμού, του μισογυνισμού, της μισαλλοδοξίας, του φόβου και του σκοταδισμού, στήνουμε αναχώματα μέσα απο την ταξική αλληλεγγύη, προτάσσοντας τη συντροφικότητα και τη δράση απέναντι στην απόλυτη απονέκρωση και βία των καιρών. Η νίκη είναι δική μας, όσο και αν οι φασίστες και συνεργοί τους επιχειρούν να ποδοπατήσουν όποιο σηκώνει κεφάλι. Δεν τρομοκρατούμαστε, μαχόμαστε, ισοπεδώνουμε τον φασισμό στις συνειδήσεις, το δρόμο και κάθε άλλο πεδίο της καθημερινότητας.


Φασίστες κουφάλες θα περάσουμε από πάνω σας


ΚΚΕ(μ-λ) 


Αντιφασιστική συγκέντρωση και διαδήλωση την Πέμπτη 15/10 στις 18:30 στην πλ. Γεωργίου


Το ΚΚΕ(μ-λ) καλεί τον λαό και τη νεολαία της πόλης στη διαδήλωση ενάντια στην επίθεση των δύο φασιστοειδών, σε αντιφασίστα την Πέμπτη 8/10 στην Ελευσίνα. Με το σύστημα να βρίσκεται σε φάση πιο ουσιαστικής εμπλοκής στα σφαγεία των πολέμων, να τσακίζει δικαιώματα και να διαλύει κατακτήσεις, οπλίζει με την πολιτική του τα χέρια των φασιστών, στοχοποιώντας αντιφασίστες, πρόσφυγες και μετανάστες, προκειμένου να τρομοκρατήσει τον λαό και να περάσει την επίθεσή του. Ο φασισμός τσακίζεται με τον λαό στον δρόμο!

author: Harriet Williamson
title: Child Psychotherapist Forced to Close Practice After Holding Sign at Peaceful Protest
content:
A child psychotherapist was forced to close her private practice after being arrested for holding a paper sign at a Palestine Action protest, Novara Media can reveal.


Alex Payne, a

UKCP-registered

 integrative child psychotherapist of 16 years and accredited member of the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy, had her professional indemnity insurance cancelled following her arrests at two protests opposing the genocide in Gaza and the ban on Palestine Action. 


She was arrested in October 2025 and April this year under section 13 of the Terrorism Act for holding signs that read: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.”


Amnesty International UK has slammed Payne’s case as “chilling”. 


Palestine Action was proscribed as a terror organisation under Keir Starmer’s Labour government in the summer of 2025, making it the first direct action group in British history to be banned in this way. 


Payne was charged under the Terrorism Act after her arrest in October 2025. She has not been convicted, but with this charge hanging over her, she hasn’t been able to secure alternative insurance. Payne told Novara Media: “I cannot practice as a child psychotherapist without insurance, so I’ve had to prematurely end therapeutic work with children and young people although I pose no risk to their wellbeing.


“It’s ironic to me that a protest motivated by frustration at the Starmer government’s weak response to the suffering of children in Gaza should have led to my work with children having to end.” 


Payne had been insured by Markel International since 2022, via insurance broker Everywhen. She told Novara Media that she has never needed to make a claim, and that she had used Everywhen as her broker for her entire career. 


In emails seen by Novara Media, an Everywhen advisor told Payne that Markel International accepted that the “matter does not relate directly to [Alex’s] professional practice” but had decided that: “Taking the overall circumstances into account, including the two arrests and the ongoing legal proceedings, we do not feel this is a risk we can continue to support.”


Markel International and Everywhen both declined to comment. 


Amnesty International UK’s law and human rights director Tom Southerden told Novara Media: “To see a child psychotherapist facing arrest, and then having to close their practice simply for peacefully holding a placard, is a chilling attack on our freedom of speech.” 


On what moved her to take action, Payne said: “There is a huge cognitive dissonance in helplessly watching a live-streamed genocide and working with vulnerable and sometimes quite traumatised child clients. You see the impact of abuse and neglect on children and on the developing brain. 


“And then you’ve got this tiny strip of land, Gaza, where you’ve got generation after generation of traumatised children growing up into traumatised adults. And it’s very hard to see that happening and not do anything.”


She added: “I feel desperately guilty because I was doing good work with clients that I’ve had for a long time and clients who I just started working with – from eight or nine-year-olds to young adults.”


Payne is not the only person to have faced professional consequences after being arrested on terrorism charges for participating in Palestine Action protests.


Rachel, a social worker and 65-year-old grandma of three who chose not to give her last name due to fear of reprisals, took part in a protest against the ban on Palestine Action in September 2025, in London’s Parliament Square. Like Alex Payne, she was arrested under section 13 of the Terrorism Act for holding a sign that read: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.”  


Rachel immediately informed her workplace of her arrest and was suspended from her job at a local authority in the south-east of England for eight weeks. According to correspondence seen by Novara Media, she’s now back at work with a formal written warning. We are not naming Rachel’s employer to avoid further repercussions. 


Rachel said while senior management at work were “wetting themselves because it was the Terrorism Act”, she was well-supported by other colleagues who understood that her decision to take part in the protest was in line with her core values as a social worker. 


Of her grandkids, Rachel said: “I want them to grow up in a better world than we’ve got now. I don’t want them growing up in a country where they can’t say what their …

author: groundxero
title: Infinite Jail Glitch: Delhi’s Pay-and-Play Public Amenities Overtaken by Delhi Police to ‘Pay-and-Imprison’ Thousands Amidst SIR Protests
content:
Delhi’s makeshift ‘detention centres’, community spaces like stadiums and public event halls repurposed as mass holding cells for thousands of protesters, are ripped straight out of an Atwoodian dystopia. 


 


by

Mouli Sharma


 


New Delhi, 15 October 2026:

On 13 June 1989, late Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi laid the foundation stone to a public sports facility in Delhi’s Surajmal Vihar, a stone’s throw away from Jhilmil. A decade later, the Delhi Development Authority inaugurated the site as the Yamuna Sports Complex, a government run pay-and-play where you can, say, play badminton on an

outdoor daylight court

 for Rs. 100 a turn or take a ‘daily dip’ in the members’ exclusive swimming pools for Rs. 82.60 per head. 


 


On 10 October 2026, this sports complex, which serves as a public funded self sustaining recreational facility whose primary userbase consists of children and senior citizens, was turned into a hostage centre into which protesting lawyers of the supreme court were packed, after they marched toward the blockaded Jantar Mantar protest site demanding the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar. 


“I managed to get away somehow,” said Adv. Awstika Das, one of the few left behind on the Mandi House Circle after around 70 protesters were “detained” and driven away, forcibly dispersing the small march. “They’ve taken the rest to the Yamuna Sports Complex, there are senior advocates there, too. They’ve been beaten,” she said. 


 


While the lawyers were released shortly afterwards in less than two hours—in stark contrast from the many thousands in Delhi who have been detained day after day in an ongoing cat and mouse game between state and citizen since the start of the SIR protests on 2 October—due to a “special, unprecedented”

intervention

 by the Chief Justice of India, the question remained, why were they taken to the complex in the first place, as opposed to a police station with a notified holding facility or lock-up?


 


“I’m not sure that there is any statutory authority supporting this… this repurposing of public spaces or government offices for detention,” said Advocate Archit Krishna, who specialises in criminal law. Advocate Vertika Mani, a human rights lawyer, similarly expressed skepticism about the legality of such repurposing.


 


“It should be challenged in court,” she said. “There is no legal basis for this.”


 


The Delhi Police Act, 1978, which governs the operations of the force in charge of security operations in the capital, which is now overwhelmingly being described as “under siege” of said forces (‘an undeclared Emergency’), provides a wide array of protections and special powers to the Delhi Police official, distinguishing him from the common man to the degree that an FIR may not be filed against him even if he is accused of commiting a cognisable offence, say murder or rape. Such has been the case with one former ACP Vivek Bhagat, who was accused of molestation by a woman journalist on 3 October 2026, against whom an FIR has still not been filed under these special powers. Instead, he has been promoted, and an FIR has been registered against the woman complainant, NewsDiggy reporter Rosy.


 


Notably, though, even

this

legislation does not empower the police to use public amenities as detention centres or give any authority to detain people within them under any circumstances, qualifying the detentions of 10 October as false imprisonment. Chapter IV, Section 36 of the Act allows for the police to temporarily reserve for themselves and therefore prevent public entry into public spaces or streets, but even this reservation requires for a written public notice to be issued by the Commissioner of Police. 


 


“The Commissioner of Police may, by public notice, temporarily reserve for any public purpose any street or other public place and prohibit persons from entering the area so reserved, except on such conditions as may be specified,” the Act says.


Daulatpur Community Centre turned into a detention centre for protesters


As of 14 October 2026, no such public notice has been given, but at least 7 public facilities in addition to the YSC have been “identified” and “prepared” to be used as makeshift prisons during protests, as reported by various mainstream broadcasters including the Hindustan Times, attributing unnamed “government sources”. Many of them have also revealed themselves after repeated mass detentions, which included the illegal detentions of minors …

Seitdem wir unseren Guide vor einigen Wochen rumgeschickt haben (

Wir haben uns relativ schnell aktiv dagegen entschieden, kurzfristig eine WordPress-Infrastruktur aufzubauen, die eure Blogs aufnehmen kann. Das hat folgende Gründe:


 Unser Ziel ist es eine Struktur aufzubauen, die langfristig agiert. WordPress zu hosten ist aufwändig und anfällig für Angriffe und zu wenige von uns möchten das langfristig tun.


 Wir wollen Alternativen zu WordPress in die Bewegung bringen. Alternativen, die besser zu unseren Werten passen. Auch welche, die das NoBlogs-Backup importieren können.


 Wir wollen unseren sozialen, organisatorischen und technischen Prozessen ausreichend Zeit geben, damit sie sich gut anfühlen und sicher sind.


 Wir denken, dass es mehr Dezentralisierung in der linken Hosting-Landschaft braucht, und wollen euch nochmal dazu animieren, selbst aktiv zu werden.


Die guten Nachrichten


 Mittelfristig ist unser Ziel wieder eine Struktur aufzubauen, mit der ihr einfach und unkompliziert Websites & Blogs anlegen könnt

 Nur keine WordPress-Seiten – NoBlogs wird es also in diesem Format bei uns nicht geben – aber dafür andere Formate, die wir ähnlich niedrigschwellig gestalten wollen.


 Alle Noblogs Seiten, die bis zum 18.09. online waren, wurden unter *.

nublogs.org

de.indymedia.org/node/862106

uberspace.de

u8manual.uberspace.de//apps_in…

Wenn ihr eine Kleingruppe seid, die überlegt dies zu tun, nehmt gerne Kontakt mit uns auf. Einen Kurs findet ihr hier:

.

systemli.org

immerda.ch

title: Pınar Güneş’in öldürülmesiyle ilgili soruşturmada 4 tutuklama
content:
İzmir’in Çeşme ilçesinde, Pınar Güneş’in (28), öldürülmesine ilişkin yürütülen soruşturmada gözaltına alınan 5 şüpheliden 4’ü tutuklandı.

Olay, 14 Ekim’de gece saatlerinde Alaçatı Mahallesi'nde meydana geldi. Pınar Güneş (28) ile Y.U. ve A.M. isimli iki erkek arasında belirlenemeyen nedenle tartışma çıktı. Şüpheliler, Güneş'i tabancayla ateş edip, yaraladı. Çevredekilerin ihbarı üzerine olay yerine sağlık ve polis ekipleri sevk edildi. Olay yerinde ilk müdahalesi yapılan Güneş, ambulansla, Çeşme Alper Çizgenakat Devlet Hastanesine kaldırıldı. Burada tedaviye alınan Güneş, kurtarılamadı.

Olayın ardından kaçan şüpheliler Y.U. ve A.M., polis ve jandarma ekiplerinin ortak çalışması ile Urla ilçesinde suç aleti tabancayla yakalandı. Soruşturmanın devamında G.C., Ö.A. ve M.F. de ekiplerce gözaltına alındı.

İşlemlerinin ardından adliyeye sevk edilen Y.U, A.M, G.C. ve Ö.A. çıkarıldıkları sulh ceza hakimliğince tutuklandı. M.F. ise adli kontrolle serbest bırakıldı. Kadına ateş eden şüphelinin 17 yaşındaki A.M. olduğu öne sürüldü.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: IHD and ÖHD: Human rights violations are occurring in prisons in Adana
content:
The Adana branch of the Human Rights Association (IHD) and the Adana representative office of the Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD) released a report on human rights violations in prisons covering the period from July to September 2026. The report drew attention to solitary confinement, access to healthcare, and other human rights violations at Adana Suluca High-Security Closed Prison and Kürkçüler F-Type Closed Prison.


Serhat Ökmen, a member of the ÖHD, stated that the “pit-type” architecture and penal regime at Suluca Prison cause severe psychological pressure.


Ökmen explained that prisoners spend 23 hours a day in single-person cells and are allowed only one hour outdoors in the exercise yard. Drawing attention to the conditions of isolation in the prison, he said that a prisoner named Nurettin had recently died by suicide.


One of the key issues highlighted in the report was the alleged practice of “intraoral searches” during hospital transfers. Ökmen said that prisoners who refuse to submit to this practice are not transferred to hospitals and are therefore being denied their right to medical treatment.


He reported that there are 38 ill prisoners in the two facilities, including some in serious condition. He noted that some prisoners suffering from chronic illnesses or requiring surgery have been unable to receive treatment for years. He added that prisoners who are transferred to hospitals are made to wait for hours in transport vehicles, handcuffed and in conditions unsuitable for their health.


Ökmen also referred to a letter from Savaş Geçirgen, who is held at Suluca Prison, alleging that he was subjected to insults, threats, and physical violence during a hospital transfer.


The report stated that meals are insufficient and have low nutritional value, that drinking water is rationed at Suluca Prison, and that hygiene problems persist. It also noted that quotas are imposed on the number of books available to political prisoners, that certain newspapers and publications are withheld, and that sports, social interaction, and workshop activities are restricted.


The IHD and the ÖHD further reported that disciplinary penalties they consider arbitrary, imposed by observation and classification boards, are preventing prisoners from being released.

author: Oyunga Pala
title: When Baba Died: One Year Later
content:
Last October, two weeks before Baba died, I was returning to Nairobi after a two-year hiatus. The last time I was home was during the first-year memorial of my sister, Nyangi, who was now the prominent character in my book.


Home had changed in many ways, yet it had not, in a kind of same old but different way. The vibe was familiar, the actors younger, the pace faster. Roads once familiar were now dwarfed by high-rise towers sprouting around the city like wild mushrooms. The expressway from the airport straddling the city dominated the cityscape, a marker of a city in a hurry to grow up.


I used to wonder whether I would change. Would I be like the other diaspora Kenyans I had seen who lost all sense of belonging after just a few miserable winters abroad, and began to look down on their own? Stepping away seemed to have had the opposite effect on me.


This notion of belonging was immediately tested as I faced my former public self. When I announced that I had published a book and would be going on a book tour, the reception was warm. I was reminded of how big

Mantalk

 was, the weekly national column in the Daily Nation that I laboured over for a decade and that has now become part of the country’s cultural landscape, a reference point to a bygone era, for many stuck in nostalgia. I was no longer the Mantalk guy. I had traveled far both within and without. I had grown up, but to many of my readers, I was still that guy, who showed up every Saturday, a mysterious figure who ruffled feathers. The man some female readers used to love to hate.


I had been part of several life journeys unwittingly. And like all fans of urban culture, I was a mascot for those bygone times. Yet here I was, older, perhaps wiser, certainly a lot humbler. I had just poured my soul into a book that detailed my own journey away from the glam and fame of the national spotlight and delved into trying not only to make sense of my unresolved grief but also the grief of a nation. The shift in persona was stark: From a young man who used to critique modern rules of chivalry to one sharing lessons on how to navigate the profound loss that follows the death of a loved one.


To reach these moments of connection, I first had to navigate the city itself. My first stop the night after my arrival was the Prestige Bookshop and Nairobi traffic- well, what has changed? The roads remained clogged, and nothing quite captures Nairobi’s class dynamics as the expressway, raised above, smooth and scenic, with arresting views of flashy high-rise buildings obscuring the reality of chaos that rules just underneath it, bottleneck traffic, matatu madness, and boda bodas that now make matatus appear quite tame. It became a metaphor in hindsight of how we process grief: stoic and contained on the surface, but underneath the facade, a bubbling volcano waiting to erupt.


I remember Prestige bookshop from another time, when the city centre was a little more serene, and Mama Ngina Street still had a taste of the bourgie back when 20th Century Plaza, the Hilton hotel and the International Life House were iconic landmarks in the city centre. Yvonne Adhiambo Owuor was launching her second novel, The DragonFly Sea, in the small bookshop. The shelves had been pushed to the side to create space for the fans, and I was the MC of the day, here to celebrate one of Kenya’s finest novelists. I looked at the bookshop now, wondering how we had pulled it off, for there seemed to be hardly any room to swing a cat.


When the people started to come through, I knew this was going to be special. Odd that despite 28 years of a public writing life, I had never signed an autograph. I remained struck that people would endure Nairobi traffic to meet over a book and demand my bad handwriting on their personal copies.


I didn’t know what to expect as a new world and role began to unfold for me. Lost connections revived. People I had gone to school with, names I hadn’t seen or heard from in years. Friends, family, acquaintances, total strangers, with entwined pasts and reminders of a time once spent in communion; between the firm handshakes and tight embraces, it took me a minute to realise what was happening.


I was being honoured and celebrated. When I went to Ukombozi Library to donate a copy of my book, I met Ogutu, who told me how the story of my father’s funeral process was also his story. At the United Kenya Club, I met Clifford Derrick, who had just buried his mother, and the book …

title: 6e assemblée anticarcérale paname et environs : 25 Octobre à la Parole Errante !
content:
La sixième Assemblée Anticarcérale Paname & Environs aura lieu le dimanche 25 Octobre à la parole errante (9 Rue François Debergue, Montreuil). Le lieu sera ouvert dès 15h30 pour s'installer, écrire ensemble des lettres à des prisonnier·es ou parcourir l'infokiosque, et l'assemblée même commencera à 16h. On conseille d'essayer autant que possible de venir sans téléphone (ou au pire, de l'éteindre en avance) pour réduire la surveillance que l'on s'impose à travers l'omniprésence des mouchards technologiques dans nos milieux. Il y aura aussi un coin et des activités pour les enfants, pour permettre aux personnes qui ont des enfants de pouvoir participer à l'assemblée.


L'assemblée anti carcérale paris & environs a pour vocation d'être un espace d'organisation ouvert se réunissant mensuellement afin d'agir collectivement en solidarité avec les mouvements des prisonnier.es et tisser des liens avec les prisonnier.es et leurs proches sans passer par des cadres partisans ou syndicaux.


Lors des dernières grosses révoltes qui ont eu lieu, la réalité sociale de la répression nous a laissé-es face à un constat amer : nous sommes bien loin d'avoir les outils nécessaires pour réagir correctement face à l'appareil d'État, ainsi qu'amplifier la voix des prisonnier·ères et de celleux qui font les frais du système carcéral.


Pourtant, les mouvements ne manquent pas d'inventivité pour s'opposer de front aux prisons, que ce soit par des actions telles que l'attaque de la prison de Fresnes lors des révoltes de 2023, les attaques répétées de comicos dans cette même révolte comme lors des gilets jaunes, ou encore les attaques et intimidations de matons à domicile comme lors de

DDPF

.


Nous voulons nous en inspirer pour pousser nos luttes anti-carcérales plus loin, à la fois pour dépasser nos milieux anarchistes et adopter une position qui ne soit pas simplement défensive, en simple réaction à la répression.


La prison est — et sera toujours — l'un des symbole les plus éloquents de la puissance de l'État, de sa capacité à réprimer, enfermer et isoler l'ensemble des individu·es qui menacent son existence. La prison est au centre même de l'appareil colonial qui constitue l'État français : elle sert à mater et punir les révoltes des colonies comme récemment en Kanaky, Guadeloupe ou Martinique, à intensifier le tri aux frontières comme à Mayotte, et à tracer des frontières intérieures en incarcérant massivement les populations racisées, colonisées et les plus pauvres.


Attaquer les lieux d'incarcération - par les mots, la solidarité, le feu ou la bombe - c'est alors s'attaquer à ses outils privilégiés.


Rompre l'isolement des/avec les détenu·es est alors devenu rapidement pour les mouvements anticarcéraux un moyen d'affaiblir l'appareil carcéral et l'État colonial. En exposant la voix des personnes enfermé·es, on se donne le moyen de penser «

 

la prison

 

» (son fonctionnement, ses outils, etc.), mais aussi de la rendre moins «

 

extérieure à nos vies

 

». Des surgissements tels que

DDPF

 ou les révoltes pour Nahel parviennent à la remettre au centre de l'attention en s'y attaquant ouvertement, créant des fissures dans lesquelles nous désirons nous engouffrer pour mettre fin à la trop commune realité de l'incarcération et des assassinats policiers.


Une des prouesse des États dits «

 

démocratiques

 

», est d'avoir réussi à faire de la notion d'enfermement un impensé pour toute une partie de la population. Une situation si lointaine que l'on ne prend même pas la peine de l'envisager, alors que c'est pourtant le quotidien de beaucoup de personnes...


Cette nécessité de destruction est d'autant plus présente dans une région parisienne qui concentre à elle seule une densité collossale d'institutions d'enfermements : que ce soit les taules, tribunaux, comicos, ou prisons pour sans-papiers, mineur-es, enfants, fols, tox, handi-es, animaux non-humains...


Pour nous, s'organiser signifie construire des nouvelles formes de lutte, de solidarité et de décision, par notre capacité collective à rompre avec l'ordre existant, à expérimenter, à créer, à inventer...


Depuis le début du 20

e

 siècle, les Anarchist Black Cross (

ABC

) et leurs réseaux ont cet avantage de se présenter sous une forme autonome et souple, fondée sur un internationalisme radicalement anti-carcéral, d'où notre envie de nous réaproprier cette forme et de s'inscrire dans un réseau pour abattre les prisons proches de chez nous comme à l'autre bout du …

author: Josh Richman
title: In Memoriam: Barry Steinhardt
content:
Barry Steinhardt, a lifelong privacy champion and an early leader in the battle for digital civil liberties who served as EFF’s president in 1998-99, died last week at age 73.

 


A Connecticut native, Steinhardt led the Vermont and Pennsylvania affiliates of the American Civil Liberties Union before becoming associate director of the national ACLU. There, he helped spearhead the fight to overturn much of the Communications Decency Act, resulting in the U.S. Supreme Court’s landmark

Reno v. ACLU


ruling in 1997.

 


When the internet was still young,

Steinhardt

became one of

the first

attorneys to

specialize in the intersection of technology and privacy

.

In early 1998 he took a leave of absence from the ACLU to become EFF’s president, and then returned to the ACLU in 1999.

 


In 2002 he founded the ACLU’s Program on Technology and Liberty. After retiring from the ACLU, he continued on as a senior advisor to London-based

Privacy International

.

 


Steinhardt chaired the 2003 Computer Freedom and Privacy Conference and served on a wide variety of significant panels and boards, including the Department of Transportation’s Negotiated Rule Making on national driver’s license standards, the Advisory Committee to the US Census, and the Blue Ribbon Panel on Genetics of the National Conference of State Legislatures. He also was selected to be a member of the US delegation to the G-8 Government and Private Sector Tokyo conference on Cyber Crime and served as an advisor to the Czech Helsinki Committee.

 


“Barry led many critical technology and civil liberties fights and was an important mentor to me and others in the field,” said EFF Executive Director Nicole Ozer. “Barry’s influential work across strategy to defend and advance privacy rights and safeguard people against surveillance has made its mark on the law and policy of our digital world and protected the rights and safety of people across the United States and around the world.”

author: Chris Walker
title: ICE Is Fast-Tracking a Nationwide Domestic Spy Program Across Dozens of Cities
content:
The agency plans to contract with around 142 agents to take part in domestic spying operations.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is reportedly fast-tracking a program designed to expand its domestic surveillance capabilities in dozens of cities across the United States.

Details of the new spy program, entitled the Enforcement and Removal Operations Overwatch and National Security Enforcement, or ERO ONE, were published on a federal website in September. The American Prospect reported on ERO ONE earlier this week.

Around $100 million is expected to be allocated from the Department of Homeland Security to the program, which intends to contract 142 intelligence agents who will be placed in at least two dozen cities throughout the country. Those agents would coordinate with nearby ICE offices, as well as with a central hub located in Washington, D.C.

The published plan doesn’t specify what these agents will do while in the field, but it does indicate that they will analyze classified and nonclassified information to create “network, link, and relationship” analyses. Such research examines not only a specific person, but also their connections — including members of their household, extended family members, friends, and even acquaintances.

The government’s explainer of the program states that agents will “provide research, analysis, evaluation, reporting, coordination, and related intelligence support to ERO ONE headquarters and designated field locations.”

The document places some restrictions on ERO ONE agents, who will not be allowed to engage in actions such as “arrest, detention, search, seizure, interrogation, inspection, investigative, or other law enforcement authorities.” However, given that ICE agents have repeatedly overreached their own enforcement powers or blatantly lied to residents during enforcement operations, it’s not unreasonable to believe these restrictions could be ignored.

ICE has already expanded its domestic spying capabilities through facial recognition and mobile phone location data software, as well as artificial intelligence (AI) technologies as part of its mass deportation efforts. ICE has also used “zero-click” technology that allows the agency to access encrypted data on an individual’s phone by sending a link to the user that doesn’t require them to click it at all.

Critics warn the new program is not only set to target immigrants in the country, but could be the precipice of a new domestic surveillance paradigm.

“It looks dangerously like the construction of an internal spying agency,” Jay Stanley, senior policy analyst with the American Civil Liberties Union’s Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project, explained to The American Prospect. “It’s a nightmare in the making.”

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Dulce Amor Rodriguez
title: Social media ban may exclude children instead of protecting them, advocates warn
content:
Child rights advocates have warned that a proposed social media ban could restrict children’s access to information, education, expression, and participation without addressing the perpetrators and platforms responsible for online abuse.


The warning followed the Senate’s approval of Senate Bill No. 2424, or the proposed Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (SMART KIDS) Act, on third and final reading on October 8.


The Senate approved the measure by a vote of 16-1, with no abstentions, advancing a proposal sponsored by Sen. Robinhood Padilla that would restrict minors’ access to digital services classified as high-risk.


Salinlahi Alliance for Children’s Concerns argued that the government must protect children from online exploitation, grooming, bullying, and other forms of digital harm without treating their access to digital spaces as the problem.


“Banning children from social media does not make the internet safe. It impedes children’s right to participation while the perpetrators remain,” said Teacher Elle Buntag, Salinlahi secretary general.


The group warned that restricting children’s access would not, by itself, establish whether platforms would respond more effectively to abuse or whether authorities would investigate and prosecute offenders more consistently.


Instead, Salinlahi called on the government to strengthen investigations into online sexual abuse and exploitation, require platforms to detect and remove abusive content, improve reporting and rescue mechanisms, and provide survivors with psychosocial and legal support.


“If the government’s answer to online abuse is simply to remove children from the platform, then we are asking children to bear the burden of a problem created by perpetrators and enabled by weak systems,” Buntag said.


The group maintained that children have rights to information, expression, education, participation, and connection in digital spaces, and urged the government to protect these rights while making online environments safer.


“The state must not confuse restricting children’s access with protecting children. Protection means making the digital spaces they inhabit safe and holding those who exploit them accountable,” Salinlahi said.


Different approaches


The debate over the Senate measure centers partly on whether an under-18 restriction offers a proportionate response to online harm or whether lawmakers should adopt age-specific safeguards.


Sen. Risa Hontiveros, the sole senator who voted against the measure, argued for a more targeted approach that would allow older adolescents to use social media with adequate safety measures.


Hontiveros had proposed restricting access for children under 13 while allowing those aged 13 to 18 to use social media if platforms provided adequate safeguards.


The Child Rights Network Philippines’ explainer questioned the basis for setting the minimum age at 18, and urged lawmakers to examine the evidence behind a blanket restriction before limiting children’s digital rights.


Sen. Win Gatchalian, a co-author and co-sponsor of the Senate measure, argued that aligning the age threshold with the legal definition of a child under existing laws would make enforcement more consistent and easier for authorities, according to the network’s explainer.


Padilla, meanwhile, said lawmakers could amend the measure after assessing its effects, and cited other countries’ experiences with restrictions and subsequent policy reviews, the explainer said.


The Child Rights Network challenged the idea that ease of enforcement should determine the age threshold, arguing that lawmakers must also consider the measure’s effects on children’s rights and daily lives.


The debate therefore goes beyond whether authorities can enforce an age restriction and asks whether the restriction would protect children effectively without imposing unnecessary limits on their participation.


Beyond entertainment


Child rights advocates said children use social media for more than entertainment, including research, learning, creative work, communication, and maintaining relationships.


The Child Rights Network noted that children also use digital platforms to connect with friends and peers and to communicate with parents working overseas.


Salinlahi argued that the government must account for these uses when designing online safety policies, rather than assuming that removing children from platforms would resolve the …

author: dev
title: Du backlash écologique au backlash IA
content:
À quand une psychanalyse des nouveaux contes de fées ? Le vent serait-il en train de tourner ? Entre les Docteur Frankenstein de l'IA qui prennent peur de leur créature et les manifestations contre l'implantation de data centers un peu partout aux USA, mais aussi maintenant en France, l' 'IA mania', qui avait débuté comme un cyber-conte de fées, commence à virer au cauchemar.


Les fournaises estivales devenues habituelles (« il ne fait que 30°C… ça va ») entretiennent des torpeurs mentales qui convergent opportunément avec un aveuglement salutaire pour la santé mentale, sacrée cause nationale. Peut-on être assez inconscient pour se féliciter de la douce moiteur de cet été indien sans en voir ni les causes, ni les conséquences à bien trop court terme ? Comme l'a montré une anthropologue, Elise Boutié, à propos des méga-feux en Californie, les victimes de la catastrophe elles-mêmes (du moins les survivants, car il y a eu des morts) restent souvent dans le déni quant à l'origine climatique de ces incendies et les attribuent au simple hasard

 [

1

]

, un peu comme Emmanuel Macron avec son « Qui aurait pu prédire... ? » en 2022. C'est sans doute la même chose avec l'IA. "Qu'est-ce qui réveille ?" se demandait Lacan. Il semble en tout cas facile de continuer à ignorer le vase communicant entre la courbe des investissements dans l'IA et celle des investissements dans la transition écologique, désormais nettement inférieurs

 [

2

]

. On s'alarme du niveau d'endettement, mais quid de ses causes ? Une transition chasse l'autre : il n'y aura pas assez pour le numérique et pour l'environnement. Et il pourrait ne pas y avoir assez pour aucun des deux. Oui, mais : aux USA, 75 projets de

data centers

 ont été annulés rien qu'au premier trimestre, sous la pression des citoyens de toute sorte

 [

3

]

. Républicains comme démocrates,

rednecks

 ou cols blancs se révoltent contre ces gigantesques aspirateurs à eau et à énergie.


Et en France ? On part de loin : le problème, médiatiquement et politiquement construit, ce sont, semble-t-il, les éoliennes, approuvées sur le principe et en théorie, mais en fait très mal tolérées quand elles s'implantent dans le champ d'à côté. L'IA et le numérique, au contraire, c'est virtuel : comme disent les élèves, « mais comment ça peut émettre du CO2, un téléphone ? Où est le pot d'échappement ? » Si l'on ajoute la fable de la prétendue neutralité du nucléaire sur le plan environnemental, et de son coût prétendument faible, le piège se referme. Et pourtant un rapport récent à la Commission Européenne montre que non seulement le coût de l'énergie produite par les nouveaux EPR sera plus de 3,5 fois supérieur à celui des renouvelables, mais aussi que ces EPR2 bénéficient d'aides à l'investissement inédites (et de conditions particulièrement arrangeantes et coûteuses pour le budget de l'État)

 [

4

]

. A l'heure où l'EPR de Flamanville est à nouveau à l'arrêt, à peine un an après sa mise en service complète, il y a de quoi faire réfléchir au prix de l'électricité.


La France cherche à "rester dans la course" : "attirer les investisseurs", c'est-à-dire d'abord les data centers ("Choose France"), cela veut dire offrir aux GAFAM sur un plateau nos ressources en eau, notre électricité pas (trop) chère, en échange de... hum. Pas de transferts technologiques en tout cas. Quant à Mistral, il semble avoir renoncé à la compétition sur les LLM pour faire du business autrement, en contrats avec les Américains (... et avec Total). "Mistral AI veut être présent", dixit, "sur toute la chaîne de valeur, des data centers aux applications chez les entreprises, pour contrer la domination américaine" : c'est justement le contraire qui est en train de se passer. Et la France, sous l'influence de ses start-ups (théoriquement) souveraines a longuement renâclé avant de finir par signer un texte présenté à l'ONU pour renforcer les mesures de sécurité sur l'IA, sans engagement clair cependant.


Faisons confiance à la communication de la "marque France" : les éléments de langage nous livrent le bon message, mais sous forme inversée. Encore du Lacan !
