author: Unknown
title: Из колонии вышел Василий Куксов, осужденный по делу «Сети» в 2020 году
content:
По данным «Медиазоны», вчера, 16 октября, 38-летний Василий Куксов освободился из колонии №16 в Нижегородской области. Сегодня утром он доехал на поезде до Сердобска в Пензенской области и встретился там с родными.

В 2020 году Куксова, музыканта и инженера-конструктора, приговорили в Пензе к девяти годам колонии по делу «террористического сообщества "Сеть"» (всего обвиняемые по этому делу получили до 18 лет заключения).

Дело возбудили в октябре 2017 года. Сотрудники ФСБ тогда обвинили антифашистов и анархистов, многих из которых объединяло увлечение страйкболом, в том, что они создали «террористическое сообщество» и планировали «раскачать народные массы для дальнейшей дестабилизации политической обстановки в стране».

Тогда в течение месяца силовики задержали Куксова, а также Илью Шакурского, Дмитрия Пчелинцева, Андрея Чернова, Армана Сагынбаева и Егора Зорина. Формальным поводом для начала уголовного преследования стала явка с повинной Зорина. Молодого человека задержали с наркотиками, и он дал показания о террористическом сообществе. Впоследствии дело против него прекратили. В январе 2018 года в Петербурге по тому же делу были задержаны Виктор Филинков и Игорь Шишкин. 11 апреля обвинения предъявили еще одному петербуржцу — Юлию Бояршинову.

Сначала большинство фигурантов дали признательные показания, но позже отказались от них, заявив о пытках. О насилии и применении тока со стороны силовиков сообщали Виктор Филинков, Дмитрий Пчелинцев, Илья Шакурский, Арман Сагынбаев и Андрей Чернов. Следственный комитет не возбудил дело ни по одному заявлению обвиняемых о пытках. О пытках и давлении со стороны силовиков также рассказывали пятеро свидетелей по делу.

Василий Куксов говорил в суде, что сотрудники ФСБ при задержании избили его со словами: «Ты попал, жизнь твоя кончена», — и угрожали отрезать палец. Несмотря на это, он никогда не давал признательных показаний. Во время следствия в пензенском СИЗО-1 у него перед приговором диагностировали открытую форму туберкулеза. Его не госпитализировали и продолжили содержать c другими фигурантами дела. После вступления приговора по делу «Сети» в силу Куксова в ноябре 2020 года доставили в нижегородское ЛИУ-3 для больных туберкулезом. Его выписали в январе 2022 года. В нижегородской ИК-16 после этого его несколько раз отправляли в штрафной изолятор.

author: Said Alsaloul
title: My Study of Dystopian Fiction Never Prepared Me for Reality Here in Gaza
content:
As a teacher of English literature in Gaza, I’ve seen my relationship to books be overturned by the violence around me.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

As a 27-year-old English literature graduate and English teacher from Gaza, I have always been passionate about teaching. I enjoy helping my students learn to speak English by reciting stories aloud.

I connect with them through English, so I collected every English-language book my hands could reach. Before October 7, 2023, during my fourth year in university, I used to visit a bookshop in Gaza City to buy English novels for enhancing my linguistic link with my job and the students. In 2022, shortly before I graduated, I wrote a short story about our tough conditions in Gaza and submitted it to a writing competition. It ranked seventh out of 80 stories, and I received a reward. What began as a practice to improve my English turned into a way of life. Whenever I had money, I bought a few novels until I gathered a large collection and built my own English library. Sometimes I purchased novels I would never open, but it felt satisfying to have them on my shelf. I could sense linguistic progress: a future.

After lectures, I went to a park near the university where I enjoyed the shade from trees and a soft breeze. It was my place where I could sit on a bench under a big tree, a cup of coffee in one hand, a novel in my bag. The novels were all fiction. What I loved was the way the writers chose words. That gave me the literary sense to generate a unique language over time.

In that shady spot, I opened The Alchemist by Paulo Coelho and began to read: “Tell your heart that the fear of suffering is worse than the suffering itself.”

I recalled Gaza’s 50 percent unemployment rate. I would graduate after a few months and start desperately seeking a job, competing with tens of thousands of unemployed graduates who were also fighting over the same positions. Young men used to dream of building families and marrying the girl they loved. Now they watch their hopes crumble under occupation and blockade. I recalled the constant wars every two years, the terror and psychological traumas they inflict. The patient people who can’t leave because of the blockade and the exorbitant travel fees. The eight-hour daily electricity cuts that devastated us for years.

Thinking about these forms of suffering is unavoidable. They deteriorate your life. But coexisting could be our only key to survival. We learned to carry the weight without collapsing. We learned to read between the lines of our own destruction. Knowing that everyone is suffering gives one a strange kind of comfort.

“And that no heart has ever suffered when it goes in search of its dreams, because every second of the search is a second’s encounter with God and with eternity,” Coelho wrote.

I believed it. Tomorrow will be better. The suffering is temporary. I let out a breath I didn’t know I was holding and turned the page.

When I closed the novel, I was certain Coelho had written it for Gaza. For us. For the young people who struggle so much until we believe it is part of life to keep suffering. For those who are still dreaming no matter what.

Then I saw the word on the cover: fiction.

What was fiction to the world was not fiction to us.

I took a pen and crossed it out. I wrote: reality.

I started to read fiction not just to escape, but to understand, to see how fictional worlds were constructed, to learn how to change our reality, or at least adapt to it. Reading became my life, not just for language, but as a chain of subplots that I recognized in my own existence.

One day I turned to Shakespeare:

To be, or not to be: that is the question:

Whether ’tis nobler in the mind to suffer

The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune,

Or to take arms against a sea of troubles…

I once saw Shakespeare’s words as distant, beautiful meditations on grief — something to study, not to live by. In university lectures, the beloved professor Refaat Alareer, who was killed by an Israeli airstrike in 2023, always asked us: “How can you relate to this as a Palestinian?”

“We lack freedom, suffer the devastating blockade and limited resources to thrive. We are the exception case for the world’s rules,” students would reply. “So shall we stay silent and say it is okay to suffer or shall we rebel?”

Refaat took up arms with a pen. He wrote our suffering in …

author: Marianne Dhenin
title: California Is Home to 200 Billionaires. Organizers Say It’s Time to Tax Them.
content:
If passed, California’s Proposition 40 would generate funding for health care, education, and food assistance programs.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Thousands of volunteer canvassers are hitting the streets across California, fighting for a first-of-its-kind wealth tax on the state’s ballot on November 3. Those mobilizing for Proposition 40 — which would generate revenue to backfill federal funding cuts to health care, education, and food assistance programs — are up against hundreds of millions in spending on competing ballot measures from the billionaires who would be taxed by Proposition 40. Whether or not it passes, experts told Truthout the citizen-led ballot initiative is a historic measure that could serve as a model for future efforts to tax the ultra-rich.

“Either way, even if it doesn’t, but definitely if it wins, it’s going to set a new standard for the type of tax that people can demand via ballot initiative,” Benjamin Case, project lead on the Ballot Initiatives Project at Arizona University’s Center for Work and Democracy, told Truthout. “It’s the first wealth tax in the U.S., and first wealth tax of its kind in the world, and it’s also the first tax specifically on billionaires.”

The ballot measure was announced last October by high-profile progressive economists Emmanuel Saez and Robert Reich, as well as the Service Employees International Union’s (SEIU) United Healthcare Workers West, which represents 145,000 health care workers across California. Proposition 40, also called the Billionaire Tax Act, would levy a one-time 5 percent tax on the total net wealth of each of the state’s billionaires, using a retroactive residency date of January 1, 2026. It would apply to roughly 200 billionaires, including Silicon Valley titans like Mark Zuckerberg and Peter Thiel. These individuals have seen their average annual income rise 7.5 percent on average per year over the last four decades, while wages for the average American stagnate and a growing number struggle to meet their basic needs.

Most taxes are levied on income or real estate, not wealth. The latter is meant to capture a person’s net worth, including real estate, cash, and stock holdings, minus debts. Wealth taxes remain relatively novel, outside of some examples in European nations. A recent analysis of a similar wealth tax implemented in Norway found that it did not spur significant outmigration of the ultra-rich or deter founders from starting their companies in the country. The relatively few business owners who did leave Norway under the new tax program maintained their businesses and did not stop investing in the country, according to the analysis.

“If you think about the wealthiest billionaires in California, they have a net worth of somewhere in the range of $250 billion, and our highest income tax bracket applies to everybody who makes essentially more than a million dollars. The difference between a million dollars in income and $250 billion in wealth is just astronomical,” Chris Hoene, executive director of the California Budget and Policy Center, told Truthout. “It’s an innovation to try to tax wealth, and you can do it at a very small margin and produce a lot of revenue quickly.”

Proposition 40 is expected to generate about $100 billion over the next five years. About 90 percent of that revenue would be used to replace the tens of billions of dollars that will be stripped from California’s 15 million Medicaid recipients over that same period under President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. That bill slashed taxes for the wealthiest Americans and is expected to undercut health care and social services programs nationwide. The cuts are expected to create a $100 million shortfall in California’s Medi-Cal program alone over the next five years, stripping over a million Californians of coverage and forcing clinics to shutter. SEIU estimates 145,000 health care workers could lose their jobs. The bulk of the cuts are expected to hit after the midterm election, but many across California are already bracing.

“Frontline health care workers that are in the facilities with the patients are already seeing this,” Renee Saldaña, United Healthcare Workers West’s press secretary, told Truthout. “Patients are already getting nervous about things like ‘Am I going to be able to afford my medicine? title: Whereabouts of man summoned by Iranian Revolutionary Guards remain unknown
content:
A 40-year-old man has been detained in the city of Piranshahr in East Kurdistan (Rojhilat) after being summoned by the intelligence service of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). His whereabouts have remained unknown since his detention. The man, Ahmad Mostafanejad, has been denied access to legal counsel and contact with his family.


According to the human rights organization Kolbarnews, Mostafanejad was summoned by telephone to the Revolutionary Guards’ intelligence department in Piranshahr on Wednesday, October 14. After complying with the summons, he was detained and taken to an undisclosed location.


No information has yet emerged about the reasons for his detention or any possible charges against him. His health condition and detention conditions also remain unknown. Iranian authorities have neither disclosed his whereabouts nor allowed him to contact his family.

title: Jineolojî Conference: Women’s liberation must become a force for shaping society
content:
How can the ideology of women’s liberation become a politically effective force in society? This question was at the center of the second day of the European Jineolojî Conference in Haelen, the Netherlands. Around 150 delegates discussed building a democratic and communal society, overcoming hierarchical forms of organization, and integrating Jineolojî more deeply into everyday social life. Shortcomings in previous work were also openly addressed.


Alongside Jineolojî activists, the conference brought together representatives of women’s councils, communes, cultural and faith communities, media outlets, and civil society organizations, as well as mothers. The session on the transition from the ideology of women’s liberation to organized political practice featured contributions from scholar Dilar Dirik, Meral Çiçek of the Kurdish Women’s Movement in Europe (TJK-E), and Elif Kaya of the Jineolojî Academy.


Dilar Dirik: ‘Transformation requires courage’


Dilar Dirik raised the question of the internal conditions necessary for social transformation. She argued that simply continuing existing activities or establishing new organizational structures was not enough. Instead, deeply entrenched ways of thinking, taboos, and patriarchal patterns of behavior must also be overcome, she underlined.


Dirik critically examined the state-centered legacy of actually existing socialism, arguing that its failure to sufficiently question its own foundations had led to the emergence of new hierarchies. Contemporary forms of organization, she added, could also unintentionally reproduce social divisions and power relations.


“Transformation requires courage,” Dirik emphasized.


https://1649452211.rsc.cdn77.org/20261017125111_2026-10-17-haelen-jineoloji-konferasi-2-nci-oturum-1.mp4


It was therefore crucial, she argued, not to limit social organizing to political actions. “People must be directly involved in decision-making and be able to develop alternatives that meet their actual needs. This also includes economic opportunities.” Dirik advocated establishing cooperatives and alternative economic models, noting that the need to secure an individual livelihood makes it difficult for many people to participate consistently in social activities.


She also called for closer cooperation with environmental initiatives, migrant movements, and other social forces. Socialism, she argued, must be reflected not only in political objectives but also in interpersonal relationships. “Socialism emerges by responding to the needs of others, through love and affection,” Dirik explained.


Çiçek: Women’s organizing is the foundation of social transformation


Meral Çiçek continued the discussion by raising the question of how the ideology of women’s liberation could be transformed into an organized political force. She argued that social bonds had been increasingly weakened by capitalist living conditions. “Communal organizing must therefore strengthen solidarity, shared responsibility, and collective decision-making processes. The most fundamental characteristic of society is its communal nature,” Çiçek said. Under current conditions, the commune offers a way to preserve social values and communal life, she added.


Referring to the political transformations in the Middle East, she emphasized the importance of the Kurdish people developing an independent capacity for political action. “To defend their achievements and take advantage of new opportunities, Kurds in all four parts of Kurdistan and in the diaspora must develop strong political representation,” Çiçek said, noting that this process is inseparable from women’s organizing. “The democratic transformation of society is only possible through an organized women’s struggle. Women’s liberation must not be limited to political representation but must transform social relationships, decision-making structures, and everyday life,” she stated.

“Democracy means more than participation in elections. Communes must be based on shared needs, act independently, and develop democratic connections with one another,” Çiçek stated. title: Saturday Mothers demand answers about the disappearance of Fehmi Tosun
content:
At their 1,125th vigil in Galatasaray Square in Istanbul, the Saturday Mothers commemorated Fehmi Tosun, a Kurd from Lice who was abducted in front of his family 31 years ago and has been missing ever since. Holding photographs of their relatives and red carnations, participants once again demanded that cases of enforced disappearance be investigated and those responsible brought to justice.


The gathering focused on the still-unresolved abduction of Tosun, who was 35 years old and a father of five at the time. Ikbal Eren, whose brother Hayrettin Eren also disappeared while in police custody, recalled that numerous people had witnessed Tosun’s abduction and that his family had concrete information about the perpetrators.


On the evening of October 19, 1995, three armed men in civilian clothes brought Tosun to his home in Istanbul’s Avcılar district in a white Renault. When he saw his wife and five children, he shouted, “They are going to kill me!” Before his family could reach him, he was forcibly dragged into the vehicle and taken away.


His wife, Hanım Tosun, immediately reported the abduction to the police and provided officers with the vehicle’s license plate number. Although the officers checked the license plate and made phone calls, they eventually stated that there was nothing they could do. The authorities later denied having taken Tosun into custody. His friend Hüseyin Aydemir, with whom he had eaten breakfast that morning, has also been missing since that day.


Human rights violation acknowledged, investigation closed


Ikbal Eren pointed out that in 2003, during proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), the Turkish government acknowledged that the investigation had been inadequate and that it had violated its obligations under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The government had also pledged to take measures to prevent similar cases.


Nevertheless, Tosun’s disappearance was never effectively investigated. The case was closed on the grounds that the statute of limitations had expired, and the family’s legal appeals were unsuccessful. An individual application to Turkey’s Constitutional Court also failed to shed light on his disappearance.


“The government’s acknowledgment of the rights violation and payment of compensation are no substitute for justice,” Eren stated. She emphasized that the state was obliged to establish the fate of the disappeared and hold those responsible accountable. The practice of paying compensation without ending impunity ultimately encouraged the continuation of such crimes.


‘Why have you put up these barricades?’


Hanım Tosun, the wife of the disappeared man, made a particularly impassioned appeal to the state authorities. She criticized the police barricades that continue to restrict access to Galatasaray Square. “You should not speak of justice, the judiciary, or the law. If you truly speak of justice, then look at Galatasaray. Why have you put up these barricades here?” Tosun asked. She emphasized that the families were not insulting anyone but were simply demanding the truth about their disappeared loved ones.


She called for state archives to be opened, pointing to records that remained in the possession of the authorities. “If you speak of peace and justice, you must first speak about the Saturday Mothers. You must finally show us a grave. You must open your archives. Only then can you speak of justice and peace.”


Tosun reaffirmed that the families would continue their protests until the fate of all those who had disappeared was clarified and the perpetrators were brought to trial.


The vigil concluded with the laying of red carnations in Galatasaray Square.

title: Tora Pekin: Süreklileştirilmiş bir darbenin gölgesindeyiz, yasal tutukluluk süreleri aşıldı
content:
Sayın Başkan, Sayın Üyeler öncelikle bu ek savunmalarla ilgili olarak da tabii ki kendi aramızda değerlendireceğiz ve gerekli beyanlarda bulunacağız ama asıl olan müvekkilimin 4. gününde yapmış olduğu savunma. Geçen buradan içerikten sonra tekrar size beyanda bulunacağız.


Şimdi 578 gündür süren bir tutuklamanın gölgesi altında müvekkilim Sayın Ekrem İmamoğlu'nun sorgusuna ek beyanlar için söz aldım. Öncelikle aslında ben almamalıydım bu sözü. Sözü Avukat Mehmet Pehlivan almalıydı. Hem bir hukukçu, hem savcılıkta o vardı. Şüpheli evresinde, savcılıkta benim müvekkilimle birlikte o vardı.


O da burada olmalıydı, bu savunmayı da o yapmalıydı, ben de bunu kendisine diye düşünüyorum. Bununla ilgili olarak ek beyanlarımı aktarmam gerek. Evet, tutuklamanın gölgesinde söz aldım diye söyledim ama üzerimize düşen tek gölge değil. Biz 19 Mart'tan bu yana süren sürekli kılınan bir darbenin gölgesi altındayız. Bu ülkede sayın İmamoğlu ve yargılananların çoğu bunları dile getirdiler, davasıyla da. Şimdi bu dava bitecek mi? Yoksa Adalet Bakanının da ifade ettiği gibi ek iddianamelerle sonsuza kadar sürecek mi, bunu bilmiyoruz.


Bu belirsizliklerin gölgesi altındayız. Bunu sayın İmamoğlu söylemişti. Ben ekliyorum; sizin de bildiğinizi düşünüyorum, sizin de zorlandığınızı düşünüyorum. Neden çıkartıldı bu söylem de demeyeceğim çünkü bu beyanla beraber duruşma saatleri bir normale geldi.


Duruşma saatlerimiz gece yarılarından doğru 10'a kadar çekilmişti herhalde o da bence normal saat değil ama bu beyandan sonra biraz daha rahatladınız. Yani tamam ben bu yargılamayı sıktıracağım diyorsunuz ondan sonra da takdir edenler gerçekten dediğiniz gibi itirazımız da olsa. Ama 400'den fazla yargılananı dinlediniz, beyanını sorguladınız.


İddianame sayısı


O aşama bu beyanın arkasından o hız, yine bitirelim dediniz bence zaten hani fazla da uzatmamışız ama makul saatlere geldi, 6'ya, 7'ye geldi saatler. Ben biraz sezgisel, şöyle düşündüğünüzü düşünüyorum yani: Ya sürekli bana ek iddianame göndereceklerse, 2 gün gönderiyorlar. Yaptığına sonrasında basının yayın, daire başkanlıkları. 


İddianamesi geldi, siz de kabul ettiniz. Sürekli buradaki sayı artacaksa, yargılanan sayısı ve bu sayısı artacaksa, gece yarılarına kadar yapmaya gerek yok yani. İşi bitiremiyoruz. Ondan sonra o makul saatlere geldi, 18.00'e dedik, 19.00'a dedik, ona gerek yok diye düşünüyorsunuz diye düşünüyorum, tahminimce.


Şöyle; evet, bu gölgeleri anlattım. Nelerin üzerimize gölge düşürdüğünü anlattım ama bu kısır döngü sonsuza kadar gidebilir. Çok kötü bir dönemde, dava denilmeyecek bir zor kullanmayla karşı karşıyayız Sayın Başkan, Sayın Araştırmacılar. Şimdi bence bu zor kullanmaya karşı, bu darbeye karşı sürekli kılınmıştır. Bir darbeye karşı asıl olan Sayın İmamoğlu'nun 4. günündeki söyledikleridir. Yani sorgu aşamasında bu beyanın üzerine daha fazla söz söylemeye anlam da yok diye bunu düşündüm. Tabii sorgunun bitmesi sırasında Sayın Başkanım, siz kurmadan, biz çalışıyorduk.


Orada bir dile getirilmesi var, 4. gün dile getirilmesi var, yüreklere seslenen bir dile getirilmesi var. Doğrusu isterseniz bunun üzerine, bu sesi yankılamak dışında, daha fazla bir şey söyleyelim söylenmez mi? Bunu düşündüm. Bu soru, beni başka bir soruya götürdü.


O da şu; Sayın İmamoğlu, vekaletimi üstlendiğimden beri doğal olarak, en şık dosya. En başlarda aynen. İlk FETÖ operasyonu olduğu zaman doğal olarak her operasyonda doğal bir reflekstir, her şeyi inceleyip varsa yalan söylenen bir şey. Niye alındı, yani müvekkilim niye alındı? Bir şey var mı? Yani dosyada bir şey var mı, 2 tane soru.


Bu soruyu ilk duyduğum andan itibaren, iddia edenin yanıtı şuydu: Ha tamam, aynen bu yanlış. FETÖ'nün abisi veya sözcüsü izlemiş biliyorsunuz kendilerini söyledikleri öyle bir ilgisi var, delili var. Ki şu an hakikat, bu konuştuğumuzun başlamasından itibaren, önce FETÖ. Sonra geçen hafta, ATV kapanacak, onlar yok falan filan sadece suçlama falan.


Bir şey soracaksa soracak aynen. Sinem Hanım niye alındı? 1,5 senedir anlatıyor çocuklar. Bu soru yanlış bir soru. Niye alındı sorusu yanlış bir soru. Dosyada bir şey var mı sorusu yanlış bir soru. Tamam mı? Dosyada bir şey yok. Yokluğunu değil, ama yanlış bir soru. Bu soruyu sormak bizi muhalefet iktidarına götürür.


Belediyelere çökmek

author: Ross Kirshenbaum
title: Washington State Invests My Pension in Genocide. I’m Demanding Divestment.
content:
Workers across the US are demanding divestment from firms that profit from weapons and surveillance. I’m one of them.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Last month, I joined more than 45 bus drivers, teachers, and government workers to testify before the Washington State Investment Board, demanding responsible investment of our pension funds. I arrived grateful to be surrounded by fellow pensioners who were grounded in a shared commitment to fighting for investments that reflect our values.

Quickly it became clear that the Washington State Investment Board was going to strictly enforce the 45-person speaker limit that it implemented last year after beneficiaries began regularly demanding divestment at their meetings. This meant that my friend, a Palestinian member of my union who had taken off the day to testify, was barred from speaking. I had a minute to speak and yielded my time to him. We would not allow their bureaucratic procedures to silence us. We spoke out because we believe our state’s investments should earn money for our retirement funds without compromising our values.

This mobilization of beneficiaries began with Washington’s Cut Ties with Genocide campaign, launched by Washington for Peace and Justice and Jewish Voice for Peace Seattle. Sitting in an early meeting of the campaign, I was heartbroken to learn that the Washington State Investment Board invests my pension money into companies that enable genocide abroad, surveil and warehouse my neighbors, and contribute to climate chaos around the world. When I began my career as a bus driver in 2016, I was proud to have a pension. Now I felt like my pension was tainted. I could see clearly that my future financial stability was built on the destruction of other people’s futures.

What are these harmful investments? The Washington State Investment Board has invested over $204 million in Lockheed Martin, one of the world’s leading weapons manufacturers. Lockheed Martin produces the F-35 fighter jets that have been crucial to the Israeli military’s genocide in Gaza. These jets have the capacity to carry and detonate 2,000-pound bombs — bombs that destroy whole families, buildings, and neighborhoods in Gaza, leaving behind craters in the earth. In just one horrifying example from 2024, the Israeli military used F-35 jets to drop three 2,000-pound bombs on an Israeli designated “safe zone” in Khan Younis, killing 90 Palestinians and injuring hundreds.

The Washington State Investment Board has also invested more than $73 million in Palantir, a secretive data and AI company whose technology enables mass surveillance in the U.S. and across the world. In March, immediately after the horrifying Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) occupation of Minneapolis, the ACLU reported that Palantir technologies “form the backbone for ICE’s mass deportation regime.” Palantir’s leaders embrace surveillance and provide essential data to Donald Trump’s fascist forces. When the Washington State Investment Board invests in these companies, us pensioners are conscripted into complicity with Israel’s genocide against Palestinians, the mass deportations of our neighbors, and global climate devastation.

As a pension beneficiary, I care deeply about ensuring that our state’s public investments are both moral and profitable. The Washington State Investment Board manages over $230 billion in assets, which include retirement funds of public employee pensions for over 600,000 workers like me. Studies show that ethical investing can generate about the same or even more income than investing in war profiteers and human rights abusers.

The Washington State Investment Board has invested over $204 million in Lockheed Martin, one of the world’s leading weapons manufacturers.

We in Washington are not alone in our call: We’re part of a movement across the country of pensioners demanding that our retirement stop enabling human rights violations.

In Maryland, the Baltimore Teachers Union has joined community allies to demand an end to the Maryland State Retirement and Pension System’s investment in Israel Bonds.

Pensioners in Maine have been involved in a legislative push to get Maine’s state pension fund to divest from corporations and countries enabling severe human rights violations — companies like Lockheed Martin.

author: Unknown
title: Yurttaş mevcut siyasetten umutsuz, çareyi ‘halk meclislerinde’ arıyor
content:
Fotoğraf: Elif Ekin Saltık/ Evrensel

Elif Ekin Saltık [email protected]

Saha Araştırmaları Merkezi (SAMER), “Yurttaşların Siyaset Algısı, Alternatif Siyaset Arayışı ve Demokratik Katılım Olanakları” başlıklı araştırma raporunun sonuçlarını paylaştı. 14 kentte 428 kişiyle çevrim içi ortamda gerçekleştirilen araştırma, temsili siyasete yönelik derinleşen krizi, yurttaşların mevcut siyasal işleyişe olan tepkisini ve doğrudan demokrasi arayışını verilerle ortaya koydu.

Araştırmaya göre katılımcıların yüzde 45,1’i siyasi kararların alınma biçiminden “memnun değilim”, yüzde 33,9’u ise “hiç memnun değilim” yanıtını verdi. Mevcut işleyişten memnun olmayanların toplam oranı yüzde 79’a ulaşırken, memnun olanların oranı yalnızca yüzde 6’da kaldı.

Öte yandan yurttaşların yüzde 73,1’i siyasete katılımın sadece sandıktan ibaret olmadığını, seçim dışı yolların da varlığını kabul ediyor. Hak arama yöntemleri arasında ise barışçıl gösteri ve yürüyüşe katılmak (yüzde 36,2), sivil toplum kuruluşlarına katılmak (yüzde 26,2) ve imza kampanyaları (yüzde 21) öne çıktı.

Yurttaşlar, siyasetin yalnızca siyasi partiler ve seçilmişler eliyle yürütülmesini yetersiz buldu. Katılımcıların yüzde 77,3’ü, yerel kararlarda bölge halkının görüşünün doğrudan alınması gerektiğini savundu.

Araştırmanın en çarpıcı sonuçlarından biri ise “halk meclisleri”ne olan destek. Yurttaşların yüzde 84,1’i mahalle ve yerel konulardaki kararların doğrudan halk meclislerinde alınmasını “gerekli” veya “çok gerekli” buluyor. Yurttaşların yüzde 73,9’u, böyle bir meclis ya da toplantı kurulması halinde kesinlikle veya muhtemelen katılacağını beyan etti. Ancak bu güçlü talebe karşın, halkın doğrudan katılımına dayalı bir siyasetin Türkiye’de yaygınlaşma olasılığı düşük (yüzde 61) görüldü. Bu durum, katılım talebiyle siyasetin gerçekte dönüşebileceğine duyulan güven arasındaki uçurumu yansıttı.

Mahalledeki önemli bir sorunun çözümü için yurttaşların inisiyatif alma eğilimi (yüzde 39,7) yüksek olsa da bu durum doğrudan aktif ve örgütlü siyasete tahvil edilemiyor.

Aktif siyasetin önündeki en büyük engeller şöyle sıralandı: Yüzde 15,4 ile “katılımın etkili olduğunu düşünmeme”, yüzde 15,2 ile “baskı ve korku ortamı”, yüzde 14 ile “zaman yetersizliği” ve yüzde 10,3 ile “yeterli bilgi ve donanıma sahip olmama”. Katılımcıların yüzde 26,2’si ise doğrudan siyasete katılmak istemediğini belirtiyor.

Rapor, siyaset mekanizmalarındaki toplumsal cinsiyet ve yaş eşitsizliklerine de ayna tuttu. Kadınların yüzde 33’ü aktif katılım hakları konusunda hiç bilgisi olmadığını veya çok az bilgisi olduğunu belirtirken, bu oran erkeklerde yüzde 11,8’de kaldı. Aktif siyasete katılmak istemediğini belirten kadınların oranı (yüzde 39,3), erkeklerin oranının (yüzde 18,1) iki katından fazla.

Gençlerde ise güvensizlik ve uzaklaşma eğilimi dikkat çekti. 18-24 yaş arası gençlerin yüzde 47,6’sı aktif siyasete katılmak istemediğini belirtirken, halk meclisi veya halk toplantısına katılma isteği gençlerde yüzde 56,3 düzeyinde kaldı. Bu oran, yaş ilerledikçe artış gösteriyor ve 65 yaş üzerinde yüzde 100’e yaklaşıyor.

Araştırma sonucu, halkın karar alma süreçlerine doğrudan müdahale edebileceği demokratik, eşitlikçi, güvenilir ve sonuç üreten mekanizmaların kurumsallaştırılmasına duyulan ihtiyacı ortaya koyuyor. Katılımcıların beklentilerinin ilk sıralarında katılım mekanizmalarının artırılması, siyasi haklar konusunda bilgilendirme ve örgütlenme olanaklarının güçlendirilmesi yer alıyor.

Raporun tamamına ulaşmak için tıklayın.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: İzmir Barosu Olağan Genel Kurulu başladı: 'Hukukun üstünlüğünü savunmaya devam edeceğiz'
content:
İzmir- İzmir Barosu 2026-2028 Olağan Genel Kurulu, Bayraklı’daki Mustafa Kemal Atatürk Spor Salonu’nda başladı.

14.670 avukatın üye olduğu baro yönetiminin belirleneceği genel kurulun ilk gününde avukatlar, mesleki sorunlarını tartışmak ve yeni dönem yönetimini seçmek üzere bir araya geldi.

Dört adayın yarıştığı seçimlerde Çağdaş Avukatlar Grubu’nun adayı Emre Öktem, Cumhuriyetçi Avukatlar Grubu’nun adayı Serhat Sökmen, İzmir Avukat Hareketi’nin adayı Volkan Gültekin ve bağımsız aday Tacettin Çolak yarışıyor.

Genel kurul saygı duruşuyla başladı. Saygı duruşunun ardından oy birliği ile divan seçildi.

İzmir Barosu Genel Kurulu’nun divanı adına konuşan Av. Çetin Turan, baronun hak ihlallerine karşı mücadelesine dikkat çekerek, “İzmir Barosu hukukun her alanında yapılan hak ihlallerinin karşısında çıkmıştır. İnsan, çevre haklarını savunmak İzmir Barosunun görevleri arasına girmiştir” dedi.

Ülkedeki hukuki ve siyasi tabloya değinen Turan, mevcut yönetimin hukuk kurallarına uygun hareket ettiğini söylemenin mümkün olmadığını belirtti. Anayasal güvencelerin fiilen ortadan kaldırıldığını ifade eden Turan, yargı organlarının kararlarının uygulanmadığını, bağımsız olması gereken mahkemelerin görev alanlarını aşarak kararlar verdiğini söyledi.

Sulh ceza hâkimlerinin otomatik tutuklama hâkimlerine dönüştüğünü, yurttaşların yasalar karşısında eşit olmadığını belirten Turan, “Yasalar kimine uygulanıyor, kimine uygulanmıyor. Hukuki güvence kavramı terk edilmiş. Gazeteciler tutuklanıyor, televizyon kanalları kapatılıyor. Avukatlık mesleği günlük geçim sorunu dışında müdafiliğini yapamıyor” dedi.

İzmir Barosunun barışı ve toplumsal değerleri savunduğunu vurgulayan Turan, güncel gelişmeler karşısında baronun söyleyecek sözünün olacağını belirtti. Barışa ilişkin tartışmalara değinen Turan, İzmir Barosunun tek adam rejimlerine karşı çıktığını ve hukukun üstünlüğünü esas alan parlamenter sistemi savunduğunu söyledi.

Turan, “Bu karanlığın elbet dağılacağına inanıyoruz. Gelecekten umudumuzu kesmiş değiliz çünkü haklıyız, tarihsel akışın doğru tarafındayız” diye konuştu.

Dünyanın çok sayıda siyasi dava gördüğünü hatırlatan Turan, Türkiye Barolar Birliği kurucu başkanının 1971’de siyasi davalara ilişkin yaptığı tespiti anımsattı. Turan, “Sokrates’i ölüme mahkûm eden hâkimlerden hiçbiri bugüne kadar ulaşamadı ama Sokrates’in savunması devam ediyor” sözleriyle konuşmasını tamamladı.

İzmir Barosu 2026-2028 Olağan Genel Kurulu’nda açılış konuşmasını yapan Baro Başkanı Av. Sefa Yılmaz, hukukun üstünlüğü, savunma mesleğinin karşı karşıya olduğu sorunlar ve ülkedeki hak ihlallerine dikkat çekerek, “Anayasası olan bir ülkeyiz ama anayasanın hiçbir hakka ilişkin maddeleri uygulanmaz. Anayasal bir ülke değiliz” dedi.

Savunma mesleğinin adil yargılanma hakkı ve adalete erişim açısından vazgeçilmez olduğunu vurgulayan Yılmaz, “Savunma mesleğinin olmadığı yerde adil yargılanma hakkından bahsedilemez, adalete erişimden bahsedilemez. İzmir Barosu her zaman savunma mesleğini önceleyen ama hiçbir zaman hukukun üstünlüğünden ödün vermeyen bir anlayışı hayata geçirmek için çalışmıştır” dedi.

Türkiye’nin uzun süredir ağır bir hukuksuzluk döneminden geçtiğini söyleyen Yılmaz, 2010 ve 2017 anayasa değişikliklerinin bu sürecin önünü açtığını ifade etti. Bu ülke dört yanı demir parmaklıklarla çevrilmiş cezaevi” dedi.

Yılmaz, insanların söyledikleri sözler nedeniyle gözaltına alınıp tutuklandığını, hatta neden tutuklandıklarını bilmediklerini ifade ederek, “Hukuksuzlukların temelinde bu tek adam rejiminin olduğunu biliyoruz. Faşizm konuşma yasağı değil, söyleme mecburiyetidir” diye konuştu.

author: Brad Reed
title: Rule Lets Fossil Fuel Companies “Unintentionally” Kill Polar Bears and Walruses
content:
The Trump administration’s rule change was a major priority for the Alaska Oil and Gas Association.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Oil and gas companies will now be permitted to kill polar bears and Pacific walruses off the northern coast of Alaska so long as such killings are “unintentional,” according to a new Trump administration rule.

The US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) on Friday finalized a rule change that would shield fossil fuel companies from legal liability if they engage in the “incidental, unintentional” killing of the animals “during year-round oil and gas industry activities in the Beaufort Sea… and adjacent northern coast of Alaska.”

Under the rule change, which is scheduled to last through 2031, the FWS “will issue letters of authorization” that sign off on the incidental killing of wildlife upon request by oil and gas companies.

As noted by a report in Bloomberg Law, the proposed rule change “drew more than 85,500 public comments, nearly all in opposition,” before the FWS ultimately signed off on it.

The rule change was a major priority for the Alaska Oil and Gas Association, which represents fossil fuel giants and requested the revision in September 2025.

Allowing for the incidental killing of polar bears isn’t the only controversial rollback of environmental regulations made by the Trump administration in recent weeks.

In September, The New York Times reported that FWS had gutted a key provision in the Endangered Species Act by arguing that only the intentional killing or wounding of protected species counts as illegal “harm.”

Last week, it was revealed that the US Department of the Interior is moving ahead with a plan to let fossil fuel companies conduct specific wintertime operations at the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska without undergoing reviews mandated by the National Environmental Policy Act.

Even though the Trump administration has prioritized the development of domestic fossil fuel production by gutting environmental standards, these policies have not translated into the promised cheaper oil and gas prices, which have spiked over the last half year thanks to the president’s illegal war with Iran.

title: Deforestation on Mount Dorşîn in Amed countryside expands
content:
Deforestation on Mount Dorşîn in the Kulp district of Amed (Diyarbakır) province continues to advance. The tree felling has now spread to a new area near the hamlet of Zimak in the rural part of Eskar.


The affected area has been closed to the public on “security” grounds. While access is strictly controlled, the felled trees are transported out without obstruction. Trucks carry the timber through military checkpoints all the way to Amed.


According to information from the region, at least two truckloads of timber are transported away every day. The trees, felled by village guards under the supervision of the Turkish military, are transported through military checkpoints to Amed.

Since October 13, the Iranian regime has deployed a large force of Revolutionary Guards (Pasdaran), along with heavy weapons and kamikaze (explosive-laden) unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), to the Shaho region. On October 13, the enemy bombed and shelled the Qilbê Plain area using heavy weapons and kamikaze drones.


Furthermore, in the early hours of October 15, the Kela Terzan area was attacked by four UAVs, followed by further bombardment by Revolutionary Guard forces that continued until noon. The regime has increased the number of troops in the region, indicating its intention to continue military operations and attacks against our forces in this area.


We would also like to emphasize that our forces have issued the necessary warnings in response to these attacks. However, this does not mean that our response will always be limited to warnings. If these attacks continue, we, as the East Kurdistan Defense Units, will fully exercise our right to self-defense and respond accordingly.”

title: News quiz Oct. 17 | Videography and Valentine’s Day volunteers
content:
A news quiz? Why not. Let’s get into it!


1.

 Nunavut Premier John Main spoke to Nunatsiaq News last week to give an update on the GN’s stalled elder van project. What did he say?


A.

 “The vans are ready to rock and roll.”


B.

 “We’ve got the vans, we just need drivers.”


C.

 “The update is, as of right now, they’re still not operating.”


2.

 Kinngait’s youth group won a volunteer award on Oct. 3. It has run a number of events, including a breakfast on what holiday?


A.

 Valentine’s Day


B.

 Christmas


C.

 Nunavut Day


3.

 Sonia Caron, Quebec’s new representative for the Ungava Riding, is a member of Parti Québécois, which has promised to revisit a referendum on Quebec separatism. What did she say to Nunatsiaq News about what that might mean for the province’s Inuit?


A.

 She said she would ask her constituents what they think.


B.

 She declined to comment.


C.

 She said she would defer to the premier on the issue.


4.

 The Kivalliq Inuit Association is holding an election in December for a few positions, including vice-president and secretary/treasurer. When can people put their names forward as candidates?


A.

 Oct. 20


B.

 Oct. 26


C.

 Oct. 31


5.

 A person in Gjoa Haven was assaulted earlier this month while doing what?


A.

 Canvassing for Statistics Canada.


B.

 Driving a water truck.


C.

 Taking video for a hamlet-organized clean energy initiative.


What did Sonia Caron, Quebec’s MNA for Ungava, say to Nunatsiaq News when asked about a potential referendum on Quebec separatism? (File photo courtesy of Parti Québécois)


Answers:


1.

 C — The vans are

not on the road yet

, Nunavut Premier John Main told Nunatsiaq News. The territorial government allocated $1.25 million last year towards their operation. They are now developing a policy and a call for proposals to run the vans.


2.

 A — The Kinngait Youth Group

served 200 residents

 for a Valentine’s Day breakfast this year.


3.

 B — Quebec’s Ungava MNA Sonia Caron

declined to comment

 when asked about how her party’s separatism ambitions could affect her Inuit constituents. For now anyway, the separatism question has been shelved, at least as long as U.S. President Donald Trump is in power.


4.

 B — The nomination period for the Kivalliq Inuit Association’s elections

open

 Oct. 26. Voting day is scheduled for Dec. 14.


5.

 C — A videographer was

assaulted

 while working on promotional materials for a hamlet-sponsored environment initiative, according to Gjoa Haven Mayor Raymond Quqshuun Sr. No report was made to police, but the hamlet is taking the incident seriously, he said.

author: Sasha Draeger-Mazer
title: Texas Woman Sues Anti-Abortion Group Under Law It Helped to Pass
content:
The woman is suing Students for Life for the cost of raising the children of two unplanned pregnancies.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

A Texas woman is using a state law banning the transport of abortion pills to sue members of the anti-abortion organization Students for Life of America.

In the suit filed Tuesday in a Harris County district court, plaintiff Maria Puerto, a 26-year-old mother of two using a pseudonym to protect her family, alleges that four anti-abortion activists had ordered abortion medication on their phones in March 2026 outside of the Space Center Houston. The lawsuit cites, among other things, a now-expired social media post by one of the defendants captioned “Guess what we are doing? Ordering abortion pills undercover? Yep. Stay tuned.”

Known as the Woman and Child Protection Act, House Bill 7, which went into effect in December, prohibits providing an “abortion-inducing drug” to or from anyone in the state of Texas. The law is enforced by allowing almost any person, regardless of whether they have been impacted by the incident, to bring a civil suit against a provider of abortion medication. Plaintiffs may seek an injunction and a minimum of $100,000. If the person bringing the suit has no connection to the incident, the plaintiff receives $10,000, with the remainder of the award going to a charity selected by the plaintiff.

The lawsuit does not specify how the defendants violated HB 7. While the law does not explicitly bar the ordering of abortion medication, it does prohibit the transport of the drug within the state.

“What the statute says is that transporting abortion drugs from one location to another within the state is a violation of HB 7 … By the plain language of the statute, this would seem to be a violation,” Puerto’s attorney Molly Duane told The Texas Tribune. “This is the problem with writing such a confusing and vague law.”

While pregnant women cannot be prosecuted under HB 7 for actions taken to have an abortion, none of the four defendants — Kristan Mercer Hawkins, Lydia Taylor Davis, Jamie Curry and Megan Roos — were pregnant at the time, according to the lawsuit.

Duane, who is with Amplify Legal, the legal arm of advocacy group Abortion in America, said she and her client are hoping that the lawsuit will eventually surface more about what the defendants did with the abortion pills once they ordered them.

Hawkins is the president of Virginia-based Students for Life, which lobbied heavily for the passage of HB 7 last year. In a video posted to X on Tuesday, Hawkins called the lawsuit “frivolous” and a “publicity stunt,” and urged Texas Child Protective Services to investigate Puerto.

Puerto is suing for $459,782, “the average cost of raising two children from birth to age 18 in the state of Texas.” According to the lawsuit, both of Puerto’s pregnancies were unplanned and occurred despite the use of contraception, and she was unable to end the pregnancies due to the state’s abortion ban and the expenses associated with traveling out of the state. The suit also says that her first pregnancy directly resulted in her having to quit college and losing her job.

If she wins the lawsuit, Puerto would be entitled to $10,000 of the award, as she has no connection to the defendants. According to a Tuesday statement by Abortion in America, she plans to give the remaining award to Jane’s Due Process, a nonprofit that helps young Texans confidentially access abortion and birth control.

In an essay she published Tuesday, Puerto said Texas laws regulating her pregnancy effectively controlled her future, and described the financial struggle she has faced as a result.

“I’ve filed a lawsuit against those who helped build these horrible laws — and then had the privilege to break them in an attempt to trap women like me who still need help,” Puerto wrote. A statement by Students for Life Vice President Kristi Hamrick called the suit a “backhanded compliment” and vowed to fight it in court.

A request for comment from the defendants was directed to Students for Life’s initial statement on the lawsuit.

author: Randi Beers
title: The world is ending, and I feel fine
content:
A friend told me a story this summer about

 a smokey day in Minnesota, where she lives. When she complained about the haze to her 13-year-old nephew, he responded: “That’s just summer.”


It wasn’t long ago that wildfire smoke was a characteristic of summer mostly limited to western North America, where conditions are drier.


But, in just a few years, that has drastically changed. Evidence of climate change is everywhere: it’s in the sea ice of the North — much less predictable now — and unbreathable air across the south. (And

parts

 of the North.)


When we think about and imagine the collapse of civilization, the conversation usually revolves around the world becoming uninhabitable due to climate change.


Nunatsiaq News reporter Miriam Lafontaine recently

wrote about

 one recent study that predicts Arctic winters will be, on average, 10 degrees warmer by 2100.

A change like that could bring Iqaluit’s mean daily temperature in January from -26 C to -16 C. 


For comparison, Iqaluit’s average daily temperature

increased

 by one degree between 1991 and 2020. 


Even more recently, artificial intelligence has emerged as a potential threat, with leaders in the field warning AI could kill us all by the end of the decade.


Of course predicting the end of the world — and being wrong about it — is a constant throughout history.


We braced ourselves for Y2K, in anticipation that computers wouldn’t understand the calendar flipping from 1999 to 2000.

Before that, we thought global petroleum reserves would wane with demand still soaring.

Before that, during the Cold War, the threat was nuclear.


In 1947, after the first nuclear weapons were developed, the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists created the Doomsday Clock to assess risks to humanity. It was originally set to seven minutes to “midnight,” or the end of the world.


Today, it sits at 85 seconds to midnight.


Is the end of the world nigh? Nobody knows — not even ChatGPT. But it did acknowledge it’s a fair question.


No single person can control climate change or any other threats to civilization but we can control our own lives. Like Iqaluit’s Derek Allerton, who

collects cans

 every day in the hopes the Nunavut government will reinstate a beverage recycling program.


We can buy into renewable energy programs, compost, limit our consumerism, and do other small things to make our communities better.


Even if the path forward isn’t clear, I’m confident we will find ways to adapt to anything.


Except maybe an asteroid.

author: Marjorie Cohn
title: As Trump Sabotages the ICC With Sanctions, There Are Many Ways to Fight Back
content:
Trump officials now face a temporary restraining order for violating the First Amendment by sanctioning US groups.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The U.S. government has long sought to incapacitate the International Criminal Court (ICC), the world’s first global court that was created to prosecute the most atrocious crimes. As the ICC seeks to provide accountability for Israeli crimes, the Trump administration has become increasingly aggressive in its attempts to hobble the court. On October 9, 2026, Team Trump imposed punitive sanctions against the court itself, which constitutes the gravest intensification of its war on the ICC. But there are several strategies available to mitigate the worst effects of these sanctions.

In February 2025, Donald Trump issued Executive Order 14203, which authorizes the imposition of sanctions against the ICC. The sanctions amount to illegal unilateral coercive measures because only the UN Security Council has the authority to impose sanctions.

The executive order prohibits U.S. persons from providing material support or services to certain designated persons and entities, including financial services. It exposes non-U.S. persons to secondary sanctions for engaging in conduct prohibited under the order. U.S. persons who violate it may face criminal penalties of up to 20 years imprisonment and fines of up to $1 million.

Trump’s 2025 order has led to the sanctioning of nine of the ICC’s 18 judges, three ICC prosecutors, the ICC president, and a senior ICC trial attorney. The Trump administration also sanctioned three highly respected Palestinian human rights organizations — Al-Haq, Al Mezan, and the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights — for their assistance to the ICC. Francesca Albanese, UN Special Rapporteur on Occupied Palestine, who wrote three courageous reports documenting Israel’s genocide in Gaza, was sanctioned as well.

In December 2025, a top Trump administration official told Reuters there was “growing concern” that “the ICC will turn its attention to the president, to the vice president, to the secretary of war and others, and pursue prosecutions against them,” adding that this was “unacceptable, and we will not allow it to happen.” He said the ICC had been warned that unless it amended the Rome Statute to ensure it would not investigate Trump and his top officials, new and very severe U.S. sanctions would be imposed on the court.

Sure enough, in an attempt to permanently paralyze the court, the Trump administration sanctioned the entire ICC on October 9, pursuant to Executive Order 14203. These harsh financial sanctions prevent the court from using U.S. dollars and U.S.-based financial services and technology companies. They bar U.S. citizens and companies from supplying the court with funds, goods, or services without a license from the U.S. Treasury.

U.S. sanctions have serious impacts on targeted individuals, whose bank accounts can be frozen or closed. Their financial transactions can be rejected, and they can be denied access to digital services and entry into the United States. Sanctions have a chilling effect on non-U.S. banks and other companies outside the jurisdiction of the United States; they themselves could lose access to the U.S. banking system. The ICC could lose access to companies on which it relies for its critical functions, including banking, information, technology, and travel.

Although the sanctions contain a six-month wind-down period and exemptions for certain services, they still pose significant risks. In the face of global reliance on the U.S. financial and IT systems, even non-U.S. service providers, including banks, might stop providing services to the ICC for fear of penalties or reprisals by the U.S. Treasury. This could affect the court’s ability to maintain a bank account, receive financial contributions from States Parties, pay staff, make payments, and maintain essential operations.

The imposition of these outrageous sanctions is the latest, and most devastating, chapter in the U.S.’s long campaign to undermine the ICC. Moreover, these sanctions were imposed on the same day that the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay, a South African lawyer who served as a judge on the ICC for five years and led the UN Commission of Inquiry in 2025 that confirmed Israel’s commission of genocide in Gaza.

title: Öcalan: The future of the Middle East lies not in new wars but in building a democratic society
content:
A conference titled “Democratic Confederalism in Kurdistan: A Perspective for Peace in the Middle East” has begun in Turin, Italy.


The conference, organized with the support of the Kurdistan Information Office in Italy (UIKI) and the Verso il Kurdistan Association, is being held at the conference hall of the Metropolitan City of Turin on Corso Inghilterra.


The conference, attended by Kurdish politicians, Italian parliamentarians, local government officials, academics, and representatives of the women’s movement, is discussing a democratic solution to the Kurdish question and the prospects for peace in the Middle East.


https://1649452211.rsc.cdn77.org/20261017113704_2026-10-17-torino-demoktatik-konfederalizm-konferansi-acilis-1.mp4


The conference is attended by Davide Nicco, President of the Piedmont Regional Council; Michela Favaro, Deputy Mayor of Turin; Ayşe Serra Bucak Küçük, Co-Mayor of Amed Metropolitan Municipality; Antonio Olivieri, President of the Verso il Kurdistan Association; and Yılmaz Orkanda, Director of UIKI.


The conference consists of three sessions. The first session will address democratic confederalism as an alternative model for the Middle East, developments in Rojava, and the struggles in Iran and Shengal.


The afternoon sessions will focus on the Peace and Democratic Society Process in Turkey, Öcalan’s freedom, international solidarity, and the struggle for women’s liberation.


Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan sent a message sent to the conference, stating the following:


“Dear friends,


I greet you from İmralı with feelings of international solidarity and freedom. I hope your conference will contribute to equality and freedom among peoples and the establishment of lasting peace in the Middle East.


The Middle East is currently at a critical turning point. Wars, conflicts, nation-state solutions, and security-oriented policies have failed to bring peace and freedom to the peoples of the region. This is now clear. Therefore, our fundamental task is to abandon the politics of war, embrace democratic politics, organize society, and build a new era that guarantees the equal and free coexistence of peoples.


Democratic confederalism and the perspective of a Democratic Republic are among the central issues in this search for a solution.


The dissolution of the PKK and the end of its strategy of armed struggle should be seen as the beginning of a new era. This change also requires a new perspective on the issue.


It must be stated clearly that the end of armed struggle does not, in itself, mean peace. For peace to become lasting at the end of this process, the root causes of the conflict must be eliminated, Kurdish identity, language, and culture must be guaranteed, obstacles to democratic politics must be removed, and equal citizenship must be secured by law.


Democratic integration does not mean unilateral adaptation or unconditional participation in the existing system. On the contrary, it must be a democratic transformation in which differences are not denied, rights are recognized, and coexistence is established on the basis of equality.


The political expression of democratic politics is the Democratic Republic, while the guarantee of a democratic society is the rule of law. Without legal guarantees, democratic politics cannot become sustainable, nor can the peace process succeed.


The resolution of the Kurdish question cannot be considered separately from the democratization of Turkey. Likewise, Turkey’s democratization is inseparable from the emergence of a political will that enables peoples to live together freely and equally.


This is precisely where the significance of the democratic confederalism perspective for the Middle East lies. The solution is not to assimilate peoples into a single identity, turn borders and differences into sources of new conflicts, or create new forms of state domination.


What is needed today is this: democratic politics instead of the politics of war, recognition instead of denial, law instead of coercion, and free and equal coexistence instead of social fragmentation. This transformation requires states and political actors to assume responsibility, democratic institutions to be strengthened, and society to have a voice and decision-making power over its own future.

content:

Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan’ın Helsinki’ye büyükelçi tayin ettiği Ayşe Hilal Sayan Koytak, güven mektubunu Finlandiya Cumhurbaşkanı Alexander Stubb’a önceki gün sundu.

title: Manisa'da tur otobüsü kazasında can kaybı 12'ye yükseldi
content:
Manisa – Akhisar ilçesinde 11 kişinin öldüğü, 27 kişinin yaralandığı kazada ağır yaralanan yaşlı kadın, tedavi gördüğü hastanede hayatını kaybetti. Kazada hayatını kaybedenlerin sayısı 12'ye yükseldi.

Gebze-Orhangazi-İzmir Otoyolu'nun Akhisar Gişeleri mevkisindeki kazada ağır yaralanan ve Manisa Şehir Hastanesi'ne kaldırılan Zülfiye Arıca (70), 6 gün süren yaşam mücadelesini kaybetti.

Arıca'nın cenazesi aynı hastanenin morguna kaldırıldı.

Böylece kazada ölenlerin sayısı 12'ye yükseldi.

Gebze-Orhangazi-İzmir Otoyolu'nun Akhisar Gişeleri mevkisinde 11 Ekim'de H.K. idaresindeki çekici, Bursa'dan Denizli'ye giden M.A. yönetimindeki tur otobüsüne çarpmıştı.

Kazada 11 kişi hayatını kaybetmiş, yaralanan 27 kişiden birine olay yerinde müdahale edilmiş, 26 kişi hastanelere sevk edilmişti.

Yaralılardan 13'ü taburcu edilmişti.

Gözaltına alınan tur otobüsünün sürücüsü M.A. ve çekicinin şoförü H.K. tutuklanmış, otobüsün sahibi ve yedek sürücüsü M.Y. ise adli kontrol şartıyla serbest bırakılmıştı.

title: Özgür Özel Yozgat'ta: 'Ya otokrasi ya demokrasi'
content:
Yeni Parti Genel Başkanı Özgür Özel, partisinin Yozgat'taki il başkanlığı ön seçiminde yaptığı konuşmada, Türkiye'nin kritik bir dönemece yaklaştığını belirterek, "Ya otokrasi ya demokrasi ya bir otokrat ya bütün demokratlar gelip ülkenin kaderine el koyacaklar" dedi. Özel, fon vurgunu üzerinden Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan'a da tepki gösterdi.

Yeni Parti'nin Birinci Olağan Kurultay takvimi kapsamında 81 ilde düzenlenen il başkanlığı ön seçimleri başladı. Yeni Parti Genel Başkanı Özgür Özel, Yozgat Büyük Sinema'da gerçekleştirilen ön seçime katıldı. Özel'i Yozgat Kurucu İl Başkanı Abdullah Yaşar ve ilçe başkanları karşıladı.

Konuşmasında partisinin kuruluş sürecini anlatan Özel, il ve ilçe başkanlarının yanı sıra genel başkanın da üyelerin katıldığı ön seçimle belirleneceğini söyledi. Özel, "Ben bu tarihi adımın ilk adımını Yozgat'tan sizinle birlikte atmak istedim" dedi.

Partisinin kuruluşuna giden süreçte yaşananları anlatan Özel, CHP'nin yargı müdahalesiyle ellerinden alınmaya çalışıldığını belirtti. Bu süreçte iki ay mücadele ettiklerini belirten Özel, yurttaşlardan gelen yeni parti kurulması çağrısına yanıt verdiklerini söyledi.

Özel, "Yeni bir yol bulamadık belki ama yepyeni bir yol açtık ve talimatını milletin verdiği, adını bizzat meydanlarda milletin koyduğu, bütçesini milletin oluşturduğu ve bugün sokak sokak, meydan meydan milletimizle birlikte büyüttüğümüz Yeni Parti'yi sizlerle kurduk" ifadelerini kullandı.

Yozgat'ın iki ay içerisinde partisine 2 bin 912 üye kazandırdığını açıklayan Özel, "Yozgat artık kimsenin kalesi değildir. Yozgat milletin kalesidir" dedi.

İl başkanlığı için Abdullah Yaşar ve Berkay Apsalmış'ın yarışacağını belirten Özel, parti yönetiminde üyelerin iradesinin belirleyici olacağını vurguladı.

Türkiye'deki siyaset anlayışının değişmesi gerektiğini söyleyen Özel, parti üyelerinin karar alma süreçlerine doğrudan katılacağı bir yapı oluşturacaklarını belirtti. Partisinin 770 bin üyeye ulaştığını, hedeflerinin 1 milyon üye olduğunu aktaran Özel, mahalle, ilçe ve il meclisleri oluşturmayı planladıklarını anlattı.

Özel, "Türkiye'de siyaset yapma biçimi değişmeyince ülkenin kaderi değişmiyor" diyerek önümüzdeki seçimlerin önemine dikkati çekti:

"Olsun olsun en çok 1 - 1,5 yıl sonra tarihin en kritik dönüm noktasında olacağız. Ya otokrasi ya demokrasi ya bir otokrat ya bütün demokratlar gelip ülkenin kaderine el koyacaklar."

AKP iktidarını eleştiren Özel, seçim sürecinin yalnızca parti yöneticileriyle yürütülemeyeceğini, bütün üyelerin sahada çalışma yürütmesi gerektiğini söyledi. Yozgat'taki ön seçimi de partisinin iktidar yürüyüşünün başlangıcı olarak nitelendirdi.

Eski siyaset anlayışında kararların yukarıdan verildiğini, bunun bedelini ise halkın ödediğini söyleyen Özel, yeni dönemde kararların üyeler tarafından alınacağını, yöneticilerin de hesap vereceğini savundu.

Liyakat yerine sadakatin esas alınmasını ve kamu olanaklarının iktidarın çıkarları doğrultusunda kullanılmasını eleştiren Özel, hayat pahalılığı, devlete güvenin azalması, gençlerin gelecek kaygısı ve kayırmacılığın mevcut siyasi düzenin sonucu olduğunu ifade etti.

Özel, "Bunların hepsi üst üste konulmuş yanlış tuğlaların eseridir. Yanlış tuğlayla doğru duvar örülmez" dedi.

Konuşmasında fon vurgununa da değinen Özel, 10 milyondan fazla kişinin yaşananlardan etkilendiğini belirti. Fon vurgununun ekonomiye maliyetinin önce 20 milyar dolar, ardından 90 milyar dolar olarak açıklandığını söyleyen Özel, uzmanların bu tutarın 110 milyar dolara ulaştığından söz ettiğini aktardı.

Söz konusu rakamı 6 Şubat depremlerinin ekonomik kaybıyla karşılaştıran Özel, yaşananları "asrın soygunu" olarak nitelendirdi. Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan'ı sorumlu tutan Özel, "Sorumlusu kim? Hiç sorumlu aramayın oradan, buradan. Sorumlu Recep Tayyip Erdoğan" dedi.

Fon şirketlerinin yöneticilerinin iktidar tarafından atandığını belirten Özel, Erdoğan'ın fon vurgununa ilişkin dış güçleri işaret etmesine tepki gösterdi. AKP'li eski Aile ve Sosyal Politikalar Bakanı Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya'yı da anan Özel, "Ya Sayın Erdoğan, fon şirketlerinin yönetimine o AK Partili isimleri dış güçler mi atadı? Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya Hanım'a 2,2 milyarlık vurgunu dış güçler mi yaptırdı?" diye sordu.

Yeni Parti'nin mağdurların zararlarının karşılanması için Meclis'e kanun teklifi sunduğunu söyleyen Özel, haksız kazançların tespit edilmesini, sorumlulardan tahsil edilmesini ve mağdurlara geri ödenmesini talep etti.

title: The legacy of France can and should only be remembered as one utterly stained by (or, more…
content:
The legacy of France can and should only be remembered as one utterly stained by (or, more accurately, formed from) its brutal colonialist and imperialist endeavours.

this part is especially triggering for me, since i learnt this past 17th October, that my Grandmother, who was 15 years old at the time, arrived with her mother at this horrific scene a bit too late and was nearly arrested by the police. I can’t imagine what would have happened to her if they had left the house earlier.

The rare white people who witnessed this on the right side of history said that one of the things they won’t forget is how they fellow white parisians turned into informants for the police and how during all of the night they called the cops on the Algerians who managed to hide or escape.

Over 200 Algerians were killed that night over 500 if you count the one killed in the following nights but thousands more were arrested (over 10000) every single ministry was an accomplice they used to public buses to transport them kept them in a stadium because the precincts were not big enough… While the people killed were men and women, the people arrested were a huge majority of men. So the following days the women and children started calling for a peaceful march to ask for their husbands and fathers to be released. This time they knew that the public opinion wouldn’t look kindly to it if they killed them. So the police instead arrested the women and sent them to a psychiatric hospitals saying they were unstable and needed to be locked inside. Luckily the director was a good man so he refused to lock the women inside the hospital saying they were perfectly sane but he also refused to let the police take them. So he waited until the police left to help the women leave back to their places.

There’s a documentary about it (I don’t remember if the psychiatric hospital was in this documentary or in an other) made by an Algerian woman in the diaspora in France. It’s filled with testimonies and a woman explains that when her husband left for the protest he told her to take care of the children and that if something happened to him she needed to make sure their children would go to school school and be good students. He survived to October 17 but was found and killed by the police on the 19th.

Lastly in 2021 Macron pretended to atone for what happened and with the police prefect they went to pay their respect on the bridge where most of the massacre happened and they went to put flowers. He was the first president doing it. Except after doing it in front of the camera the police then stopped the peaceful march that the survivors and the families of the victims organize every year and they kept them from putting flowers there and pay their respect. Macron did a lot of fucked up shit but pretending to acknowledge a massacre from the police while using the police to stop Algerians from paying their respects to the victims was really the thing that stayed in my mind the most. Nothing says “we actually don’t regret sending the police against a peaceful protest of Algerians and will do it again” as well as sending the police against the peaceful march organized by the descendants of those killed and by the survivors…

title: Seven workshops held at European Jineolojî Conference
content:
Seven workshops were held at the European Jineolojî Conference, organised under the slogan “Building a free communal life through Jineolojî”.


Ahead of the workshops, a group of women performed a song they had written about the sacred nature of women's resistance and struggle and the expansion of women's organisation on the basis of the women's revolution.


The workshops, entitled “The Jineolojî Organisational Model in Europe”, “The Pedagogy of Jineolojî”, “The Family as the Most Fundamental Communal Space, Social Transformation and the Transformation of Men”, “Women's Memory and Cultural Resistance”, “Young Women and Jineolojî”, “Ecologically Based Social Life and Jineolojî”, and “The Importance and Organisation of Media and Publishing Activities in Uncovering and Sharing Knowledge”, explored how Jineolojî could become more deeply rooted in society, how it could be organised and what role it could play in building a democratic communal society.


 


Organisational and educational methods discussed


The workshop entitled “The Jineolojî Organisational Model in Europe” examined more than a decade of experience gained through committees, local initiatives, Europe-wide organisational networks and academies. Discussions focused on how this experience could be developed into a stronger, more widespread and sustainable organisational structure.


The “Pedagogy of Jineolojî” workshop explored how Jineolojî could reach broader sections of society. Participants examined alternative pedagogical methods for transforming education, camps and research activities into spaces for collective knowledge production, social engagement and organisation.


Family, social transformation and women's memory


The workshop entitled “The Family as the Most Fundamental Communal Space, Social Transformation and the Transformation of Men” addressed patriarchal relations reproduced within the family, the gender-based division of labour, relations between women and men, and intergenerational ties. Participants also focused on the transformation of men and discussed how communal life could be organised to develop a culture of free living and new social relations.


 


The “Women's Memory and Cultural Resistance” workshop focused on uncovering women's collective memory and passing it down through generations. Discussions explored how women's knowledge could be made visible and shared collectively through oral history, personal narratives, art, music and mythology. The aim was to transform women's memory into a resource that strengthens contemporary cultural resistance, social bonds and organisation.


Young women and ecological living discussed


The “Young Women and Jineolojî” workshop addressed the growing isolation experienced by young women, their search for identity and belonging, and the relationship between Jineolojî, digital life and changing means of communication. Participants discussed developing spaces for social engagement and organisation where young women could build connections between generations, produce knowledge and play an active role in constructing a democratic communal life.


The “Ecologically Based Social Life and Jineolojî” workshop examined the relationship between women, society and nature. Participants exchanged ideas on ecological knowledge and memory, everyday life, patterns of production and consumption, and experiences of collective living.


The importance of media and publishing activities


The workshop entitled “The Importance and Organisation of Media and Publishing Activities in Uncovering and Sharing Knowledge” discussed the role of written, visual and digital media in bringing the knowledge produced through Jineolojî to wider audiences. Participants focused on developing a consistent and lasting editorial approach that examines women's lives and struggles from a Jineolojî perspective.


The findings of the seven workshops, organised in line with the conference's strategic objectives, will be shared with delegates on the final day of the conference.


The first day of the conference concluded with the workshops. Two main sessions will be held tomorrow under the titles “Building a Communal Democratic Society” and “The Socialisation of Knowledge and the Decolonisation of Science”.


Women discuss Jineolojî experiences and the needs of the new period

title: KON-MED criticizes CDU MP over remarks about Öcalan
content:
The Confederation of Kurdish Communities in Germany (KON-MED) has strongly criticized remarks by Tijen Ataoğlu, a member of the German Bundestag from the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), regarding the imprisonment of Leader Apo, and called on the CDU/CSU parliamentary group and the German government to clarify their positions on the matter.


On 15 October, during a Bundestag session on German-Turkish relations, Tijen Ataoğlu said: “Abdullah Öcalan belongs in prison, and that is absolutely right.”


In a statement published on Friday, the Kurdish umbrella organization described the remark as unacceptable. It said the statement ignored the human rights dimension of Öcalan’s imprisonment and the case law of the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR). The fact that Ataoğlu herself serves on the Legal Affairs and Human Rights Committee of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe made the remark particularly serious, it added.


“We expect a lawyer in this position to take European human rights rulings seriously, rather than categorically justifying a person’s imprisonment,” the confederation stated.


ECHR ruling remains unimplemented more than twelve years later


In its statement, KON-MED recalled the European Court of Human Rights ruling issued on 18 March 2014 concerning Abdullah Öcalan. In that ruling, the ECHR found that the aggravated life sentence imposed on Leader Apo violated Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture, because there was no realistic possibility of a review of the sentence or release.


The right to hope requires that people serving life sentences have a genuine prospect of having their sentences reviewed and potentially being released. Öcalan still has no such possibility. “This right must not be called into question for political reasons,” KON-MED emphasized.


Ataoğlu’s remarks also come at a decisive stage in the process for peace and a democratic society. With his appeal of 27 February 2025, Öcalan opened the way toward ending the PKK’s armed struggle and finding a political solution to the Kurdish question.


Since then, steps toward disarmament and the establishment of a legal framework have been initiated. KON-MED considers blanket support for his continued imprisonment a politically dangerous signal. Such statements, it argues, undermine efforts to achieve a negotiated settlement and contradict the importance of Öcalan to the ongoing process.


The Federal government urged to fulfil its responsibilities


The Kurdish organization also referred to the position taken by Germany’s Federal Foreign Office on 27 February 2025. At the time, the ministry welcomed Öcalan’s peace appeal as a historic opportunity to end the decades-long conflict and declared Germany’s willingness to support a political solution. Respect for the cultural and democratic rights of the Kurdish population was also identified as a prerequisite for lasting peace.


Against this backdrop, KON-MED is demanding a clear position from the federal government and the CDU/CSU parliamentary group in the Bundestag. Ataoğlu must publicly clarify her remarks and affirm that the right to hope also applies to Öcalan. The CDU/CSU parliamentary group should explain whether it shares the position of its MP and state its position on implementing the ECHR ruling.


KON-MED is also calling for concrete action at the European level. From 1 to 3 December, the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe will once again address the implementation of human rights judgments. As a member of the body, Germany shares responsibility for ensuring that Turkey fulfils its obligations.


The umbrella organization is therefore demanding that both the federal government and the German delegation to the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe take a firm stand in favour of implementing the ruling. “The right to hope is not a political concession, but a human right. It applies to Abdullah Öcalan as well,” the statement concludes.
